Dolly Parton was far more than a musician, actor, writer, philanthropist, or theme-park mogul. Parton, who died Tuesday at 80, occupied a unique place in global culture — a figure of American mythology who was truly larger than life. Yet at the core of all her achievements, she was primarily a songwriter.

Distilling 11 songs from her vast, decades-long catalog is a formidable task, but certain classics stand out. Here is a key selection from her body of work — ranging from country tracks that challenged traditional gender norms to what remains the greatest ballad ever recorded.

open image in gallery Distilling 11 songs from her vast, decades-long catalog is a formidable task, but certain classics stand out ( Getty Images for SXSW )

1968: “Just Because I’m a Woman”

Parton was long celebrated for the feminist themes throughout her music. That progressive sociopolitical stance is evident from the beginning of her career, which overlapped with the emergence of the women’s liberation movement. On the country classic “Just Because I’m a Woman,” Parton’s protagonist reminds her partner he need not judge her for having previous sexual partners — after all, he's had some, too. “My mistakes are no worse than yours,” she sings, “Just because I’m a woman.” She said the song was inspired by a conversation with her late husband, Carl Dean, who asked her if she’d been with any men before they met.

1971: “Coat of Many Colors”

The quintessential example of Parton the raconteur is “Coat of Many Colors.” It’s an autobiographical tale about her mother, who made a coat for Parton out of rags. She was mocked by other kids but understood its value. “Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be,” she sings, “In my coat of many colors my momma made for me.”

1973: “Jolene”

It is not only one of Parton’s best-known hits, but also one of the best-known country music songs of all time. “Jolene” was inspired by Dean; Parton told NPR in 2008 that she wrote the song about a flirty bank teller who seemed to take an interest in him.

“She got this terrible crush on my husband,” she said. “And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us — when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So, it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one.”

1974: “I Will Always Love You”

The second single from Parton’s 13th studio album, “I Will Always Love You” is most known for its rendition by Whitney Houston. But the Parton original was written for Porter Wagoner ahead of her departure from “The Porter Wagoner Show.” (She left in 1974, having collaborated with him since 1967.) There have been several versions, but none as resonant as Houston’s, recorded in 1992 for the soundtrack to “The Bodyguard.” The song topped the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for a then-record-breaking 14 weeks.

1977: “Here You Come Again”

Parton wrote an overwhelming number of her hits, which makes “Here You Come Again” an interesting outlier. It was penned by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, first recorded by B.J. Thomas and originally conceived with the idea that Brenda Lee would record it. The song made its way to Parton and became a tentpole pop crossover hit for the country artist. But make no mistake — Parton made sure the steel guitar was heard loud and proud.

open image in gallery Parton wrote an overwhelming number of her hits ( Getty Images )

1980: “9 to 5”

Enter Parton, the Hollywood star. It begins with the sound of a typewriter. (That clacking sound? Parton originally conceived of it by striking her long acrylic nails together.) The ebullient “9 to 5” was written for the 1980 film of the same name, which starred Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Parton in her acting debut. The song also appears on her album “9 to 5 and Odd Jobs.” Lyrically, it celebrates women in the workplace and serves as a battle cry for pay equity; it earned Parton her first Oscar nomination.

1983: “Islands in the Stream,” with Kenny Rogers

By the 1980s, Parton had fashioned herself as a mainstream celebrity. On “Islands in the Stream” with Kenny Rogers, her clarion soprano makes for perfect harmonies. That shouldn’t come as any surprise, but perhaps this will: The song was written by the Bee Gees. Barry Gibb maintained it was meant for Diana Ross, while Robin Gibb said it was meant for Marvin Gaye. Whatever the case, it got to Parton and Rogers, and the rest is history. It's also a reminder of how R&B and country music are inextricably linked.

open image in gallery On ‘Islands in the Stream’ with Kenny Rogers, her clarion soprano makes for perfect harmonies ( Getty Images )

1989: “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That”

Before this triumphant return to capital-C country music, there was a deeper detour into ’80s drum machine-heavy pop. (If there's a single Parton album to consider skipping, it is 1987’s “Rainbow.”) But what came after, 1989’s “White Limozeen,” should be celebrated for “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That,” with its steel guitar, banjo, mandolins, Pedabro and a fierce fiddle courtesy of Ricky Skaggs — all while Parton playfully objectifies a man with a cheeky wink.

1999: “The Grass Is Blue”

“I’ve had to think up a way to survive,” Parton opens the title track to her 1999 album “The Grass Is Blue.” She said she wrote the bluegrass ballad in 30 minutes, during a lunch break while filming “Blue Valley Songbird,” a made-for-television musical drama about a woman who tries to leave an abusive partner. It features her scratch vocals — a demo meant to serve as a blueprint for the final recording — providing an additional rawness to a song of impossible pain. “And the sky is green / and the grass is blue,” she sings. “And I don’t love you.”

2001: “Little Sparrow”

If there is anything resembling a dip in Parton’s overwhelming popularity, it arrived in the ’90s, when country listeners instead embraced the glossy pop-country of Shania Twain and LeAnn Rimes. A pivot arrived at the end of that decade and into the one that followed, when Parton endeavored to make roots albums — pulling from bluegrass, country, gospel and Appalachian folk — that reinvigorated her music career. The heartbreaking a cappella harmonies of the title track on her 2001 album “Little Sparrow,” released one year after the death of her father and dedicated to him, are further evidence of her greatness. Parton’s is a voice that knows no bounds. But to remind people of that fact? Sometimes it takes going back home.

2014: “Blue Smoke”

No one writes place like Parton. On “Blue Smoke,” with its youthful choo-choo spirit, Parton brings the listener into her childhood home in the Blue Ridge Mountains, gorgeous, desolate and nostalgic. “Blue Smoke climbin’ up the mountain, Blue Smoke windin’ ’round the bend / Blue Smoke is the name of the heartbreak train that I am ridin’ in,” she sings. “I left a note, I wrote, ‘I’m leaving and I won’t be coming back’ / Blue Smoke rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling down the track.”

Kacey Musgraves is facing backlash from some fans after she showed support for immigrant families during a birthday performance.

The Grammy-winning country singer celebrated her 38th birthday on Friday by marking the opening night of her Middle of Nowhere tour in Chicago. At one point during the performance, she paused the show and urged the audience to donate to the Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights as her “birthday wish.”

“It’s a wonderful organization, and they help give aid — legal aid — and money to children whose parents have been deported unfairly,” Musgraves said on stage. “It’s not a political thing. It’s just, these kids need help.”

She continued: “They have no guidance and no way to get through this thing without their home base or their parents. So anyway, 50 cents, whatever the hell, I don't know, whatever you want to do, but that would mean a lot to me. If you don't want to, that's totally fine too.”

The plea was met with applause and cheers from her crowd at the United Center. However, once videos of the moment started circulating online, conservative political commentators were quick to unleash their wrath on the “Follow Your Arrow” singer.

open image in gallery Kacey Musgraves is facing backlash from MAGA warriors after she showed support for immigrant families at a recent concert ( Getty )

Fox News’ Tomi Lahren posted in response to the video on X, “what is an unfair deportation?” while conservative commentator Vince Langman complained, “what happened to the country music industry?”

“Lost me young lady, no more listening to you,” one former fan wrote to Musgraves on X. Another angry user commented on her Instagram: “Might want to know the majority of your audience before talking out against illegal aliens being deported!”

One fan countered in the comments of her latest post: “We love you Kacey! People upset and surprised she would support the Young Centre clearly know nothing about her: she's always been a progressive, and not quiet about it.”

The Independent has reached out to Musgraves for comment.

open image in gallery The Grammy winner is currently on her ‘Middle of Nowhere’ tour ( Getty )

This is not the first time that Musgraves has upset conservatives. She has spent her career backing progressive causes, from supporting immigrants to gun control and LGBTQ+ rights.

Her pick of charity also does not come out of nowhere: Musgraves has repeatedly championed the Young Center, a national nonprofit that advocates for children separated from their families. Earlier this year, she partnered with Depop to sell pieces from her music videos and her personal wardrobe to raise money for the organization.

Law & Order’s Mariska Hargitay said she nearly stepped away from her role as the fierce commanding officer Olivia Benson after more than 25 years in the role.

In a new interview, the 62-year-old Law & Order: Special Victims Unit actor, who has portrayed Captain Benson since the show’s launch in 1999, revealed she nearly left the series to pursue new opportunities, including her comedy career.

“The comedy thing was painful to me because I felt like I was only exercising one part of myself,” she told Variety in a recent interview. “People would say, ‘You need to get off that show and do comedy. You need to get off that show and have a talk show.’”

But Hargitay realized she wasn’t ready to leave after a conversation with her friend Julianna Margulies about potentially departing the series. That is when she managed to fit different entertainment opportunities between shooting Special Victims Unit.

“Because I loved it,” she explained. “And then I got to do all this other stuff, and that’s why I don’t think about leaving right now.”

open image in gallery Mariska Hargitay was worried she was only exercising one of her talents as the star of ‘Law & Order: Special Victims Unit’ ( Getty )

“Do I want to quit now? No,” she said. “Why? I made a movie while shooting; I did a play for six weeks on hiatus. I’m hosting the Emmys.”

She added that starring in Every Brilliant Thing on Broadway made her excited for the other projects she can pursue when she has breaks from filming the series.

“Next summer, if I don’t make another movie, I’ll probably do another play. And I love it!” she said. “After I made my film, it was unleashed. Something got unleashed, or broken open, or freed.”

Hargitay is set to be the first woman to host the Emmys in 15 years when the ceremony takes place in Los Angeles on September 14.

“Bringing important stories into the light has been the heartbeat of my career,” Hargitay said in a press release. “It's my great honor to host the 78th Emmy Awards — in the 100th birthday year of my beloved NBC — and celebrate this extraordinary community of storytellers.”

open image in gallery Mariska Hargitay has portrayed fierce commanding officer Olivia Benson on ‘Law & Order: Special Victims Unit’ since its premiere in 1999 ( Getty )

Special Victims Unit has undergone various cast shake-ups in recent years.

NYPD captain Donald Cragen, played by 75-year-old Dann Florek, was killed off from the series last September after 35 years appearing in the franchise.

In the season 27 premiere of Special Victims Unit, which is TV’s longest-running live-action series, Hargitay’s character Olivia Benson paid tribute to her former leader, calling him the best boss she’s ever had.

“Everything I know about being a captain, I learned from him,” she said.

The main Law & Order series will also welcome a new senior detective, played by James Badge Dale, for the 26th season, premiering in October, following the departure of Reid Scott’s character Senior Detective Vincent Riley.

Hargitay has appeared in nearly 600 episodes of Special Victims Unit, as well as featuring in crossover appearances on the original Law & Order, Chicago P.D., and Law & Order: Organized Crime.

For years, Maine residents and visitors alike have flocked to Popham Beach in Phippsburg expecting to see a variety of shells, seabirds and rock outcroppings. This summer, visitors also encountered the occasional Christmas tree carcass strewn along sections of the beach’s uppermost sand dunes. These old trees are not the result of a holiday mishap — they were intentionally laid out to help rebuild the dunes after they were ravaged by harsh winter storms in December 2023 and January 2024.

Beaches in Maine are dynamic: shaped by wind and tides, they shift over time. But the changes at Popham have been particularly dramatic in recent years. The beach eroded, on average, roughly 92 feet annually between 2017 and 2025, according to data from the Maine Geological Survey’s beach mapping project, in part because of the migration of the Morse River, whose swift currents have cut into the dunes at the river’s edge. This, along with increasingly intense storms, has resulted in extensive changes to the shoreline of the beach, one of Maine’s most popular day-use state parks.

After the winter storms several years ago, the Popham Christmas tree project, in which volunteers arranged more than 500 trees in rows meant to trap sand and reform the dunes, became one of the most visible examples of nature-based shoreline stabilization techniques in the state. These projects, often called “living shorelines,” reflect an approach the Maine Department of Environmental Protection has been pushing for years as an alternative to rigid coastal structures such as concrete seawalls.

This is because seawalls can be counterproductive — wave energy is reflected off them, increasing erosion at the base of the wall and accelerating erosion at its edges. The structures also block sand from being deposited on the dunes behind them. Living shorelines use natural materials and vegetation such as logs, plants, sand and even oyster shells to stabilize the shoreline.

But living shorelines face challenges in Maine. The state’s long winter season substantially shortens the time period for construction and initial growth, often leaving young vegetation susceptible to cold and ice. As sea levels rise and heavier winds come into the Gulf of Maine, ocean waves carry increased amounts of energy, speeding up the erosion process.

Without continued maintenance, living shorelines in Maine often struggle. The one at Popham Beach lasted around a year. Today, while the regrown dune grass and the uppermost dunes remain intact, the Christmas trees have been scattered across the beach by storms and no longer contribute to dune replenishment. “It was a system that we knew could eventually be taken out by the incoming tide,” said Sean Vaillancourt, park manager and lifeguard coordinator for Popham. Vaillancourt said the park viewed it as a temporary solution. Permanent solutions for Popham’s erosion problem may include relocating the parking lot and second bath house or artificially changing the Morse River’s course — time-consuming and expensive options.

Still, Vaillancourt views the Christmas tree project as a success. “If we had not done this, it would have been a lot worse,” he said.

Landowners who install living shorelines must have the time and financial resources for extra watering during dry seasons, yearly replanting after harsh storms and possible restructuring in response to coastal changes, said Peter Slovinsky, a marine geologist with the Maine Geological Survey who has worked extensively on living shorelines around the state.

“Living shorelines are like tending to a garden,” he said.

A mixed record

Last May, the Maine Board of Environmental Protection made significant updates to the state’s shoreline rules, making it easier for landowners to get permission to plant a living shoreline on their land. Now, under the Natural Resources Protection Act, most nature-based proposals qualify for permit-by-rule, in which landowners file notice with the DEP, a process that takes around twenty working days.

“There was always interest in trying to make it as easy as possible to do the designs that were the most beneficial to natural resources,” said Jordan Kimball, assistant nonpoint source training coordinator for the DEP.

Now, if landowners want to go the hard armored route, they will have to prove why nature-based solutions do not work on their property through a more expensive and time-consuming individual permit application.

To aid coastal homeowners, the Maine DEP also began developing a living shoreline guidance program in early 2022. Known as O.U.R. S.H.O.R.E, the program set guidelines for homeowners and established training for contractors and landscapers.

The guidelines, drafted in 2024, include information on how to select vegetation, identify shoreline functions and understand different erosion processes.

Since the shoreline rule changes took effect last summer, DEP has received 170 permit-by-rule applications for shoreline stabilization activities, according to Nathan Robbins, a climate change specialist with the department. This includes both riprap-based and nature-based projects, the latter of which have seen increased interest since the new standards went in place.

But living shorelines in Maine, including the Maine Geological Survey’s own demonstration projects, have had mixed results.

In 2017, as part of a two-year grant through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Maine Geological Survey selected three project demonstration sites across Maine at which to experiment with different living shoreline techniques.

Two of these sites were in Brunswick: one at Maquoit Bay Conservation Land and one at Wharton Point, on sections of eroding land at the edge of marshes. Both are also subjected to waves, tides and ice in the winter. Each project cost less than $5,000 to implement, using volunteer labor for the initial construction, according to Slovinsky.

Staff from the Geological Survey used dead oyster shells for stabilization on both sites, placing half of the shells in biodegradable bags and half in synthetic mesh baskets. At the Maquoit Bay site, the team also used “tree runners,” 10- to 12-foot-long tree trunks designed to provide a ramp for ice to ride up and over during the winter months.

The installation techniques were experimental, explained Slovinsky, so not everything was expected to work. The biodegradable bags containing the oyster shells fell apart too quickly, unable to withstand storms, while the tree runners at Maquoit Bay were incorrectly anchored and did not provide the necessary protection.

The team has monitored the projects over the years, replacing the biodegradable bags with the mesh baskets. Both shorelines have remained stable and at Wharton Point mud and sand has begun accumulating atop the mesh baskets.

Neither site, however, has seen increased natural recruitment of oysters, said Slovinsky, in part because the living shorelines were placed too high in the intertidal zone. Any natural growth of oyster spat that occurs during the summer dies in the winter, as it is exposed to sub-freezing temperatures for too long. The third test site cost approximately $65,000 and was located on Lanes Island in Yarmouth, in an area that has been experiencing severe, long-term erosion. The team arranged fallen trees from the area into a terraced structure, placing root balls at the edges of the structure to help decrease erosion at the base of the structure.

Slovinsky explained that even in 2017, the erosion was so severe that natural solutions alone could not address the problem.

“It didn’t matter what we did. It got one hundred percent outflanked and basically there’s not much left of it,” Slovinsky said.

While the method turned out to be inadequate for the high levels of erosion on Lanes Island, Slovinsky said that the same method has worked successfully on a 1,500-foot private shoreline i n Blue Hill that was constructed in 2021 .

Different techniques

Living shorelines will look and work differently in different places, said Seth Wilkinson, a certified ecological restoration practitioner who works around New England.

“Site analysis is so important. You’ve really got to understand where you are,” said Wilkinson. “Each of the different techniques allowed under Maine’s regulation have their place.”

Wilkinson has found that because these projects can become complicated, it’s helpful to take an interdisciplinary approach. “It’s good to have an engineer, possibly an environmental consultant — if it’s complicated on the regulatory side — and a restoration ecologist,” he said.

An official with the Portland Water District who was involved in a living shoreline project at Sebago Lake State Park’s popular Songo Beach swimming area said they did not budget for or anticipate the continual upkeep needed.

The project was intended to deal with erosion at Songo Beach, where intense wind, waves and high water levels had repeatedly stripped away beach sand. By 2022, the erosion had become severe. Trees had also been toppled as their roots were exposed by the retreating shoreline.

In response, in 2023, park staff and project partners began constructing a living shoreline designed to absorb wave energy and capture sand.

The team used roughly 75 oak trees harvested from the park, leaving their root balls attached. The trees were incorporated into engineered structures positioned along approximately 300 feet of chronically eroding shoreline. Live stakes — branches from dormant, native trees and shrubs — were planted alongside the structures to encourage vegetation and provide additional stabilization as the shoreline recovered.

The techniques were adapted to address the unique erosion challenges of Sebago Lake, said Chad Thompson, the water district’s source protection coordinator.

“In my mind, it was the most cutting-edge living shoreline project done in Maine,” he said.

While the trees are helping to protect the shoreline from erosion and the brush bundles are capturing some sand, the project has required enormous maintenance, said Thompson, especially after storms ripped out many of the live stacks.

The state park and water district did not have the ability to dedicate their whole season to maintaining one project, said Thompson. The project was supported by $40,000 in federal funding via the Clean Water Act, but the grant covered only initial construction, not additional upkeep.

“It ultimately fell through due to lack of resources,” said Thompson.

The water district has not given up on living shorelines, however. In June, the district, along with the Maine Department of Transportation, planted a shoreline stabilization project at an underground granite culvert in Standish Brook.

For years, Standish Brook flowed through an underground granite culvert, built in the early 1900s as part of the railroad system, before emptying into Sebago Lake. In recent years, the culvert has continually collapsed, causing major flooding and draining issues upstream. Staff from the water district and the transportation department eventually determined the only long-term solution was to remove the culvert and restore the stream to an open channel.

Working with the Cumberland County Soil and Water Conservation District’s engineer Chris Baldwin, the Portland Water District and state transportation department excavated the granite culvert to create a natural ravine with sloping sides for the brook to flow through. The initial phase of the project cost $120,000.

To stabilize the sides of the ravine, the water district worked with Paul Larrivee, a local forester, to plant native vegetation, including juniper, sweet fern and purple coneflower. They also used live-staking with dogwood and pussy willow, and put down temporary erosion-control mats and blankets — rolled materials made from natural fibers designed to stabilize bare soil and protect newly seeded areas from rain and wind. Purchasing, planting and maintaining the vegetation cost around $30,000, which was paid for by the water district.

The planting was done in June, ideally giving the vegetation enough time to grow and stabilize before the winter months. The forester comes out and monitors the plants and live stacks once or twice a week, providing extra watering during dry spells.

“With this project, there’s a lot of initial work to make sure the plants survive and grow, but hopefully, once they’re established, we won’t have to do much maintenance,” Thompson said. If successful, the Standish Brook project will stabilize the ravine, prevent further flooding in the area and help keep invasive plant species at bay.

Nature-based solutions, said state officials, are dynamic and complex, and if they are going to serve as long-term solutions, they require continual monitoring and care.

“One of the unique things about this kind of work is you can’t just say at the end of the project, ‘That worked,’” said John Maclaine of the DEP, who assists with O.U.R. S.H.O.R.E. “Living things take time and get stronger over time. Part of this is continually going back to look at what you’ve done.”

Dolly Parton died with a net worth of over $450 million, according to estimates.

The Queen of Country’s death at the age of 80 was announced Tuesday by her family in an emotional statement.

She was born in a two-room log cabin in rural Tennessee and described her upbringing as “dirt poor,” but went on to become one of the wealthiest performers in country music.

Parton retained ownership of her vast music catalog, which numbered some 3,000 songs and included indelible hits such as “Jolene,” “9 to 5” and “I Will Always Love You,” which was famously covered by Whitney Houston. In June 2025, Forbes estimated that her song catalog alone was worth $120 million.

The singer-songwriter also had a significant stake in her own amusement park, Dollywood, in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

open image in gallery A significant portion of Dolly Parton’s wealth came from her amusement park Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee ( 2024 Invision )

Parton died with no immediate family. She never had children, and her husband Carl Dean died last year at the age of 82.

She did however have a large extended family, with her death being announced by her nephew, Bryan Seaver.

The family have not yet announced Parton’s plans for her extensive fortune, but it is widely expected that they will be used to further the philanthropic interests she supported throughout her life.

During her life, Parton raised millions for numerous good causes, including the American Red Cross and several HIV/AIDS-related charities, and was involved in charitable campaigns ranging from relief from wildfires in the Great Smoky Mountains to the American Eagle Foundation's efforts to preserve the bald eagle.

open image in gallery Parton died Tuesday at the age of 80 ( Getty )

In 1995, she founded Dollywood Foundation’s Imagination Library, a program which she described as her proudest achievement. The program mails a new, free book to children from around the world, from their birth until they begin kindergarten.

Parton funded the project in memory of her father. “My own father didn't get a chance to go to school,” she told CNN in 2016. “He couldn't read and write, and that hindered him a great deal because he was so smart. It really bothered him a lot.”

At the time of her death, Parton’s Imagination Library was mailing books to almost 850,000 children each month in 1,600 communities across the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Australia and the Republic of Ireland.

“I want to be remembered as somebody who took her work serious, but not herself,” she told The Independent, when asked about her legacy. “Someone who brought books to children all over the world.”

News.content:

Dolly Parton, who was born in a two-room log cabin and rose to become the world’s wealthiest country music star with timeless hits including “9 to 5” and “Jolene,” has died aged 80.

Her death was announced by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, in an Instagram video posted Tuesday afternoon.

“This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago,” Seaver said. He served as Parton’s head of security for more than two decades.

“Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus,” he continued. A cause of death was not revealed. However, Parton had been open about struggling with her health in recent months, forcing a slew of concert and public appearance cancellations.

Most recently, Parton was forced to pull out of attending the opening night of a new attraction at Dollywood, her Tennessee theme park last week. The singer suffered dizziness and dehydration and her doctor advised her against travel.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton photographed in London in 1977, the same year she released her first million-selling album ‘Here You Come Again’ ( Keystone/Getty Images )

Parton became one of the most beloved singer-songwriters of all time and sold more than 100 million records globally, earning her the nickname the “Queen of Country,” over the course of her six-decade career.

She wrote more than 3,000 songs, and a record-breaking 44 of her albums reached the top 10 on the country music charts. She won eleven Grammy Awards, three Emmy Awards and was set to receive an honorary Oscar for her humanitarian work in 2026.

She was believed to be the world’s wealthiest country music star, with an estimated net worth of $500m, and became a noted philanthropist. She was known for her efforts to encourage literacy around the world through her Dollywood Foundation’s Imagination Library, and also used her money to fight the HIV/Aids crisis, fund the American Red Cross and develop a Covid vaccine.

In 2022, she was awarded the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy and commented: “I just give from my heart. I never know what I’m going to do or why I’m gonna do it. I just see a need and if I can fill it, then I will.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton attends the opening of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum exhibition 'Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker' in Nashville, Tennessee in May 2025 ( Jason Kempin/Getty Images )

Born on January 19, 1946, in a two-room log cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River in Tennessee, Parton was the fourth of 12 children. Her father was an illiterate sharecropper who worked his way up to owning a small tobacco farm.

Parton later described her family as being “dirt poor” but credited her mother with passing on her love and deep knowledge of traditional folk ballads and her father for his work ethic. “He raised that whole family on his brains and hard work,” she wrote in a 2020 memoir. “He knew how to count money. He knew what everything was worth.”

Parton started performing when she was a child. By the age of 13, she had appeared on local radio and television in East Tennessee; performed at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville; and recorded her first single "Puppy Love". When she graduated high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville the next day and began establishing herself as a songwriter.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton in 1980’s ‘9 to 5’. She also wrote and sang the title song, which became a number one hit and was nominated for an Oscar ( 20th Century Fox )

She released her debut album Hello, I’m Dolly in 1967, the same year she joined the weekly television program The Porter Wagoner Show. Wagoner was an established country star who mentored Parton, and they released a string of successful albums as a duo.

In 1973, Parton decided to concentrate on her solo career and wrote the ballad “I Will Always Love You” about their professional separation. The song was a hit for Parton and again for Whitney Houston, who recorded a 1992 power ballad cover that topped the charts for a then-record-breaking 14 weeks.

Parton once said that she wrote “I Will Always Love You” the same day she wrote another of her signature hits, “Jolene”. She later qualified the claim, telling an interviewer: “When we found an old tape, they were on the same cassette. That could have been a few days apart. They were certainly written within a very short span of time.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers had a chart-topping hit in 1983 with 'Islands in the Stream' ( Rick Diamond/Getty Images )

open image in gallery Dolly Parton, seen opening a new ride in 2010, bought an interest in a Tennessee theme park in 1986 and renamed it Dollywood ( AP )

Both songs were included on her 1974 album Jolene, which brought her to a wider audience outside of country music. 1977’s Here You Come Again was her first album to sell a million copies, and gave her a first Grammy win after almost a decade of nominations.

In 1980, Parton took on her first acting role when she was cast alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in the subversive workplace comedy 9 to 5. She also wrote the film’s theme song, which became a number one hit, earned an Oscar nomination for Best Original Song and made her an icon to women everywhere.

The film’s success helped Parton launch a secondary career as an actor, appearing in movies including The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (1982), Steel Magnolias (1989) and Joyful Noise (2012).

open image in gallery Dolly Parton and Carl Dean were married for 58 years ( Instagram/@DollyParton )

Parton kept up a prolific rate of productivity throughout her life, releasing a new album at least every couple of years alongside diverse business ventures including TV specials, frozen food and her own Dollywood theme park in Tennessee. Among various rides and attractions, the park features a replica of the tiny log cabin where she was born.

She married just once – to her husband of 60 years Carl Dean, a businessman who she met aged 18, on the same day she moved to Nashville. The singer once wrote she was “surprised and delighted” that while Carl talked to her, he looked at her face.

“He seemed to be genuinely interested in finding out who I was and what I was about,” she said.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton performing with Miley Cyrus, her goddaughter, at the Grammy Awards in Los Angeles in 2019 ( Kevin Winter/Getty Images for The Recording Academy )

open image in gallery Dolly Parton, seen here launching her first 'Imagination Library' in the UK in Rotherham in 2007, was a noted philanthropist ( Getty Images )

The pair married two years later on May 30, 1966 in Georgia. For years they kept their relationship strictly private, with Parton telling the AP in 1984: "A lot of people say there’s no Carl Dean, that he’s just somebody I made up to keep other people off me."

Parton’s health concerns first became public in September 2025, when she was forced to postpone her Las Vegas residency.

She made the announcement with a joke about her history of cosmetic surgery, writing: “As many of you know, I have been dealing with some health challenges, and my doctors tell me that I must have a few procedures. As I joked with them, it must be time for my 100,000-mile check-up, although it’s not the usual trip to see my plastic surgeon!”

A Broadway show based on Parton’s life is slated to open in 2027.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

News.title: This summer’s wildfire epidemic is one of the worst in decades – so why are deaths so low?
News.content:
Wildfires in Britain and Europe this year are among the worst in decades, yet direct deaths are at some of the lowest levels, according to a Telegraph analysis.

As of early August, 505,683 hectares of land have burned across Europe, forcing the evacuation of more than 360,000 people as uncontrollable flames reach major cities, towns, and villages.

The problem is global – in the US, Nevada declared a state of emergency over the weekend after a wildfire caused more than 42,000 people to evacuate their homes.

But what sets 2026 apart isn’t just the vast areas of land burned, but how few deaths have been caused by the fires.

This summer, just 14 people are reported to have died in European wildfires, the vast majority in a single blaze in Almería, southern Spain.

By comparison, more than 130 people were killed in the summer of 2017 – a toll driven largely by the Pedrógão Grande disaster in Portugal, where more than 60 people died on a single stretch of road.

In 2018, at least 100 others died in a single afternoon in the Mati disaster near Athens, despite total hectares burned that year being roughly a third of current levels.

Since the modern phenomenon of summer wildfires exploded in Europe a decade ago, the direct death toll has broadly trended downward, as the chart below shows.

News.title: Swine flu outbreak in Delhi swamps clinics and hospitals
News.content:
India is battling a surge in H1N1 flu infections, prompting the federal health ministry to step up surveillance and hospital preparedness.

The national capital New Delhi has recorded 1,777 cases this year, almost eight times the number (229) reported during the same period in 2025.

Dr Randeep Guleria, a senior pulmonologist and director of Medanta Medical School, Gurugram, says the H1N1 cases are much higher than reported.

“It’s quite likely that the reported numbers are an underestimate because they depend on how many people are tested,” Guleria said. “If you speak to patients admitted to hospital who test positive for H1N1, you often find that other members of their family have similar symptoms, although they have not been tested.”

“There is a surge and we are seeing a lot of patients. We are testing only those who come to hospital and are more seriously ill,” Guleria said.

H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A. It is a contagious respiratory infection that can cause fever and cough and in severe cases it can lead to pneumonia and respiratory failure.

Officials at the Indian Council of Medical Research said the rise did not mean the emergence of a new strain of the virus.

The surge comes during India’s rainy season, when seasonal influenza and other respiratory infections typically increase.

Doctors in Delhi say they are seeing more patients with high fevers, persistent coughs and flu-like symptoms, although most cases remain mild.

The H1N1 cases have been reported beyond New Delhi. The metro cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Bangaluru have reported a high number of cases, although the pattern is not uniform across the country.

Doctors in Bangaluru have reported more influenza A infections among children, with some developing pneumonia and respiratory distress.

India’s health minister JP Nadda said there was a need for continued vigilance and robust surveillance. He has asked officials to monitor unusual increases and clusters of cases and ensure hospitals could respond quickly.

“Swine flu (H1N1) can show up through symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, headache, runny nose, body aches and fatigue… If you experience these symptoms, seek medical advice at your nearest healthcare centre,” the health ministry said on X.

Delhi’s health minister, Pankaj Kumar Singh, said the capital had enough beds, doctors, medicines and medical equipment to manage the increase. “Delhi is fully prepared to deal with the present health situation,” Singh said.

India has had several waves of H1N1 since the virus emerged globally in 2009.

The infection, commonly called swine flu, became a recurring seasonal respiratory illness after the 2009 pandemic rather than disappearing from circulation.

India recorded 3,320 H1N1 cases and 14 deaths in 2025, according to Ministry of Health data.

News.title: Newcastle and Liverpool serve up thrilling tribute to Kevin Keegan
News.content:
It is fitting that Newcastle United vs Liverpool is a Premier League opening weekend fixture following the death of Kevin Keegan at the age of 75 last month.

All corners of St James’ Park will pay tribute and show their appreciation for the former player and manager who means a great deal to both sets of supporters.

Fans will find a printed message from the Keegan family on the back of black and white cards on their seat, which they will hold up to display a mural before kick-off.

As well as playing for both clubs, Keegan was Newcastle’s manager when they were beaten by a last-gasp Stan Collymore goal at Anfield in April 1996, a 4-3 defeat remembered as one of the great Premier League games.

This fixture usually delivers entertainment, and with new managers Matthias Jaissle and Andoni Iraola promising front-footed, ‘vertical’ football, there should be goals. That was certainly the case last August, when Newcastle fought back from two down with 10 men, before Rio Ngumoha scored a memorable winner.

It has been a summer of tumult for Newcastle, losing manager Eddie Howe, as well as key players Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes. There has been bullish talk of “Newcastle 2.0” from David Hopkinson, the club’s chief executive, and the club believe they have found a promising coach, but fans have understandably revised expectations downwards.

Liverpool are a difficult team to read; champions only 18 months ago but brittle last season, which resulted in Arne Slot’s dismissal. Iraola’s appointment is a shift back towards Jurgen Klopp’s style. That will be music to the ears of Anfield regulars, but holes remain in the squad. Central midfield has not been replenished; they need a Mohamed Salah replacement, and their strength at full-back is questionable. Much will depend on how 21-year-old central defender Jérémy Jacquet fares alongside Vigin van Dijk but he impressed in pre-season.



Full team news on the way shortly.

Sports.title: Arsenal to shatter club record sale as Gabriel Martinelli closes in on £50m Al-Hilal transfer after being axed by Arteta
Sports.content:
ARSENAL are closing in on a deal to sell Gabriel Martinelli to Saudi side Al Hilal.

The Gunners are set to bank over £50million, which would make it a club-record sale, and talks over a fee are in the final stages.



Martinelli, 25, will receive a pay rise on his £180,000-a-week wages if he gives the green light to the move.

The winger has been deemed surplus to requirements at Arsenal, but he turned down an offer from Galatasaray earlier this month.



Martinelli’s position in Mikel Arteta’s plans has been made clearer since, though, and he was left out of the match-day squads for the first two games.

The Brazilian is into the final year of his contract at the Emirates, although there is an option to extend it by 12 months.



Arsenal have strengthened their left flank this summer by bringing in Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34million.

The Greek star impressed in pre-season and caught the eye in the Gunners’ opening Premier League win over Coventry last week.

Arteta wants to add another attacker to his squad; however, the club have failed to do so up until now.

Arsenal are interested in Atletico Madrid forward Julian Alvarez, who could move before the transfer window shuts next week.



But the Argentine has made it clear that his preference would be to head to Barcelona if he leaves the Spanish capital.

Atletico, however, are adamant that they will not sell to Barca, which has opened the door for Arsenal.

Arsenal’s current club-record sale dates back to 2017, when they sold Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain to Liverpool for £35m.

Sports.title: Chelsea make £20million profit on Liam Delap after just ONE Prem goal as Nottingham Forest agree club-record transfer
Sports.content:
NOTTINGHAM FOREST have agreed a £50million deal for Chelsea exile Liam Delap.

The Blues striker bagged just ONE goal in the Premier League last season after his £30m move from Ipswich.



He was stripped of his No9 shirt this summer and has been training separately from new boss Xabi Alonso‘s main group.

And yet the Blues are set to make a profit of at least £15m on the flop transfer.



Everton also expressed an interest in the forward.

But it’s Forest who have struck a deal for the former Manchester City academy player, with £45m upfront and an extra £5m in add-ons.

The potential £50m deal smashes Forest’s previous record transfer, which was the £37.5m spent on Ipswich’s Omari Hutchison a year ago.

Delap was not part of Alonso’s squad for Chelsea‘s Premier League opener at Fulham on Monday night as their new-look front three impressed.

Chelsea, who have already added Danny Welbeck this summer, currently have six senior strikers on their books and want to cut that number to three before the window closes.

Nicolas Jackson is a target for Aston Villa and Atletico Madrid and is expected to depart.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Marc Guiu, who signed from Barcelona in 2024, has options in Spain, Italy and Germany and looks likely to leave on a permanent deal.

That will see Chelsea go into the new season with Joao Pedro, Welbeck and Emmanuel Emegha, a summer signing from sister club Strasbourg, as their three strikers.

Delap suffered from poor form, ill-discipline and hamstring and shoulder injuries last season.

He was part of Alonso’s squad for the pre-season tour of Australia and Asia.

However, he was not involved in Chelsea’s final pre-season game ahead of the new season.



And shortly after that game against Real Sociedad it was confirmed his shirt number had been given to Pedro, who claimed a goal and an assist at Fulham.

Further star power has been spotted at the PFA Awards with Stacey Dooley, 39, featuring.

Additionally, social media stars Angry Ginge, 24, and Gemma Owen, 23, have also made appearances.

Owen has stunned wearing a sculpted black dress with dainty gold jewellery.

Meanwhile, livestreamer Angry Ginge has kept his look simple with a skinny black tie to complement his suit.

Sports.title: Newcastle cult hero, 34, appointed as club’s new loans manager and immediately tasked with flogging four players
Sports.content:
PAUL DUMMETT has been appointed as Newcastle United’s new loans manager.

The 34-year-old Premier League cult hero has already been tasked with sending four players away for the 2026-27 season.



Former defender Dummett has joined the Magpies‘ loans department in his first executive role after announcing his retirement from professional football in December 2025.

It comes after ex-Newcastle striker Shola Ameobi, 44, was moved to become the team’s head of corporate affairs, according to The i Paper.



A restructure of the team’s loans department has also seen Peter Rampage, 42, take over as the talent management lead.

Right-back Leo Shahar and striker Sean Neave, both 19, are expected to be sent away on loan after attention from Championship and League One teams.

READ MORE BRIGHTON THE MOOD Man Utd confirm £70million Carlos Baleba transfer from Brighton

Park Seung-soo, 19, and Miodrag Pivas, 21, are also expected to be sent on loan following their recent moves to the North East.

South Korean winger Park joined the Magpies’ youth setup in 2025 after making 25 appearances for K League 2 side Suwon Samsung Bluewings.

Meanwhile, Pivas joined Newcastle in July 2024, before spending last season in the Netherlands with Willem II.

Ex-Wales international Dummett will draw on his experiences as a loanee and a cult figure star in his new role.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

The former defender made 196 appearances for the Magpies between 2010 and 2024.

He was also sent on loan to Gateshead and St Mirren early on in his career, with later permanent moves to Wigan Athletic and Carlisle United.

Dummett was seen watching on as several young players were given vital experience during pre-season friendlies.

It is hoped that Newcastle’s revamped loans department can help close the gap between the club’s academy and first team.



The Magpies are continuing to spend big as the 2026-27 season swings into action with Nico Gonzalez, 24, set for a £50 million move from Manchester City.

Additionally, loan deals have been agreed for youngsters Antonio Cordero, Anthony Munda, both 19, and Alex Murphy, 22.

Newcastle opened their 2026-27 Premier League campaign with a 2-2 draw against Liverpool.

They will next travel south to face Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday, August 29.

Sports.title: Inside Cole Palmer’s amazing lifestyle, from £4.3million Surrey mansion to influencer girlfriend and Burberry contract
Sports.content:
WHAT a difference a summer off makes.

Cole Palmer put on a masterclass for Chelsea on Monday Night Football, scoring and grabbing an assist in a 3-2 win over Fulham.



That came after he was cruelly snubbed by Thomas Tuchel for England’s World Cup squad.

But, instead of wallowing in self-pity, the Blues playmaker enjoyed some downtime with pals in Ibiza, where he was spotted partying with Wayne Lineker at his Ocean Beach club.

And that’s just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to Palmer’s amazing lifestyle off the pitch.



He lives in a stunning £4.3million mansion in Surrey, dates a beautiful influencer, and even caught the eye of fashion giants Burberry, who signed him up on a modelling contract.

There’s absolutely nothing ‘Cold’ about his existence.

Mansion fit for a king

Like many Chelsea footballers, Cole 24, resides in the leafy Surrey Village of Oxshott.

His home, worth £4.3million, is situated behind private gated grounds.

It boasts six bedrooms, an expansive entrance hall and living room, as well as a modern kitchen and dining room.



While there’s also an entertainment room, where he can play video games and relax with friends after playing football.

Although his planning application to build an outdoor gym sparked objections from his neighbours.

Influencer Wag

Cole is currently dating the stunning blonde model and influencer, Olivia Holder, dubbed the ‘Pilates Princess’.



They were first spotted together last December enjoying a date at London’s Winter Wonderland.

The 24-year-old stunner reportedly runs a beauty clinic alongside her sister in Bromley in Greater London.

A devout Christian, Olivia regularly discusses her faith on Instagram.

She is becoming the ultimate Chelsea Wag, and is often seen in the hospitality section at Stamford Bridge.

Olivia has enjoyed the trappings of Cole’s lifestyle, including luxury holidays in Dubai, Ibiza, Cannes, and Marbella.



Cars

When it comes to motors, Cole has a very impressive collection.



When he began life as a Man City trainee, his trusted car was a Volkswagen Polo.

But, now on a salary of £130,000-per-week, he’s been able to branch out to more luxurious brands.

The most impressive is his Lamborghini Urus, worth a whopping £190,000. It was customized by WRAPvehicles with neon green brake calipers and gloss black wheels.



He has added a BMW i4 M50 to his garage, worth around £72,000.

Cole also was seen behind the wheel of a reliable Mercedes-Benz A-Class, which starts at £31,000.

He’s in fashion

Thanks to his persona on the pitch, earning him the nickname ‘Cold Palmer’ because of his epic goal celebration, the midfielder has scored plenty of fans.

And many have taken to his fashion style too, dubbing it Palmercore – mixing high-street luxury brands with streetwear and tracksuits.



That said, he has rocked up to high-profile ceremonies like the PFA Awards and GQ Men of the Year events in designer suits and tuxedos, so he’s not always so paired down.

His style caught the attention of British fashion house Burberry, who signed him up on a seasonal campaign deal.

Cole went viral with a nine-minute fishing film for the brand called The Duffle with Cole Palmer.

Amusingly, the clip sees him sitting by a lake fishing in complete silence for the entire duration.



The playmaker also starred alongside Arsenal star Eberechi Eze for their It’s Always Burberry Weather campaign, where he wore Burberry’s classic coats and trademark knits.

Back in June, Cole was a cover star for trendy i-D Magazine in partnership with Burberry to model their latest collection.

There’s more to come…

All of this is brewing quite nicely to build Palmer into a brand.



Last October, Cole successfully trademarked the term ‘Cold Palmer’ with the UK government’s Intellectual Property Office.

What does that mean? Well, now no one can use his nickname for commercial purposes without first getting his permission first.

Second, he can now add that trademarked term to products he wants to endorse.

Think toys, clothes, footballs, football boots, and even food.

He also managed to trademark his name, autograph, and shivering goal celebration.



There is already a partnership with Gopuff who launched a premium ice brand they’ve aptly called COLE’D.

Expect more merch to follow.

Sports.title: Why Nicolas Jackson to Aston Villa transfer is so complicated despite Chelsea outcast and Emery being perfect match
Sports.content:
NICOLAS JACKSON going to Aston Villa would make sense for everyone.

Chelsea want him off their books, Villa need a striker, and Jackson and Unai Emery would love to be reunited after their spell together at Villarreal.



But multiple factors, from Uefa’s “45-day rule” and Premier League loan regulations, to the intrigue surrounding Julian Alvarez’s future at Atletico Madrid, are putting spanners in the works.

Which is why Villa, after shadowing Jackson most of the summer, are now looking at other options, such as Crystal Palace’s wantaway frontman Jean-Philippe Mateta.



And why Chelsea, for the second summer in a row, find themselves scrambling to find Jackson a new home, preferably a permanent one.

Despite the fact the Senegal striker would be a more natural replacement for Ollie Watkins, if he joins the Villa exodus, than Mateta.



Chelsea and Villa have already done business this summer. Morgan Rogers moved to Stamford Bridge for £117m, a record for a British player, in late July.

Soon afterwards, Alejandro Garnacho moved in the other direction, on loan with a conditional buy clause.

But those deals make a Jackson move more difficult and less attractive for both clubs.

Under Uefa rules, if clubs sell players to each other within a 45-day period they are treated as a player swap – not as two separate transactions.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

In those circumstances, the clubs are not able to put any profit on the player they have sold directly on to their books for accounting purposes.

The rules are complex, but the upshot is the selling clubs cannot enjoy the full benefit of the agreed fee when it comes to calculations related to Uefa and PL financial rules.

Rogers’ transfer to Chelsea was confirmed on July 21. So if Jackson were to move in the other direction before the window closes next Tuesday, the deal would fall within the 45-day window.

The result would be Villa not being able to add all the profit on Rogers to their accounts and Chelsea facing the same restriction on what they received for Jackson.



The Uefa regulations allow wriggle room if players move initially on loan, although there are still restrictions.

But that option is not open to Chelsea and Villa. PL rules say clubs can only have one player on loan from another PL club at any one time. And Garnacho is already filling that slot at Villa Park.

An added complication is Villa and Chelsea are already in Uefa’s bad books for breaching regulations.

They are operating under settlement agreements which set them financial targets they must meet to avoid further fines and punishment.



Villa have already sold Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Ezri Konsa to help balance the books. Ollie Watkins wants to follow them out by making a lucrative move to Saudi Arabia.

Jackson would be much more of a direct replacement for Watkins than a player like Mateta.

Although Chelsea are not involved in European competition this season, they still have to meet most of the terms of their settlement.

The Blues seem to be pretty cool right now about the Jackson situation, because of interest from other clubs. But Atletico seem like the best bet.



The LaLiga side have been in talks with the Blues on and off the whole summer.

Director of football Mateu Alemany was in London earlier this month.

But Atletico have, until now, been pushing for an initial loan deal for Jackson.

And Chelsea, after another busy summer of incomings, would much prefer a permanent deal.



They value the 25-year-old at £65m. Jackson arrived three years ago for £30m on an eight-year contract.

Which means his current value for accounting purposes, after allowing for amortisation, is just under £20m. So a £65m fee would bring a profit of more than £45m.

The trick will be finding someone willing to pay that much, either up front or as a compulsory purchase after an initial loan.

Atletico have so far resisted. But their own problems with Alvarez are coming to a head.



The Argentinian star has been pushing for a move, preferably to Barcelona, all summer.

The start of the new season has upped the stakes, with Alvarez being booed by Atletico fans and a toxic atmosphere developing.

It would be a major climbdown by Atletico if they sold their star player, after insisting he would be staying.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They were already looking at Jackson because of an injury to Alexander Sorloth. But if Alvarez left, the need for reinforcements up front on a longer-term basis would become critical.

All of which leaves Jackson in limbo, waiting to see if all the different rules and all the other transfer sagas will align for him to get his move away.

Sports.title: Man Utd CONFIRM £70million Carlos Baleba transfer from Brighton as Seagulls insert genius contract clause
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER UNITED have announced the £70million signing of Carlos Baleba from Brighton.

The Cameroon international, 22, has penned a five-year deal at Old Trafford with the option of a further 12 months.



And his arrival for £65m plus £5m in add-ons should round off the Red Devils’ relentless midfield spending spree.

United bosses had already splurged £50m on Andrey Santos from Chelsea and £35m on Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa.





But they wanted a third to sure up Michael Carrick‘s squad after Casemiro‘s move to Inter Miami and Manuel Ugarte‘s long-term knee injury.

And they teased the announcement with a tweet at 4.30pm on Tuesday.

The club simply wrote: “#areyouareabaleba” which sent United fans into ecstasy.

They then replied to their own post with a video of Baleba in the red home shirt saying: “Hi, I’m a Baleba.”



The official confirmation of the deal, including photos of the midfielder putting pen to paper, dropped at 4.45pm.

Baleba said: “It is an incredible feeling to join the club of my dreams.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“Playing at Old Trafford is always special but the opportunity to do so as a Manchester United player will be a real honour.

“I cannot wait to work with Michael Carrick – his experience and knowledge of the game make him the perfect coach to help me to reach the highest level.

“The ambition of everyone at the club is extremely clear, the future is hugely exciting, and I am determined to play my part in delivering the success that we are capable of together.”



Jason Wilcox, director of football, added: “Carlos is an elite midfielder with immense potential to develop further.

“He brings a unique combination of qualities that will really complement our squad.

“We are delighted to further strengthen our midfield with the addition of another established senior international with a proven track record of performing in the Premier League.

“Carlos’ determination to join Manchester United and his confidence that we will achieve our shared ambitions mean that he is the perfect signing as we continue to build a dynamic and entertaining team ready to compete across multiple competitions.”

The fact the Red Devils have almost halved the £120m price tag they were quoted for Baleba last summer will come as some relief.



Brighton have covered their backs by inserting a sell-on clause which could bump up their earnings from the deal if United cash in down the line.

Last season was not the youngster’s finest on the South Coast as he managed only 35 goalless appearances in all competitions.

But United were long-standing admirers of Baleba, and they hope he can compete with Santos, Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo for the two deep-lying midfield spots in Carrick’s starting line-up.



The new recruit can also play at left-back, where United may need cover for Luke Shaw during a long season of domestic and European football.

Baleba has been nursing an ankle injury and is not expected to return until mid-September.

He scored four times in 112 appearances for Brighton after they snapped him up from Lille as a 19-year-old for £23.2m.

His last appearance for the Seagulls, ironically, came against Carrick’s United on the final day of last season.

Brighton sporting director Mike Cave said: “Carlos has made a significant contribution during his time with us and we’ve seen him develop both as a player and person here.



“When Carlos arrived, he was a young player with huge potential and, through his own hard work and commitment together with the support of our coaches and staff, he has developed into an outstanding Premier League midfielder.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“This is a move that Carlos was keen to make and we respect that he wants to take this opportunity at this stage of his career.

“We would like to thank him for everything he has done during his time at Brighton and wish him every success in the next chapter of his journey.”

Sports.title: Alvarez left with two options: Atletico or Arsenal
Sports.content:
Julian Alvarez must take one of two paths before the transfer deadline: stay at Atletico Madrid and try to rebuild his connection with the fans or get his head around a potential move to Arsenal.

Atletico have told him again that they will not sell him to Barcelona and that - coupled with the reaction of the club's supporters on Sunday - has left him "devastated", according to well-placed sources in Spain.

The situation is now "extremely tense", according to Atletico expert and journalist Ruben Uría.

"Neither Miguel Gil Marín (CEO of Atlético Madrid) nor the Apollo board want to sell the player to Barcelona," he told Sky Sports News. "The entire Apollo board supports Gil Marín's decision. Alvarez has been told."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the Transfer Talk podcast, Sam Tighe and Daniel Storey debate whether Arsenal should gamble on signing Julian Alvarez despite the striker clearly wanting to sign for Barcelona

According to Uría, Arsenal sporting director Andrea Berta has remained in contact with his former Atletico employers in recent days after Alvarez was booed off by supporters in the opening LaLiga game against Villarreal.

But Arsenal will need Alvarez to put Barcelona out of his mind and show he really wants to join Mikel Arteta's project before any serious negotiations or any offers can be made. In that vein, Arsenal are not currently hopeful of getting him in before September 1 and they are certainly not currently expecting it at the Emirates.

Alvarez still has his heart set on Barcelona. The question is, will this be the case as the transfer window comes to an end? Will the deadline have any effect? Arsenal will always be ready and open to Alvarez should he change his mind but, at the moment, any move looks very unlikely.

If Alvarez shifts his thinking before the end and pushes for an escape, Atletico are believed to be ready to listen to offers of around £130m (€150m) from Arsenal. Indeed, according to Uría, some people around the Argentine think it is increasingly impossible for him to stay at Atletico given the current atmosphere.

Should Arsenal complete a deal for Alvarez, it would be the 10th £100m+ signing in Premier League history.

Premier League £100m+ transfers Alexander Isak – £125m – Newcastle to Liverpool

Morgan Rogers – £117m - Aston Villa to Chelsea

Florian Wirtz – £116.5m – Bayer Leverkusen to Liverpool

Elliot Anderson – £116m – Nottingham Forest to Manchester City

Moises Caicedo – £115m – Brighton to Chelsea

Enzo Fernandez – £106.8m – Benfica to Chelsea

Declan Rice – £105m – West Ham to Arsenal

Sandro Tonali – £100m – Newcastle to Tottenham

Jack Grealish – £100m – Aston Villa to Manchester City

It would also be the fourth this summer, after Morgan Rogers' switch to Chelsea, Elliot Anderson's move to Manchester City and Sandro Tonali joining Tottenham.

Uría also told Sky Sports News: "Julian and his agent believe that everything that's happening is the fault of Gil Marín, Atletico Madrid's CEO, who publicly asked them to say they wanted to leave Atletico.

"For their part, Atletico Madrid argues that Julian already knew how Atletico played under Diego Simeone when he signed for the club, that he knew what contract he was signing and what its clause was, and they deny that Atletico told him he could leave for a direct rival.

"We are waiting to see how events unfold regarding Julian, waiting to see how Arsenal reacts, and if they have genuine interest in the Argentina player. Atletico Madrid will not sell to Barcelona.

"Our information today is that the Julian Alvarez situation has become very tense, and according to several reliable sources, right now, in this crucial week, there are only two paths: stay at Atletico Madrid to fulfil his contract or listen to Arsenal's offer and sign for the London club. Julian will have to make his decision."

Sports.title: Liverpool hold fresh Barcola talks with PSG
Sports.content:
Liverpool are holding further talks with Paris Saint-Germain on Tuesday for Bradley Barcola.

There has been a gap in valuation between the two clubs throughout the summer, with PSG asking for around £145m for the France international.

However, those discussions have been described as positive and there is optimism that a deal can be struck.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Sam Blitz explains the four things Liverpool fans should know about transfer target Bradley Barcola

Sky Sports News understands there are good relations between the two clubs at the highest level. It is hoped this will help Liverpool and PSG reach an agreement.

Liverpool have also explored a move for Barcola's team-mate, Ibrahim Mbaye, who plays off the right wing.

The Premier League club's priority throughout this window has been to reinforce in wide areas.

They have been pursuing Barcola and Mbaye, while Brighton have also rejected two Liverpool offers for Yankuba Minteh, the latest being £60m.

Liverpool are currently the only club chasing Barcola, who has entered the final two years of his deal and has grown dissatisfied with his role at the European champions.

Liverpool, meanwhile, do not want to sell Cody Gakpo amid interest from Tottenham and Manchester City and would likely need two new wingers in before considering letting the Netherlands international go.

Sports.title: Forest agree club-record deal for Chelsea's Delap
Sports.content:
Nottingham Forest have agreed a club-record £50m deal to sign Liam Delap from Chelsea.

The transfer is understood to be worth at least £45m, which could reach £50m with add-ons.

The striker is scheduled to have a medical on Wednesday.

Delap had interest from a number of other Premier League clubs, including Everton, but Forest have secured his signing.

Chelsea signed Delap last summer for £30m from Ipswich and valued him at around £50m this summer.

They could be set for a £20m profit on a striker who scored two goals in 41 appearances last season.

Forest's previous record transfer saw Omari Hutchison join for £37.5m from Ipswich Town in August 2025.

Image: Delap joined Chelsea last summer from Ipswich

Forest are bringing in Delap to improve their striking options following Taiwo Awoniyi's £9m move to Coventry.

Oliver Glasner's side have been pursuing Tottenham midfielder Lucas Bergvall as an Elliot Anderson replacement, but Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi insists he is staying in north London.

Forest could also add a right wing-back, with Dodo at Fiorentina a player of interest.

Dilane Bakwa is set to join Lille on loan, while centre-backs Zach Abbott and Tyler Bindon could also depart on temporary moves amid interest from Watford.

Sports.title: Man Utd complete Baleba signing
Sports.content:
Manchester United have completed the signing of midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton.

The Cameroon international, 22, joins the club in a deal worth up to £70m, made up of a £65m guaranteed fee plus £5m in add-ons.

He has signed a five-year contract which includes the option of a further year.

Baleba is currently injured, having picked up an ankle injury in pre-season, but Sky Sports News understands he could be back by mid-September. Manchester United play Manchester City on September 13, live on Sky Sports.

Baleba's arrival at Old Trafford brings an end to a transfer saga that has lasted almost 12 months. Sky Sports News has been reporting on United's interest in Baleba since last autumn and broke the news that they enquired about signing him during the January transfer window.

He remained one of United's top targets this summer and becomes their third addition in midfield after Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans.

"It is an incredible feeling to join the club of my dreams. Playing at Old Trafford is always special but the opportunity to do so as a Manchester United player will be a real honour," Baleba told the club's website.

"I cannot wait to work with Michael Carrick; his experience and knowledge of the game make him the perfect coach to help me reach the highest level.

"The ambition of everyone at the club is extremely clear, the future is hugely exciting, and I am determined to play my part in delivering the success that we are capable of together."

Baleba joined Brighton from Lille in 2023 and made 112 appearances for the club. He featured 35 times last season and was absent for a spell while representing Cameroon at the Africa Cup of Nations.

But Brighton's reported £100m-plus valuation proved a stumbling block. The move never materialised and Baleba stayed at the Amex.

His form subsequently dipped dramatically. His numbers fell and, at times, he looked a shadow of the midfielder who had generated so much excitement the previous season.

That makes this a gamble for United. But, stylistically, there are few midfielders better suited to what they need.

Image: Baleba was among the league's leading defensive midfielders during the 2024/25 season - can he revive that form?

United require greater authority in the middle of the pitch and, crucially, someone capable of winning the ball back in deeper areas. Baleba brings exactly that. His athleticism, aggression and ability to carry the ball through midfield would add a level of dynamism and steel that is currently missing.

Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans have been astute additions, but Baleba offers something different: specialist defensive power coupled with the athleticism to drive United up the pitch.

His age is another major factor. Baleba is still only 22 and, despite his inconsistent season, there remains a belief around him that he can develop into one of the world's best midfielders.

That ambition is reflected in his influences. Baleba has spoken of his admiration for Paul Pogba, Yaya Toure and Andres Iniesta, while Neymar and Ronaldinho were among his favourite players to watch. There is a desire for self-expression in his game that goes beyond the physical qualities that made so highly rated.

There is risk attached to signing him. United would be betting on the player Baleba can become rather than simply the one he has been over the past 12 months.

But if United want to find a midfielder capable of growing into one of the best in his position, this is exactly the sort of gamble they should be willing to take.

Sports.title: Manchester United confirm Carlos Baleba signing as midfield spend nears £150m
Sports.content:
Manchester United have completed the signing of the Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba in a deal worth up to £70m. The Cameroon international is the third midfielder to join this summer, after Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans.

Baleba has signed a five-year contract with the option to extend for 12 months after United agreed a £65m deal plus £5m in add-ons and a sell-on with Brighton. It takes the club’s spend on midfielders to about £148m.

Santos and Tielemans have arrived from Chelsea and Aston Villa respectively during a summer when Casemiro left and Manuel Ugarte sustained a serious knee injury.

“It is an incredible feeling to join the club of my dreams,” Baleba said. “Playing at Old Trafford is always special but the opportunity to do so as a Manchester United player will be a real honour.

“I cannot wait to work with Michael Carrick. His experience and knowledge of the game make him the perfect coach to help me to reach the highest level.

“The ambition of everyone at the club is extremely clear, the future is hugely exciting, and I am determined to play my part in delivering the success that we are capable of together.”

United made a move to bring in Baleba last summer but cooled their pursuit when Brighton made it clear he was not leaving. Baleba was not at his best last season but that did not put off United, who stepped up their interest in the 22-year-old a week ago.

United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, said: “Carlos is an elite midfielder with immense potential to develop further. He brings a unique combination of qualities that will really complement our squad.
