World.title: Not Ready for Summer to End? 3 Places to Take the Kids Before August Ends
World.content:
The end of the summer holidays is in sight. While school supplies, pencil cases and sports shoes are already making their way onto shopping lists, there are still a few days of summer left to enjoy.

Before the September school routine kicks in, here are three ways to make the most of the final days of August with the family.



Letni Letna

When: 12–31 August

Where: Prague, Letenské sady

Letenské sady is taking on a new look until 31 August, transforming into a colourful festival village. The Letní Letná Festival isn’t just about evening acrobatics for adults. It also offers a programme for younger visitors called Letní Letná for Children.

From morning until late afternoon, the huge children’s tent comes alive with fairy-tale performances and other activities. Kids can take part in creative and juggling workshops, explore an interactive play area made from recycled materials or take a ride on the iconic hand-carved wooden carousel.

Most of the children’s activities take place under the festival tents, so an unexpected rain shower won’t disrupt the day.

The festival also offers a “Night Watch” childcare service for children aged four and up. Parents can enjoy the evening programme while experienced entertainers look after their children.

When: 24–29 August

Where: Liberec and the surrounding area

Fancy a trip beyond Prague at the end of August? Head north to Liberec from 24 to 29 August, when the city hosts Crystal Valley Week, a celebration of Czech glassmaking and jewellery.

This year’s theme focuses on the interconnection of cultures, with the Czech glass bead at the centre of the programme. Children can also enjoy a free ride aboard the special Crystal Tram, which has been decorated this year to resemble a long-distance train.

There are plenty of opportunities to make your own jewellery from glass beads, with workshops and craft sessions taking place throughout Liberec for both children and adults.

When: Sunday, 30 August, 11:00–19:00

Where: Prague, Ladronka Park

On the last Sunday of the summer holidays, skip cooking lunch and head to the F.O.O.D. Picnic in Prague’s Ladronka Park. The popular event returns for its 16th edition this year.

Entry to the festival grounds is free, with 120 food and farm stalls to explore, including food trucks. There is also a large children’s zone with games and creative workshops, as well as a raffle for younger visitors.

It’s a family-friendly way to spend the final Sunday of the holidays, combining food, activities and a relaxed atmosphere before the new school year begins.

World.title: Airbnb Accounts for 1 Percent of Prague’s Housing Stock, Analysis Finds
World.content:
Prague’s short-term rental market has grown into a professional business but Airbnb accounts for only a small share of the city’s housing stock, according to a new analysis.

In June 2026, around 7,878 entire apartments and houses in Prague were actively listed on Airbnb. With roughly 720,000 apartments across the capital, that represents about 1.1 percent of the total housing stock.

The situation is very different in individual parts of the city. In Prague 1, Airbnb-listed properties account for around one-fifth of all apartments, according to the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR). In Prague 2, the share is around 7 percent, while in some outer districts it is below 0.5 percent.



The concentration of short-term rentals has also changed the nature of the market. IPR data show that hosts managed an average of two apartments in 2019. By 2024, that figure had risen to three, while more than half of Prague’s Airbnb listings were operated by hosts with at least five properties.

This means short-term accommodation is increasingly being run as a business rather than as occasional home-sharing.

Prague’s housing shortage is much larger

Despite the impact Airbnb can have in central neighborhoods, the analysis points to a much bigger problem behind Prague’s housing crisis — a long-term shortage of new construction.

Since 2006, Prague has accumulated a housing deficit of more than 91,000 apartments, according to the analysis. That shortfall is about 11.5 times larger than the number of apartments currently listed on Airbnb.

Even if every Airbnb property in the city were suddenly returned to the long-term rental market, Prague would still be short more than 83,000 homes.

The accumulated construction deficit reportedly became larger than the number of active Airbnb apartments around 2009 or 2010. Since then, the gap has continued to grow.

This suggests that Prague’s housing crisis began well before short-term rentals reached their current scale.

Tourism brings other concerns

Housing availability is also not the only issue surrounding short-term rentals.

Residents in central Prague have complained about noise, disruption and visitors staying in residential buildings.

The city also collects accommodation fees from short-term stays, although payment is not automatic because apartment owners must register and pay the fees themselves.

The debate over Airbnb in Prague therefore extends beyond housing. While short-term rentals can change the character of central neighborhoods and create problems for residents, the latest figures suggest that the city’s wider housing shortage is primarily the result of years of insufficient construction.

World.title: ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival Returns to Prague for Its Fifth Edition
World.content:
The ASEAN Committee in Prague (ACP), representing the embassies of ASEAN member states, together with the embassies of China, Japan and the Republic of Korea, will host the fifth edition of the ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival (APTFF).

The festival will begin on Monday, September 7, 2026, at the Municipal Library of Prague.

Organised in cooperation with the Municipal Library of Prague, the festival will run until September 14 and feature seven full-length films, alongside a curated selection of short films from across the ASEAN Plus Three region.



Since its launch in 2022, the APTFF has introduced Czech audiences to the diverse cultures and cinematic voices of ASEAN and its Plus Three partners.

Previous editions have featured acclaimed films including Escape from Mogadishu (Republic of Korea), Father and Son (Viet Nam) and Yuni (Indonesia).

This year’s programme includes Solata: Friends Are the Family We Choose (Indonesia), Babah (Malaysia), The Beginning (Myanmar), I’m Perfect (the Philippines), 4 Tigers (Thailand), Song of the South (Viet Nam) and One and Only (China).

A selection of short films will also be screened during the opening night on September 7.

The programme includes Mbiyodo/Communal Work (Indonesia), Ninavau (Malaysia), Myanmar Be Enchanted (Myanmar), Lola Loleng/Grandma Loleng (the Philippines), Give to Getters (Thailand), Welcome to Viet Nam (Viet Nam), My Chinese Ecological Notes (China), Pukkulapottas and Hours in the Forest (Japan), and Persona (Republic of Korea).

Beyond its cultural programme, the festival is part of a broader effort by ASEAN and its Plus Three partners to introduce Czech audiences to the region, its societies and creative industries, as well as its shared identity as a community of more than 690 million people.

All screenings are open to the public and free of charge. Films will be shown in their original languages with English and Czech subtitles.

The full programme and schedule are available on the Municipal Library of Prague website.

World.title: GALLERY: Light Installation “Synapse” Coming to Florenc Metro Station
World.content:
Jan Poš light installation Synapse will go on display in the Florenc Line C metro passage at the end of September.

The artwork will track passengers’ movements and complement the existing Battle of Sokolovo mosaic. Prague city councillors approved around CZK 1.38 million in funding to complete and install the artwork.

“Synapse” is a light-based installation by visual artist Jan Poš (1996) and the winning entry in the “Light for the Metro” competition held in 2023.



The aim was to create a light artwork for the passage connecting the north and south concourses of Florenc metro station. A total of 23 artists and teams submitted proposals, with four advancing to the final stage, which was conducted as a competitive dialogue.

The five-member jury considered the artwork’s long-term maintenance and its ability to withstand demanding operating conditions.

According to Poš, the artwork, installed on the wall opposite the underpass’s main staircase, comes into view as metro passengers ascend or descend the stairs.

It becomes part of their daily journey while remaining elegantly set apart, creating a space where it can stand on its own and offer a moment of respite from the hustle and bustle.

Poš says the work’s format and style enliven and build on the Battle of Sokolovo mosaic, creating a bridge between the past and present of the city.

The artwork was originally due to be installed alongside the completion of the reconstruction of the station’s ceiling slab. Prague’s public transport operator, DPP, has been repairing the structure since 2022 due to corrosion.

World.title: Partial Lunar Eclipse to Be Visible From Prague at Dawn on August 28
World.content:
Prague residents willing to get up early on Friday, August 28, will have a chance to witness a partial lunar eclipse, with almost the entire Moon passing into Earth’s shadow shortly before it sets.

The eclipse will reach its maximum at 6:12 a.m. CEST. By then, only a narrow section along the Moon’s northern edge will remain illuminated.

In Prague, the Moon is expected to set at approximately 6:17 a.m., leaving only a few minutes to observe the eclipse at its peak.



The partial phase will begin at 4:33 a.m. As the event progresses, Earth’s shadow will gradually cover the lunar surface, reducing the bright portion of the Moon until only a thin illuminated crescent remains visible.

Astronomers at the Silesian University in Opava say observers will need an unobstructed view towards the southwest, as the Moon will be low above the horizon throughout the most important part of the event.

The eclipse follows another major astronomical event visible from the Czech Republic earlier this month, giving skywatchers a second opportunity to observe a rare celestial phenomenon within a short period.

Unlike a solar eclipse, observing the Moon does not require protective eyewear. The eclipse can be seen with the naked eye, while binoculars or a camera may provide a closer view.

For the best chance of seeing the maximum phase, observers should choose a location with a clear southwestern horizon and arrive before dawn. Weather conditions will also play a decisive role in whether the eclipse is visible.

World.title: September 19: Prague Hosts Indian Festival of Music, Food, and Community
World.content:
Prague will host its annual celebration of Indian culture, Ganeshotsav, on Saturday, September 19, at Kulturní dům Ládví.

Ganeshotsav, the festival honoring Lord Ganesha, is more than a celebration of Indian culture—it’s a way to bring people together.

Since 2021, the festival has grown into a space where Indian and Czech communities can meet, connect, and enjoy shared traditions.

The event is organised by Maharashtra Mandal, Czech Republic, a registered non-profit dedicated to promoting friendship and understanding between Indian and Czech residents.

The festival features traditional Indian rituals, music, dance, and food, and welcomes everyone to join in the fun.

Like last year, this year, the festival adds a charitable aspect: part of the registration fees will go to support non-profits in the Czech Republic.

“With this initiative, we want to contribute to the development of communities both in our country of origin and in the country that is now our home,” says the organizers to Prague Morning.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Maharashtra Mandal Czech Republic (@maharashtramandalczechrepublic)

By partnering with like-minded organisations, the festival encourages intercultural dialogue, mutual respect, and connections between diverse communities living in the Czech Republic.

Like last year, organizers will support small entrepreneurs from the Indian community who will present the diversity of Indian cuisine.

The project is called “”Our Annapoorna -The Taste of Every Indian Household”, and will offer visitors a diverse selection of traditional dishes from different corners of India.

The cultural program, featuring music, dance, and traditional rituals, will run from 5:00 PM to 8:30 PM

World.title: A Multi-Brand K-Beauty Pop-Up Is Coming to Prague This September
World.content:
A Korean beauty pop-up will bring eight K-beauty brands and K-pop entertainment to Prague’s Vltava River this September.

The HARUNARU K-Beauty Pop-up will take place aboard KVASOUL, a self-brewing boat restaurant, from September 4 to 8.



An industry preview for beauty professionals and influencers will be held on September 3.

Visitors will be able to discover, test and buy products from eight Korean brands, including GASH, ranked No. 1 at Olive Young, South Korea’s leading beauty retailer, and ilso, known for its pore-care products.

The event will also feature K-pop performances, a Random Dance Challenge, an idol-style makeup show and a dedicated selection of K-pop albums and merchandise.

The pop-up is aimed at introducing emerging Korean beauty brands to consumers and industry professionals in the Czech Republic and across Central and Eastern Europe.

Entry is free, although visitors are encouraged to register online in advance.

The event is organized by Bramasole Prague s.r.o., which operates several Korean restaurant brands in Prague.

World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Photos: another popular Hungarian lake dries out, Bölömbika lookout shows critical conditions
World.content:
The water level of yet another Hungarian lake has fallen to a critical low, meaning visitors to the Bölömbika lookout, which has seen better days, are now confronted with a dispiriting scene of environmental devastation rather than spectacular views and abundant wildlife. Check out the latest photos in our article below.

Photo: Facebook/Madárpart Túraközpont, Kölcsönző és Kemping Photo: Facebook/Madárpart Túraközpont, Kölcsönző és Kemping

Nature horror from Hungarian lake lookout

Nature lovers visiting one of the Tisza Lake’s best-known attractions, the Bölömbika lookout, have recently been met with a deeply disappointing sight. The landscape around the lookout has changed dramatically: areas once covered by water are now dry lakebed, leaving the structure effectively standing on dry land.

The transformation is particularly striking in new photographs taken by the Madárpart Hiking Centre, Rental Service and Campsite. From the images, it is difficult to imagine that the lookout was once surrounded by water. The present condition of the landscape illustrates the dramatic consequences of the Tisza Lake’s water level falling to an exceptionally low point.

The situation is even more pronounced in the Tiszavalk Basin. The area has almost completely dried out, while the lake itself is registering an unusually low water level. Not only has the familiar landscape disappeared; the conditions that once made the area attractive to hikers and water-sports enthusiasts have also been severely compromised.

Historic drought, drying rivers and vanishing lakes

Hungary is enduring a historic drought, with water levels in its lakes, rivers and streams repeatedly falling to record lows. Lake Velence, once renowned for its thriving tourism, sporting events and festivals, is now in its final throes. Even at Lake Balaton, Hungary’s so-called “sea”, swimmers must walk a considerable distance before reaching water deep enough for a swim.

The Danube’s level was so low in July that the Paks nuclear power plant had to be almost entirely shut down. A submerged weir was subsequently built to raise the water level and ensure that sufficient cooling water could be drawn from the river during periods of extreme low flow such as the present one.

The Tisza is also exceptionally low, while one of its tributaries, the Zagyva, has dried up altogether. The same has happened to the Tarna, the Galga, the Bózsva stream, the Morgó stream, the Tápió and the Hajta. Lake Kolon, a strictly protected habitat in the Kiskunság region, had already dried out by the beginning of summer, as had Lake Bicsérd in Transdanubia and Lake Kocs in the Balaton Uplands.

If you missed: Invasive mosquito species conquering Hungary – climate change destroys our echosystem?

Not just a Hungarian problem

Lake Öreg in Tata, like the Tisza Lake, is experiencing exceptionally low water levels; the same is true of Lake Balaton and Lake Velence. The extreme conditions require swift action from the Government, as forecasts suggest that summers in Hungary will remain hot and dry as climate change and global warming intensify.

The exceptionally dry summer is not a uniquely Hungarian phenomenon. Its consequences are being felt across every area of life, from agriculture and tourism to energy production. Romania was forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because of the Danube’s exceptionally low level, while in Italy the Isonzo – a river familiar from the battles of the First World War – has dried up.

Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan

World.title: House price growth eased in Hungary – here are the latest prices
World.content:
House price growth eased in July, with the gap between average prices per square metre reaching as much as tenfold across the country, property website ingatlan.com told Hungary’s MTI news agency on Tuesday.

House price growth eased in Hungary

Monthly price growth slowed to 0.1 per cent, while the annual increase fell to 11.9 per cent. In Budapest, prices rose by 0.9 per cent compared with the previous month, although ingatlan.com said this may have represented a correction following June’s 0.1 per cent decline, MTI wrote.

According to the company’s house price index, Budapest property prices were 8.3 per cent higher than a year earlier, despite a substantial increase in supply.

The number of newly built homes listed for sale in the capital rose from 3,742 a year ago to 5,381 this year, ingatlan.com said. The median price per square metre for second-hand homes in Budapest ranges from HUF 942,000 to HUF 2 million, while prices for newly built properties in the most expensive districts are approaching HUF 3 million per square metre.

Regional differences

The housing market presented a mixed picture nationwide. Pest County stood out with a monthly price increase of 1.2 per cent in July, while the Southern Great Plain recorded a 2.9 per cent decline.

Debrecen had the country’s highest median price for second-hand homes among regional centres, at HUF 1.04 million per square metre. Szeged and Székesfehérvár were also approaching the HUF 1 million mark. Salgótarján was the cheapest county seat, with a median price of HUF 312,000 per square metre.

If you missed – Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

Debrecen also led the expansion in the supply of newly built homes, with listings nearly doubling. Across the main provincial cities, supply increased by an average of close to 50 per cent.

The estate agency said current trends pointed to annual house price growth of less than 10 per cent this year. The last time prices rose at such a modest rate was in 2016.

World.title: How Hungary’s former Chief of the General Staff squandered taxpayers’ money – and must remain silent about it
World.content:
Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi served as the Hungarian Defence Forces Chief of the General Staff for one year and 328 days. During that period, one of the companies owned by the Defence Ministry, HM EI Zrt, spent around HUF 1 billion converting a luxury official residence in Dunakeszi, under the authority of Defence Minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky. The parties remember differently who requested what, and precisely for what purpose. But Gábor Böröndi, who succeeded Ruszin-Szendi as Chief of the Defence Staff, did not move into the property. Instead, another house was rented for him elsewhere – at considerable expense.

From one luxury property to another

A curious housing decision emerges from General Böröndi’s three-year tenure. Although the luxury property in Dunakeszi had been created specifically for the serving Chief of the General Staff, and was available to him, he did not move in. Instead, the Defence Ministry rented him another luxury property in Szentendre.

One of the ministry’s companies, the aforementioned HM EI Zrt, paid EUR 2,890 a month for the rental. Between August 2023 and May 2026, this amounted to a cost of roughly HUF 36 million to the state, depending on exchange-rate fluctuations. As a rented property, however, the house never became state property.

Gábor Böröndi is no longer Hungary’s Chief of General Staff, but he remained a reservist in the rank of colonel general. Photo: Facebook/Magyar Honvédség

The Szentendre property was no ordinary home, either. It is a three-storey family house measuring 386 square metres, set on a plot of almost 1,200 square metres. It includes, among other things, a wellness area, a jacuzzi, a sauna and a three-car garage. It is currently being offered for sale for HUF 275 million. To see what the property looks like, click here.

No one knows who wanted the luxury

The case is particularly striking because the official villa in Dunakeszi was left empty. More than HUF 1 billion had previously been spent on the property. According to an earlier report by the Government Control Office, merely maintaining the villa cost the state an average of HUF 368,000 a month.

In other words, the ministry was paying to maintain an unoccupied official residence while also covering the rent on another house for Böröndi. The distance between the two towns and Budapest cannot explain the decision, since Dunakeszi lies roughly the same distance to the north as Szentendre does to the south.

One of the most unusual aspects of the affair is that Böröndi himself is not permitted to explain why he did not use the official villa made available to him. Both 24.hu and HVG contacted the former Chief of the General Staff, who is currently a serving soldier in the reserve establishment and may speak publicly only with the Defence Ministry’s permission.

PM Péter Magyar and Minister of Defence Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi. Before, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi served as Hungary’s Chief of the General Staff for almost two years. Photo: Facebook/Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz

The ministry, now led by Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, did not grant that permission. As a result, the man at the centre of the affair is unable to explain why, instead of using the Dunakeszi property that the Hungarian Defence Forces could have provided, another high-value house was rented for him in Szentendre.

The available information therefore suggests that, for three years, the state incurred costs associated with two separate properties: the maintenance of the villa in Dunakeszi and tens of millions of forints in rent for Böröndi’s house in Szentendre.

There is still no answer as to why the second property was needed in place of the official residence. Böröndi himself cannot provide one because the ministry has refused him permission to speak.

A peculiar luxury project

The Dunakeszi property, which remains state-owned, is still empty. According to Ruszin-Szendi, it was fitted out to a luxury standard because it was intended for official and representational purposes, including receiving foreign delegations, as well as serving as the official residence of the serving Chief of the General Staff.

If you missed: Leading candidates for Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office have presented their programmes

He himself lived there with his family for several months. But according to the Government Control Office’s report, he ordered bespoke features for the villa by email, together with his wife, including a custom billiards table, panoramic terraces and a wellness area.

An April article by Átlátszó reported that the decision to undertake the luxury project had not been made by Ruszin-Szendi. Instead, it may have been taken by “either the administrative state secretary of the Prime Minister’s Cabinet Office, the administrative state secretary of the Defence Ministry, or the board of directors of the state-owned HM EI Zrt”.

However, after annulling a final court judgment, Hungary’s Supreme Court did not release the documents requested in connection with the project. The court’s president remains András Zs. Varga, who was appointed by Fidesz and has repeatedly been urged to resign by Péter Magyar.

World.title: Hungarian National Bank cuts base rate again
World.content:
The Monetary Council of the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) decided to cut the central bank base rate by 25bp to 5.50pc at a monthly policy meeting on Tuesday.

The Council also lowered the central bank’s symmetric interest rate corridor by 25bp, bringing the O/N deposit rate to 4.50pc and the O/N collateralised loan rate to 6.50pc.

In a statement released after the meeting, the Council said inflation developments were below the baseline scenario projected in June, while the risk premium on domestic assets had remained stable. “These factors have preserved the Monetary Council’s room to manoeuvre,” they added.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Hungarian National Bank Governor Mihály Varga. Varga remained in position after the government change despite serving as Orbán’s finance minister for more than one and a half decade. Photo: Facebook/Varga Mihály

The Council noted that July inflation had slowed to 1.2pc, below market expectations as well as the forecast in the central bank’s June Inflation report. They added that CPI was set to stay under the 3pc target for the rest of the year and throughout 2027 before returning to the target in H1 2028.

“Looking ahead, Hungary’s risk assessment will be primarily influenced by expectations regarding the fiscal path and the adoption of the euro, as well as the external market environment,” the Council said.

World.title: Gales, hail, showers and thunderstorms are on the way – before the weather takes another turn
World.content:
It will remain very hot in most parts of the country today, but a band of rain moving in from the south-west will reach Hungary, bringing gale-force winds, showers, thunderstorms and, in places, hailstones of up to 2cm in diameter. Another change in the weather will follow.

The darker, the drier. What’s more, extensive and long-lasting rains are not expected in Hungary this week. Photo: Facebook/HungaroMet

Gales, hail, showers and thunderstorms are on the way

According to HungaroMet, an area of high pressure is continuing to shape the exceptionally dry and hot weather over Hungary. Today, however, a band of rain will reach the country’s south-western and southern regions. This will trigger a rapid increase in cloud cover, lower daytime temperatures and bring showers and thunderstorms.

The early hours were refreshingly cool after the past few days, with temperatures remaining below 16C everywhere and falling as low as 8C in some areas. At Zabar, the country’s coldest spot, thermometers showed just 5.3C at dawn.

Weather to take another turn this week

The band of rain arriving from the south-west will provide some variety after the recent spell of monotonous weather. HungaroMet forecasts strong and occasionally storm-force gusts of up to 80 km/h in several areas, together with intense cloud formation and small hailstones measuring around 2cm across, Szeretlek Magyarország wrote.

Rain is coming. Photo: Facebook/HungaroMet

The rain band will move slowly north-eastwards before breaking up, bringing only light rain to Transdanubia. By dawn on Wednesday, even that will have cleared, and temperatures will begin to rise sharply once again. Highs of 34–35C are expected in the days ahead, while another plume of Saharan dust could settle over parts of the country.

It will be very hot again in Hungary. Photo: Anadolu/Piero Cruciatti

The heat will be broken on Saturday by a cold front, bringing scattered showers and thunderstorms.

World.title: PM Magyar presses Hungarian businesses to repay Orbán regime spoils
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar urged businesses that benefited unfairly from contracts awarded under the former Fidesz-KDNP government to repay that money voluntarily in a video message on Facebook on Tuesday.

PM Magyar: “Follow the example of Duna Aszfalt”

“To all of those who, as the anointed of the state, have built up fortunes worth hundreds of billions over the past decade and a half, I have a message: Follow the example of Duna Aszfalt. If public monies went to where they don’t belong, they should be repaid now, voluntarily,” Magyar said.

He warned that later the state would recover those monies anyway, using legal tools. Magyar noted that Duna Aszfalt, a company that won more than HUF 600bn of state contracts in 2018-2020, had decided on Monday to repay early USD 400m of bonds subscribed by the state-owned Magyar Eximbank and Hungarian Development Bank (MFB) to finance a high-risk road project in Africa.

Magyar said the state had reported to authorities more than 20 cases in which public monies exceeding HUF 1,700bn were used inappropriately under the former government. He added that those cases included HUF 640bn of exposure involving a rolling stock order from Egypt and a HUF 360bn state loan for North Macedonia, as well as procurements of alert bracelets for seniors, ambulances, school IT systems and government communications.

Probes and asset recovery

Earlier on Tuesday, he said the foreign ministry had reported a HUF 300bn procurement of ventilators placed during the pandemic under the former head of the portfolio, Péter Szijjártó.

Magyar also highlighted a probe ordered by the government of state contracts with 4iG group as well as efforts to recover assets from public asset management foundations that are not related to higher education. He said that more than HUF 3,000bn had been channelled to the foundations, known by their Hungarian acronym KEKVA, under the Orbán government.

If you missed: Leading candidates for Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office have presented their programmes

Magyar said the government measures to recover the assets had been taken even as the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) was in the process of being set up.

He said the opposition Fidesz could try to obstruct the establishment of the office, “but to no avail”. “They, too, know, just as do Orbán’s relatives, that whatever was taken illegally from the common wealth of the Hungarian people will be recovered by the Hungarian state,” he added.

Hungarian FM Anita Orbán names new ambassadors: historians tapped for Paris and Warsaw

World.title: Leading candidates for Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office have presented their programmes
World.content:
Hungary’s new National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH) is tasked with protecting public assets, investigating suspected misuse of state property and helping recover unlawfully acquired public wealth. The relevant legislation establishing the new body was accepted by the Parliament in July, and the body’s head is to be chosen by the National Assembly this Friday. Then the institution’s charter will be accepted in September, so the work can begin.

Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) is set to start its work soon, but first the Hungarian Parliament must choose its head. There are three top contestants whose hearing took place today in the Hungarian Parliament’s Justice and Constitutional Affairs Committee.

Miklós Ligeti: no witch hunt

The accountability not pursued in 1990 must finally be achieved, Miklós Zoltán Ligeti, the legal director of Transparency International Hungary, told the justice and constitutional affairs committee of parliament on Tuesday during his hearing as a nominee for the head of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH). He added that while asset recovery and accountability must begin, the office itself must be established first.

Miklós Ligeti, one of the candidates for the post of the head of Hungary’s new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Photo: MTI

NVVVH’s mandate will not be limited to the past 16 years. “It is not a NER-purging office,” he said, referring to the moniker “system of national cooperation” of the Orbán regime. A legal procedure cannot be turned into a witch hunt, he added. Ligeti emphasised that the new authority must cooperate with many other bodies in the fight against corruption. Without this, the entire process is doomed to fail, he said.

In response to a question, Ligeti stressed that the primary goal is to restore public trust in the state. On the risk of political retribution, he said he did not see why this office should be feared more than any other authority.

Anna Róza Unger: developing an immune system

The first six-year mandate of the leader of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) will suffice to uncover “what happened in this country”, but the cases are not expected to end in binding sentences within that period, political scientist Anna Róza Unger said before parliament’s judicial and constitutional affairs committee on Tuesday.

Unger, who is vying for the position of head of the NVVH, said the mandate will be enough to launch the procedures “to bring everyone responsible, be it a big man or a small one, a city mouse or a country one, before the court.” This would go for “all who committed it, those who allowed [crimes] to be committed, and for Hungarian society to grasp and learn what had happened so it can never happen again,” she said.

The NVVH will work to map the system that created and operated corruption rather than to unveil concrete cases, she said, “so that the newly forming Hungarian democracy may develop an immune system which, after a period of consolidation, makes re-occurrence impossible,” Unger said.

Nicholas Sárvári: NVVH ‘must become rule of law’

Hungary’s Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) “should become an integral part of the rule of law”, Nicholas Sárvári, the Tisza Party’s nominee to head the new organisation, said in parliament’s judicial committee on Tuesday.

Péter Magyar’s government granted unprecedented powers for the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Photo: Facebook/TISZA Párt

Sárvári noted that the structure of the authority was defined by law, and said that as its head he would “find the right experts for each task”. The candidate suggested that the way public assets had been handled in Hungary in previous years was “unacceptable”, adding that he felt “ashamed as a Hungarian”. Restoring public trust and building transparency will be one of the main tasks of the new authority, he added.

Photo: MTI

If you missed – The Guardian: Hungary is ‘de-Orbánising’ at record speed

Former PM Orbán’s party does not take part in the procedure

The Hungarian Parliament is expected to elect NVVH’s leader on Friday and adopt its charter during the autumn session, with the authority expected to be set up later in the season.

Péter Magyar’s Tisza has a supermajority in the Hungarian Parliament, so it will depend only on their MPs who the head of the new body will be. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes

The Hungarian Civil Liberties Union (TASZ), the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, the K-Monitor Public Benefit Association and the World Federation of Hungarians were represented at the meeting in a consultative capacity. Former government party and main opposition party Fidesz and its ally, KDNP, did not send their MPs to the hearing.

World.title: Hungary’s overpriced Covid ventilator mystery: Why thousands are still gathering dust in warehouses
World.content:
Anita Orbán, the foreign minister, has filed a criminal complaint concerning purchases related to ventilators purchased during the coronavirus pandemic under the previous Orbán government.

Brutal amount of money spent

The complaint concerns purchases made in March and April 2020, worth a total 300 billion forints (EUR 827m) by the previous foreign ministry led by Péter Szijjártó, Orbán said, adding that the purchases had been made outside the public procurement system.

The documents reviewed so far have raised “suspicion of embezzlement causing extreme damage and other crimes … suggesting the responsibility of top management” at the previous ministry, Orbán said, adding that the procurement had mostly targeted ventilators.

Former FM Szijjártó looking at a ventilator. Photo: Facebook/Szijjártó Péter

The ministry has established that its predecessor had “overpurchased“, buying too many equipment, while there was “a significant difference between purchase and producer prices”, she said.

Lack of staff was the bottleneck, not the number of ventilators

The minister noted that an invasive ventilator requires an ICU specialist, a qualified nurse, oxygen supply, and an ICU bed, which at the time of the pandemic limited the number of patients in intensive care to between 800-2,000. “The bottleneck was not the restricted number of ventilators … despite that fact, the decision makers considered the number of ventilators as an indicator of the full capacity,” she said, adding that “at the height of the epidemic only 2,500 ventilators had been sent to the hospitals, the vast majority of the stock is still in a warehouse.”

As for the purchase price of the equipment, the difference from the producer price was 13.4 billion forints in the case of six companies, she said. Quoting press reports, she said the average price of a ventilator was 17 million forints, while producers sold the same models between 1,000 and 5,000 US dollars.

If you missed: The Hungarian government bought Chinese ventilators known to be dangerous

Szijjártó tried to hide important details

According to the minister, the previous ministry had left behind “incomplete documentation” but added that the original documents “could not be fully erased and a lot of them could be restored, which provided a better image of what happened.” She added that her ministry’s staff had managed to restore 130,000 files concerning the procurement.

According to information from the ministry, its predecessor had purchased 16,853 ventilators, protective gear, PCR tests, and medicines in spring 2020, under the previous government’s “special legal order” introduced at the beginning of the pandemic.

World.title: Bucharest International Poetry Festival to take place in September
World.content:
The Bucharest International Poetry Festival (FIPB) is set to bring together poets and artists from around the world between September 14 and 20.

Organized by the Bucharest City Hall through the National Museum of Romanian Literature, this year’s festival proposes the theme “Slow Gun Poetry/Long-Range Poetry,” inspired by poet Cezar Ivănescu’s reflection on the power of a simple sign on a sheet of paper.

According to the organizers, the theme starts from the idea that from a word, ideas, consciences and even revolutions can be born, and that the true strength of the world does not lie in force, but in meaning.

“Poetry is not a form of escape from reality, but one of the most powerful ways of understanding it. At a time when words are increasingly used to separate, radicalize and build walls between people, the Bucharest International Poetry Festival assumes, through this edition, the mission of bringing the word back to its natural space: that of dialogue, freedom, empathy and the meeting between people and cultures,” said Ioan Cristescu, general director of the National Museum of Romanian Literature, cited in the press release.

This year’s edition features guests from the Republic of Armenia, Austria, the Czech Republic, Cyprus, China, Croatia, France, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, the Republic of Moldova, Peru, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Tunisia and Turkey, alongside numerous Romanian poets and artists. More than 50 events are included in the festival program: public readings, debates, conferences, exhibitions, concerts, performances, recitals and commemorative events.

The festival will officially open on Monday, September 14, at 18:00, in the Hall of the “Carol I” Central University Library. The opening ceremony will bring together representatives of partner cultural and diplomatic institutions, as well as ambassadors and representatives of cultural institutes from participating countries.

The evening will continue with a concert performed by the ARCO Chamber Ensemble, public readings by Romanian and international poets, and a reading-performance by Slovenian poet Aleš Šteger, recognized as one of the most original and translated voices in contemporary European literature, accompanied on accordion by Tori Jure.

An important component of this year’s edition of FIPB is dedicated to the memory and recovery of great Romanian poets. The program includes commemorative events dedicated to Cezar Ivănescu, Emil Botta, Constanța Buzea, Angela Marinescu, Marin Sorescu and Magda Isanos, organized in partnership with the Bucharest National Theatre. At the same time, this year’s edition marks 130 years since the birth of Tristan Tzara, founder of the Dada movement, through a workshop dedicated to children and adults, in which poetry meets visual art and calligrams.

Moreover, FIPB will feature programs dedicated to children and teenagers, such as comic book workshops, creative activities, literary games and numerous other projects.

(Photo source: Facebook/Muzeul Naţional al Literaturii Române)

World.title: Romania’s football team to face off against Sweden in Nations League match next month
World.content:
Romania’s national football team is set to play against Sweden on Friday, September 25, within League B of the Nations League. The match will be played in Solna, Sweden, according to an announcement on the official FRF website.

Starting Tuesday, August 25, and until Friday, September 18 (or until they run out), tickets for the game against Sweden will be available on the FRF website. The price of a ticket, set by the organizers of the match, is RON 130, with 2,200 seats in the stadium’s North Stand (sectors 116-121) allocated to the Romanian fans. Each supporter can order a maximum of 4 tickets before completing an order, and the tickets will be nominative.

Group B4 of the Nations League also includes Bosnia-Herzegovina and Poland. After the match with Sweden, the Romanian team will face Bosnia-Herzegovina on September 28, then Poland on October 2.

Rematches will take place on October 5 against Sweden, November 14 against Poland, and November 17 against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

The winner of the group will be promoted to League A of the Nations League, while the team finishing second will play a promotion play-off.

Romania managed to gain promotion to League B in the last edition of the Nations League, after winning the group with six wins in the same number of matches. This performance allowed the national team to reach the play-offs for the 2026 World Cup, although they finished third in their group in the qualifiers.

(Photo source: frf.ro)

World.title: Bucharest included in ranking of cities with highest potential for AI data center development
World.content:
Romania’s capital ranks 21st in the Savills Power and Place Index, the global ranking that assesses cities with the strongest potential for future data center development based on criteria such as energy availability, telecommunications infrastructure, access to resources and project delivery capability.

According to Savills’s report, the next wave of investment in digital infrastructure will increasingly target markets capable of supporting the accelerated expansion of artificial intelligence. The same report showed that global investment in data centers has reached record levels, fueled by the expansion of major hyperscale operators and growing demand driven by artificial intelligence. In this context, the challenge is no longer the availability of capital, but rather identifying locations capable of providing the power, land and infrastructure required for large-scale developments.

Savills highlighted that many established European hubs are already experiencing limitations related to power grid capacity, land availability and permitting processes, creating opportunities for emerging cities and markets with greater resource availability.

According to real estate consultant Crosspoint Real Estate, Romania benefits from several structural advantages relevant to digital infrastructure development. These include a high level of fiber-optic coverage, competitive internet speeds and affordable data service costs, all of which support large-scale data transfer and processing.

At the same time, data consumption continues to grow rapidly both in Romania and across the Central and Eastern European region, driven by the expansion of cloud services, the digitalization of the economy and the integration of artificial intelligence solutions into business operations. This trend is increasing the need for local and regional digital infrastructure and is supporting the development of data centers located closer to end users.

At present, however, one significant disadvantage is the cost of electricity. Nevertheless, with the commissioning of the Iernut and Mintia power plants, as well as the projected development of energy storage facilities in the medium term, Romania could become increasingly attractive for this segment.

“While traditional European hubs are facing increasing constraints related to energy access, land availability and development restrictions, Bucharest is emerging as a well-positioned market for the next wave of investments in digital infrastructure supporting AI development. For data center investors, access to power and connectivity is becoming just as important as location,” said Emilian Podaru, MRICS, Head of Industrial & Logistics at Crosspoint Real Estate, the International Associate of Savills in Romania.

The report estimated that data center expansion will also have a significant impact on the industrial and logistics sector. Across Europe, the growth of this ecosystem could generate additional demand for approximately 790,000 sq m of logistics space over the next three years, required for storage, equipment, operations, and related services.

(Photo source: Katrin Primak|Dreamstime.com)

World.title: “Seaside for Everyone” program aims to attract tourists to Romanian seaside in September
World.content:
The 49th edition of “Seaside for Everyone,” a well-known program that aims to attract tourists to the Romanian seaside through massive price cuts in accommodation, was announced on Tuesday, August 25, by the Federation of Associations of Romanian Tourism Employers (FPTR).

Initiated and coordinated by FPTR and supported through the participation of economic operators on the seaside, “Seaside for Everyone” advances holidays on the seaside at reduced rates for tourists.

The program takes place from September 1-30, 2026.

To date, 67 accommodation units from 10 resorts and tourist areas are enrolled. According to FPTR, a novelty of this year’s edition is the change in the list of participants. 24 of the units currently enrolled did not participate in the spring edition. Among them are units entering the program for the first time, as well as returning operators.

Moreover, compared with the spring edition, when the lowest rate communicated was RON 42/person/night, the current edition starts at RON 39/person/night for accommodation without meals, in Eforie Nord.

The minimum rates communicated by other participating units are RON 39 (EUR 7.43) in Eforie Nord, RON 65 (EUR 12.38) in Eforie Sud, RON 60 (EUR 11.43) in Costinești, RON 58 (EUR 11.05) in Neptun-Olimp, RON 74 (EUR 14.10) in Jupiter, RON 77 (EUR 14.67) in Saturn, RON 108 (EUR 20.57) in Mangalia, RON 80 (EUR 15.24) in Vama Veche, RON 69 (EUR 13.14) in Mamaia, and RON 65 (EUR 12.38) in Mamaia Nord.

The rates, the included services, and participation periods are established by each accommodation unit. Some offers are for accommodation, while others include breakfast or All Inclusive services. The packages can also be paid for with holiday vouchers, under the conditions accepted by each accommodation unit or travel agency.

Although the official period of the program is September 1–30, 2026, some units have submitted offers that continue into October. As such, tourists have more holiday options in the off-season, while operators can maintain their activity for a longer period.

The list of participating units, rates, validity periods and contact details is published on the official website of the Federation of Associations of Romanian Tourism Employers. The list is updated as FPTR receives new registrations.

(Photo source: FPTR on Facebook)

World.title: Romanian MP Claudiu Năsui accepts nomination as Moldova’s economy minister
World.content:
Romanian lawmaker Claudiu Năsui accepted prime minister Vasile Tofan’s invitation to join the Moldovan government as minister of economic development and digitalization. The Save Romania Union (USR) deputy said the move would require him to resign from Romania’s Parliament.

“I have accepted the position of economy minister in the government of the Republic of Moldova,” Năsui announced on Facebook. He said he strongly agreed with Tofan’s vision of turning Moldova into “the most welcoming country for entrepreneurs.”

Claudiu Năsui said he would use his experience to support economic reforms, including the liberalization and privatization process started after the fall of communism. He also linked Moldova’s economic development to its efforts to join the European Union and strengthen ties with Romania.

“I chose to accept Mr. Tofan’s invitation to join the government of the Republic of Moldova, even though this step means giving up my mandate as a member of the Romanian Parliament and dedicating my experience to a new reform effort,” Năsui said.

“A more prosperous Moldovan economy also means a more prosperous Romanian economy as part of our shared European path,” he added.

Vasile Tofan announced that Claudiu Năsui would be proposed for the position of minister of economic development and digitalization, citing his economic education, private-sector experience, and previous involvement in government reforms.

Năsui studied economics at Paris Dauphine University and finance at Bocconi University. He has worked in the financial sector, including at PwC and Romanian bank BCR, and holds the Chartered Financial Analyst certification.

He was first elected to the Romanian Parliament in 2016 and served as Romania’s economy minister between 2020 and 2021. He also founded the Open Budget platform, which tracks public spending.

According to prime minister Tofan, Claudiu Năsui’s priorities in Moldova will include reducing bureaucracy, addressing problems at state-owned companies, cutting public expenditure, and removing obstacles faced by small and medium-sized enterprises.

“We need this type of energy at the Economy Ministry,” Vasile Tofan said. “We want the Economy Ministry to become one of the main drivers of state reform and economic growth.”

The Moldovan prime minister also announced that Eugeniu Osmochescu would be proposed as minister of agriculture and food industry. His responsibilities will include preparing Moldovan agriculture for EU accession and improving the sector’s competitiveness and resilience to climate change.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Facebook/Claudiu Nasui)

World.title: Romanian Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner Fjord draws over 150,000 viewers after French release
World.content:
Fjord, the latest film from Romanian director Cristian Mungiu, attracted more than 150,000 viewers shortly after opening in France on August 19. France is the first of more than 100 territories where the Palme d’Or-winning film is due to receive a theatrical release.

The film ranked first in box-office receipts during both its previews and its official opening day, when it was seen by 30,058 people, including 11,727 in Paris, according to a press release. By the end of its first weekend, it had drawn 140,346 viewers in cinemas, with the Paris audience accounting for 51,847 admissions.

Including preview screenings, Fjord reached a total audience of 151,121 across 270 cinemas. Its distribution is expanding to 290 screens this week.

“Based on the ratio between its first-day box-office revenue and final audience figures, Fjord could attract more than 800,000 viewers in France,” reads the announcement.

The film is distributed in France by Le Pacte, which has handled all of Cristian Mungiu’s films since 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days. The latter, which won the filmmaker his first Palme d’Or in 2007, attracted around 380,000 viewers in France.

The release figures place Fjord ahead of the opening-day performance of some other recent Palme d’Or winners. Jafar Panahi’s It Was Just an Accident, the 2025 winner, debuted with 20,000 viewers and eventually reached 700,000 admissions, while Sean Baker’s Anora opened at a level close to Fjord and finished with 654,000 viewers.

Cristian Mungiu’s film won the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival in May, along with the FIPRESCI Prize, the Citizenship Prize, the François Chalais Prize, and the Ecumenical Jury Prize.

Fjord was also shown to 43,440 viewers in Romania during a one-off screening on June 13. Distribution also began in French-speaking Switzerland in August, with releases scheduled for September in Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Greece, Italy, and Belgium.

Fjord tells the story of Lisbet and Mihai Gheorghiu, a married couple who move to a small village on a Norwegian fjord. They soon befriend their neighbors, the Halberg family, while the children of the two households grow close despite differences in upbringing and values. The cast includes Sebastian Stan, Renate Reinsve, Adrian Titieni, Alin Panc, Giulia Nahmany, and Ana Bodea.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Mobra Films PR)

World.title: Center-right European groups EPP, Renew ask EC to withhold PNRR funds to Romania over integrity law
World.content:
The leaders of the center-right European People’s Party (EPP) and Renew Europe, two of the most important groups in the European Parliament, publicly asked the European Commission on Monday, August 24, to withhold EUR 770 million in PNRR funds meant for Romania due to the “Fritz amendment.” Their plea concerns the retroactive application of a new integrity law that would invalidate the mandate of Timisoara mayor Dominic Fritz.

EPP president Manfred Weber and Renew group leader Valérie Hayer both signed a letter shared by POLITICO asking Commission president Ursula von der Leyen to make it clear that the money will not be granted unless Bucharest abandons plans to amend a law that could lead to Save Romania Union (USR) party leader Dominic Fritz being banned from holding the office of mayor.

Weber and Hayer also argued that retroactive application violates EU legislation and Romania’s Constitution and accused the Romanian Social Democrats of deliberately targeting Fritz. “Under the guise of fulfilling a reform milestone for the Recovery and Resilience Facility, the Romanian Parliament has introduced a measure that directly violates Union law and constitutes a serious setback for the rule of law in Romania,” they said in the letter.

"European taxpayers’ money must never become a blank check for political power games,” Hayer told POLITICO. Weber added that “if legislation is designed to remove a political opponent, and EU funds are used as leverage to enforce it, this is no longer just politics - it is a rule-of-law issue.”

In the letter, they also urged the Commission to send “a signal” before Romanian president Nicușor Dan promulgates the law and before the August 31 deadline for the reforms that would allow access to EU funds.

The Fritz amendment

Earlier this month, in a 5-3 vote, the Romanian Constitutional Court approved the so-called “Fritz Amendment,” introduced by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) into the law governing the National Integrity Agency (ANI). The same law is a PNRR milestone with EUR 770 million attached to it.

The controversial amendment stipulates that elected officials in office lose their mandate within 30 days if they receive a final decision of incompatibility or conflict of interest, even if this decision predates the new law. This means that the law would apply retroactively. In June, Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Timișoara Court of Appeal ruling that found Dominic Fritz in an administrative conflict of interest.

As such, under the amendment, Fritz is expected to lose his position as mayor of Timișoara within 30 days of the legislation entering into force. The USR leader announced that he will challenge the decision at the European Court of Human Rights, and argued that the measure applies to a past action, although the Romanian Constitution states that laws should apply only to the future.

On course for adoption

After it was declared constitutional, the amended law was returned to Parliament and was adopted by the Chamber of Deputies with the votes of PSD, the National Liberal Party (PNL), and the minority Hungarian party UDMR. It still has to pass the Senate on Wednesday, August 26, and then go to president Nicusor Dan, who previously criticized the same "Fritz amendment," for promulgation before becoming law.

The supporters of the amended bill said its adoption secures EU funding, despite the retroactive application.

"For those who vote to violate the rule of law for fear of losing money from the PNRR: I am sure the European Commission will not accept rewarding such an abusive monstrosity with European taxpayers’ money," Fritz said on Facebook, in reaction to the bill's passing of the Chamber of Deputies.

Since the CCR decision, Fritz was also reconfirmed as leader of USR, which is part of the Renew Europe group in the European Parliament.

World.title: Romania’s Patria Bank accelerates lending in Q2 2026, loan portfolio nears RON 3 billion
World.content:
Patria Bank (BVB: PBK), a major Romanian bank listed on the Regulated Market of the Bucharest Stock Exchange, ended the first half of 2026 with a total performing loan portfolio of nearly RON 3 billion, up approximately 12% compared to June 30, 2025.

According to the bank, the evolution was supported by the acceleration of commercial activity in the second quarter across both the legal entities and retail segments.

As of June 30, 2026, the portfolio of performing loans granted to legal entities reached RON 2.40 billion, up 9% compared to the end of 2025 and 13% compared to the same period of the previous year.

The volume of new loans granted to corporate clients accelerated significantly in the second quarter, reaching RON 466 million, 44% above the level recorded in Q2 2025 and 67% higher than in the first quarter of 2026. For the first half of the year as a whole, the volume of new loans granted to corporate clients reached RON 746 million, up 2% compared to the same period of the previous year.

“Our ambition is to become an increasingly relevant bank for the clients we serve and to turn every financing granted into a long-term relationship that evolves alongside their needs,” stated Valentin Vancea, General Manager of Patria Bank.

The Agro segment recorded the fastest growth in the first half of the year, with the performing loan portfolio reaching RON 523 million, 29% above the level recorded as of December 31, 2025. New loan sales in this segment reached RON 224 million, up 35% compared to H1 2025, driven by farmers’ seasonal working capital needs and interest in projects supported by European funds. At the same time, the Bank continued its diversification towards the financing of the food industry, where financing for clients advanced 67% compared to the first half of 2025.

The Micro segment portfolio reached RON 434 million, up 3% compared to the end of 2025. New loan sales in the first half of the year reached RON 114 million, below the high base recorded in the same period of the previous year. The bank expects activity in this segment to record a positive evolution in the coming quarters, supported by adjustments to the analysis flow for financing requirements.

Across the SME and Corporate segments, the performing loan portfolio increased by 4% compared to the end of 2025, reaching RON 1.44 billion. This evolution was mainly driven by the Corporate component, which advanced by 14% in the first six months of the year. The two segments generated new financing of RON 408 million, with a strong recovery in the second quarter.

In the retail segment, the total balance of performing retail loans reached RON 584 million at the end of June, up 9% compared to the same period of the previous year. Unsecured loans remained the main growth driver of the retail portfolio, advancing by 16% to RON 275 million. This evolution was supported by sustained demand for consumer loans and credit cards, as well as by the increasing share of sales generated through digital channels, including the Patria de Oriunde platform. The balance of secured loans also returned to growth, reaching RON 309 million, 3% above the level recorded as of June 30, 2025.

New retail loan sales reached RON 138 million in the first half of the year, up 8.5% compared to H1 2025. Of this volume, RON 80 million was granted in the second quarter, 19% above the same period of the previous year. Sales of secured loans increased by 32% in the first half of the year, reaching RON 29 million, while unsecured loans accounted for approximately 79% of the total volume of new retail loans, with sales of RON 109 million.

In terms of commercial financing, corporate commercial financing increased by 17% compared to the end of 2025 and by 31% compared to June 30, 2025, reaching RON 2.20 billion. Commercial financing related to the retail segment reached RON 2.25 billion, 8% above the level recorded one year earlier. Term deposits reached RON 1.91 billion, while the balance of current accounts increased to RON 338 million.

As of the same date, SAI Patria Asset Management had assets under management of RON 1.53 billion, up 78% compared to December 31, 2025 and 177% compared to June 30, 2025. The financial performance of the two entities is not included in Patria Bank’s individual financial results. After the end of the reporting period, on August 5, 2026, Patria Bank completed the sale to BRD Asset Management SAI of its 99.9944% shareholding in SAI Patria Asset Management. As a result, SAI Patria Asset Management is no longer a subsidiary of Patria Bank.
