World.title: Why has Georgia’s government revived debate over Treaty of Georgievsk?
World.content:
In recent days, Georgian government officials have made a series of similar statements about the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the agreement with Russia saved Georgia and the Georgian nation. He argues that it laid the foundations for today’s sovereign state and helped preserve its European prospects.

Several days later, other leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party began speaking about the Treaty of Georgievsk in similar terms. They repeat not only the main conclusion but also the same arguments: Georgia faced the threat of destruction, an agreement with Russia was the only option, and that decision saved the Georgian nation, Christianity and Georgian statehood.

This level of coordination suggests that the discussion has moved beyond a spontaneous debate about history. The positive assessment of the Treaty of Georgievsk sounds more like a unified political message from Georgian Dream.

But what is the purpose of this message?

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement under which eastern Georgia (the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti) came under the protection of the Russian Empire. The parties signed the treaty in the summer of 1783 at the fortress of Georgievsk. The treaty protected Georgia from external threats but ultimately led to the complete loss of its independence.

Opposition figures say the government is preparing the public for a possible new agreement with Russia. Former president Mikheil Saakashvili, who is currently in prison, has even referred to specific draft agreements.

Other political commentators see the renewed focus on the treaty as an attempt to divert attention from important current issues. Against the backdrop of what they describe as the Georgian government’s increasingly pro-Russian course and anti-Western rhetoric, the Treaty of Georgievsk is a particularly sensitive issue for politically active Georgians and can easily provoke a strong reaction.

According to this view, the government deliberately sparked a historical debate to draw attention away from corruption within the administration. At the same time, the authorities have intensified the charges against former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili. His case goes beyond the actions of an individual official and raises questions about the scale of systemic corruption itself.

Russian media have already described Kobakhidze’s remarks as another sign that Tbilisi’s attitude towards Moscow is changing.

So why has a treaty signed 243 years ago suddenly become one of the main topics of Georgia’s current political debate?

What Prime Minister Kobakhidze said

Irakli Kobakhidze has made several statements about the Treaty of Georgievsk. His main argument is that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation.

On 18 August, Kobakhidze described the signing of the treaty as a “civilisational choice”. He said Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose fellow Orthodox Russia.

“The fact that today we are an independent, sovereign state based on traditional European values and traditional European culture is precisely the result of this pragmatic decision taken by Erekle II,” the prime minister said.

Kobakhidze has also argued that Erekle II’s decision was not only justified, but the “only correct and only possible” choice at the time. In his account, Russia honoured the terms of the agreement during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end. Almost 20 years passed between the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country was effectively saved.”

Kobakhidze presented Russia’s abolition of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti as a process that became possible only after the Georgian king’s death: “When Erekle II died, unfortunately, events took a different course.”

Georgian Dream leaders have also drawn parallels between this historical episode and modern Georgian-Russian relations.

Kobakhidze compared the Treaty of Georgievsk with the August 2008 war and said that “under Mikheil Saakashvili’s leadership, all the agreements, whether signed or unsigned, were torn up over our heads.”

Other party leaders have expressed similar views. MP David Matikashvili, for example, called the Treaty of Georgievsk a “smart and wise” decision.

“Ultimately, despite the many negative consequences, Georgia and the Georgian people managed to survive physically. The genius of King Erekle is obvious here,” he said.

More about the Treaty of Georgievsk

The Treaty of Georgievsk was signed in 1783 between the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. It was not an agreement between a united Georgia and Russia. At the time, the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia were not parties to the treaty.

Under the agreement, Kartli-Kakheti came under Russian protection. In return, Russia undertook to protect its territorial integrity and the Bagrationi dynasty.

Historian Beka Kobakhidze strongly disputes Kobakhidze’s claim that Russia honoured the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime. He writes that the period from 1783 until Erekle’s death was instead one of the most difficult periods of his reign.

In 1785, an army led by Avar ruler Omar Khan invaded Kartli-Kakheti. Beka Kobakhidze says Erekle had warned Russia about the planned attack and requested the assistance provided for under the treaty. Russia did not provide it.

Agha Mohammad Khan’s 1795 campaign had even more devastating consequences. After the Battle of Krtsanisi, his forces captured and looted Tbilisi. Thousands of people were killed or taken captive.

Beka Kobakhidze draws on these facts to write:

“Irakli Kobakhidze is falsifying history. The period from 1783 to 1798, from the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk to Erekle’s death, was the most difficult and destructive period of his reign.”

In 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. The Bagrationi royal family lost power, and some of its members were exiled to Russia. The Russian Empire later conquered and annexed the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia as well.

Was Georgia “on the brink of extinction”?

Another key element of Georgian Dream’s new historical narrative concerns demographic survival. The prime minister says the Georgian nation faced a “real threat of extinction” at the end of the 18th century. MP Matikashvili has also referred to the “physical survival” of the Georgian people.

This view is not new. The Russian imperial narrative, and later the Soviet version of history, often portrayed the annexation of Georgia as a painful but necessary step to save the country.

Historian Giorgi Ugulava wrote in a 2025 article for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that this representation was one of the main products of Russian imperial propaganda. The argument was that Georgia could not survive independently and that Russian protection was the best option available.

Why has Erekle II become a political symbol for Georgian Dream?

Georgian Dream’s political campaign around Erekle II began well before August 2026.

In 2023, literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili criticised Erekle II over the Treaty of Georgievsk. Georgian Dream leaders responded with fierce criticism of the scholar. That same year, the pro-Russian Conservative Movement disrupted one of Berdzenishvili’s lectures. He was later attacked in the street.

At the time, Georgian Dream chairman Irakli Kobakhidze said violence was unacceptable. At the same time, however, he accused Berdzenishvili of acting against Georgian identity.

In August 2024, Kobakhidze announced plans to erect a new monument to Erekle II in Tbilisi. The monument opened on 24 September 2025. At the ceremony, Kobakhidze described Erekle II as a symbol of “patriotism”, “love of the homeland” and “pragmatism”.

Kobakhidze also claimed that foreign diplomats had criticised Erekle II during meetings with Georgian Dream representatives. He did not name any of the diplomats or specify which countries they represented. However, according to his account, criticism of Erekle II formed part of coordinated actions by Western diplomats and the Georgian opposition.

Erekle II has therefore gradually evolved from a historical figure into a symbol of the current political confrontation. On one side stands the “pragmatic” king who reached an agreement with Russia. On the other are his critics, whom the government portrays as agents of Western interests.

“A new treaty”: what do pro-Russian forces in Georgia want?

While Georgian Dream highlights the positive historical significance of the old Treaty of Georgievsk, openly operating pro-Russian forces in Georgia are already calling directly for a “new treaty”.

One of the main figures in this campaign is Russian-Georgian citizen Mamuka Pipia, leader of the Solidarity for Peace party.

In July 2025, Pipia called for the signing of a “Treaty of Georgievsk 2” and an alliance treaty with Russia. His proposals included restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and removing Article 78 from Georgia’s Constitution. The article requires constitutional bodies to take all measures to ensure Georgia’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Pipia said: “Given today’s geopolitical situation, Russia and Georgia need to support each other, and they need to formalise an alliance treaty on equal terms.”

In August 2026, Pipia described Kobakhidze’s statements as a success for his own political agenda.

“I am glad that the country’s leadership now recognises the reality that we have been speaking about openly for the past two years,” he said.

Pipia says his idea of a “new Treaty of Georgievsk” means “a completely new, comprehensive and, most importantly, equal treaty with the Russian Federation”.

“We are working in this direction, and Moscow will make an appropriate statement very soon,” he added.

Georgian Dream denies coordinating with pro-Russian groups. However, Pipia’s political network maintains open contacts with Russian officials. He has appeared in public at various times with Russian State Duma deputies and other senior Russian officials.

In May 2025, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who is under US sanctions, was also in Red Square with Pipia. The US Treasury Department has described Partskhaladze as a Georgian-Russian oligarch and said Russia’s FSB used him to influence Georgian society and politics.

How closely do the two narratives align?

Mamuka Pipia’s and Georgian Dream’s ultimate political demands do not currently coincide. Georgian Dream is not officially calling for an alliance treaty with Russia, a “new treaty” or the repeal of Article 78 of the Constitution. This is a significant difference.

However, the similarities in their rhetoric are clear. In both cases, the main arguments for closer relations with Russia are “pragmatism”, peace, security and national interests. In both narratives, the West is increasingly portrayed not as a security partner but as a source of threats or pressure.

The rhetoric around the “deep state” also overlaps. For years, Pipia has spoken about Western forces allegedly trying to use Georgia against Russia. A similar conspiracy theory has become part of Georgian Dream’s official political messaging in recent years.

Now another important element has entered this shared vocabulary: the interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk as an agreement that saved Georgia.

What does the opposition say about a possible new agreement?

Against this backdrop, Georgian opposition figures suspect that the historical debate may serve to prepare public opinion for a more concrete political decision.

Mikheil Saakashvili said that the government was carrying out “ideological preparations for signing a treaty of betrayal”. He claims that Russia has even given ruling-party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili drafts of several agreements.

Saakashvili referred to restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and separate agreements on Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. He also claims that Irakli Kobakhidze is expected to travel to Moscow in the coming weeks.

There is currently no independent confirmation of this information. Neither the Georgian nor the Russian authorities have officially announced preparations for such agreements.

Former diplomat Ghia Japaridze also sees the government’s rhetoric as preparation for possible changes in foreign policy. He says the government is using the Treaty of Georgievsk to “justify a change in Georgia’s foreign policy course”.

What is the Russian media saying?

Irakli Kobakhidze’s statements have also attracted attention in Russia.

On 21 August, the Russian publication Vzglyad published an article headlined “Georgia has taken an important step towards normality”.

The article links several issues: the Georgian government’s campaign against so-called “Russophobia”, accusations against the West and the new interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk.

The publication places particular emphasis on the “restoration of respect for the Treaty of Georgievsk — an alliance with Russia that saved Georgia”.

In other words, what Georgian officials present in Tbilisi as a historical interpretation and an assessment of Erekle II’s decision is already being read by Russian media as a sign of changing political attitudes towards modern Russia.

A day earlier, even more far-reaching claims circulated in Russian Telegram channels. INSIDER-T, citing unofficial sources, claimed that Tbilisi had offered Moscow a behind-the-scenes deal: “full geopolitical loyalty” from Georgia in exchange for Russia publicly abandoning the annexation of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

These claims are also not supported by reliable evidence.

What matters, however, is the political expectations now emerging in the Russian information space in response to statements by Georgian officials.

A historical dispute or an ongoing political process?

There is currently no publicly confirmed evidence that the Georgian authorities are preparing to sign a “New Treaty of Georgievsk” or another alliance agreement with Russia.

However, it is difficult to describe what is happening as merely a dispute among historians.

On one side is a government that has sharply worsened relations with Georgia’s main Western partners in recent years and has effectively frozen the country’s EU accession process.

On the other are pro-Russian groups openly calling for a political alliance and security ties with Russia. They see the prime minister’s new rhetoric as a victory for their position.

This is accompanied by the reaction of the Russian information space, where Georgian government statements are increasingly seen as a sign that Tbilisi is turning towards the Kremlin.

Against this backdrop, the significance of the Treaty of Georgievsk is no longer confined to the 18th century. The key question now is why the government needs to convince the public that a historical agreement with Russia, which ultimately led to the annexation of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, saved Georgia.

And, more importantly, what modern political choice might this version of history be intended to justify?

Debate over the Treaty of Georgievsk in Georgia

World.title: 750,000 lari bribe and other new allegations against jailed former Georgian PM who turned against the government
World.content:
Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili

New charges have been brought against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili for accepting a large bribe. The charges came shortly after he published open letters accusing the government of persecuting him to prevent his return to politics.

Garibashvili is already serving a five-year sentence for legalising illicit income. The new charges carry a prison sentence of between 11 and 15 years.

🟥 According to the prosecution, then-defence minister Juansher Burchuladze, who is now in prison, illegally transferred 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Garibashvili in cash in several instalments.

What does the prosecution accuse Garibashvili of?

The case concerns the purchase of medical equipment and supplies for the Defence Ministry. According to the prosecution, the ministry conducted three secret procurement procedures from late 2022 onwards.

At the time, Juansher Burchuladze served as defence minister, while Irakli Garibashvili was prime minister.

According to investigators, Burchuladze and his relative, Vasil Mcheidze, reached an agreement with a local business and offered it an opportunity to take part in government tenders. With their help, the business was supposed to win the tenders and then pay them 10% of the total contract value.

The businessman demanded additional guarantees.

According to the prosecution, Burchuladze then reached an agreement with Irakli Garibashvili, who was serving as prime minister.

Investigators accuse the former prime minister of protecting the scheme and demanding his share of the proceeds.

According to the indictment, deputy defence minister Giorgi Khaindrava and procurement department head Vladimir Gudushauri then created non-competitive conditions. This allowed selected companies to win the tenders at predetermined prices.

The prosecution says the companies supplied the ministry with goods worth 18,484,960 lari (about $7.5 million). However, the actual value of the goods was 11,499,705 lari (about $4.5 million).

The prosecution estimates the damage to the state at 6,985,255 lari (about $2.6 million).

How was the 1.9 million lari divided?

According to the investigation, the businessman ultimately transferred 1.9 million lari (about $730,000) to Vasil Mcheidze in several instalments. The amount represented roughly 10% of the total value of the contracts.

Vasil Mcheidze kept 400,000 lari (about $155,000);

he transferred 1.5 million lari (about $580,000) to Juansher Burchuladze;

Burchuladze kept 750,000 lari (about $290,000);

he transferred the remaining 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Irakli Garibashvili.

Prosecutors have charged the former prime minister under Article 338 of the Criminal Code. The article covers accepting a particularly large bribe by a public or political official as part of a group.

At this stage, the prosecution is asking the court to schedule a preliminary hearing. It is not seeking a new pre-trial measure because Garibashvili is already in custody.

Who gave investigators new testimony?

According to the prosecution, Vasil Mcheidze decided to cooperate with investigators on 12 August. He provided the authorities with information in his possession.

Juansher Burchuladze is also cooperating with the investigation. The prosecution is relying on their testimony to establish Garibashvili’s role in the new case.

Burchuladze was arrested in September 2025. On 23 April 2026, a court sentenced him to 10 years in prison for abuse of power and legalising illicit income.

Burchuladze’s former deputy, Giorgi Khaindrava, and Vasil Mcheidze each received eight-year prison sentences in the same case. Gudushauri reached a plea agreement with the prosecution.

Why does the timing of the new charges against Garibashvili matter?

Just days before prosecutors brought the new charges, Garibashvili made three statements from prison. They were published on 17, 18 and 20 August.

The former prime minister said the ruling party was demanding that he admit to additional acts of corruption. He said the government feared his return to politics.

Garibashvili also said he had received a letter from prominent Georgian Dream representative Mamuka Mdinaradze. According to Garibashvili, a close friend of Mdinaradze delivered the letter to a member of his family.

“You sent me to prison for five years because of false assumptions, fantasies, envy, fears and suspicions created by a certain group within the party,” Garibashvili wrote.

He said the demand that he admit to the new allegations came with a hint that authorities could arrest his father.

“I am not fighting anyone. I am only defending myself and my family. That is why I will have no choice but to respond in kind to everything you do,” Garibashvili said.

The new charges have given the former prime minister’s statements added significance. However, his account has not been investigated or independently verified.

What does Georgian Dream say?

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze suggested that Garibashvili may have had information about the ongoing investigation. In his view, the former prime minister’s statements were pre-emptive.

“Former politicians often use this method, and legal issues are sometimes brought into the political sphere,” Kaladze said.

He said Garibashvili’s safety and rights were protected.

Mamuka Mdinaradze denies Garibashvili’s allegations. He considers the current case against the former prime minister part of the government’s fight against corruption.

Garibashvili family’s response

Garibashvili’s wife’s brother, Alexander Tamazashvili, published an extract from the public registry after prosecutors brought the new charges. He said the document showed a property transaction involving Zurab Tukvadze, a businessman and one of the prosecution’s witnesses.

The prosecution’s public statement does not name the businessman. However, Tamazashvili claims that Tukvadze transferred a country house in the Tskneti settlement to Vasil Mcheidze in 2023. Tamazashvili suggested that the property transfer amounted to a bribe.

The statement can also be seen as an ironic rebuttal of the allegations. However, the published property transaction neither proves nor disproves that anyone may have given cash to Garibashvili.

Garibashvili himself has not publicly responded to the details of the new charges.

Opposition raises two possible concerns

Opposition representatives have highlighted two issues in the case.

The first is possible corruption in defence procurement.

The second is the suspicion that the law may serve as a tool of political pressure.

Levan Samushia, a member of the opposition Strong Georgia – Lelo party, said Garibashvili’s earlier statements give grounds for such suspicions.

“Is the law not being used in this case to exert pressure based on clan interests? Otherwise, how could Garibashvili have known in advance that he might face charges?” Samushia said.

Zurab Japaridze, leader of Girchi – More Freedom, drew attention to the scheme described in the indictment. He linked Garibashvili’s alleged receipt of cash to his previous case.

“He artificially inflated the price, received his share in cash in lari, then exchanged it for dollars and gold and kept the bundles in a safe,” Japaridze wrote.

Garibashvili’s first case

Garibashvili first faced corruption charges in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising a particularly large amount of illicit income.

According to the prosecution, Garibashvili provided false information in his property declarations. In doing so, he allegedly attempted to give illegally obtained income a legitimate appearance.

In January 2026, Garibashvili pleaded guilty and reached a deal with the prosecution. The court sentenced him to five years in prison.

Garibashvili has not pleaded guilty in the new case. The main grounds for the charges are testimony from Burchuladze and Mcheidze. The court will have to assess the credibility of their statements, along with the other evidence.

The case now brings together two parallel questions.

One concerns possible corruption in secret Defence Ministry procurement procedures.

The other concerns Garibashvili’s claim that the government demanded that he admit guilt in advance.

Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

World.title: $12m dispute and house sold at auction: where has former Georgian PM Nika Gilauri gone? – RFE/RL
World.content:
Nika Gilauri case

At the end of 2024, former prime minister Nika Gilauri became one of the most vocal critics of the ruling Georgian Dream party. Over the following months, he faced serious problems: authorities seized his foundation, while a court ordered him and his companies to pay $12 million in compensation to former business partners. Gilauri himself stopped appearing in public.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty published an investigation into the case. The circumstances described in the report raise suspicions that the legal proceedings against Gilauri may amount to political persecution. Georgian and German lawyers have called the court ruling unfounded.

The material draws on a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty investigation.

Gilauri’s house put up for forced auction

On 16 July 2026, the National Bureau of Enforcement put Nika Gilauri’s house in Tsavkisi up for auction. A 3,368-square-metre plot of land and a 1,157-square-metre villa sold for almost four million lari (about $1.54 million).

The property had an estimated value of 4.876 million lari (about $1.87 million), but bidding started at 10% of that amount. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, businessman Vano Sturua bought the house. He is a former business partner of Nika Gilauri’s brother, Irakli.

Since 2018, this house has remained the only property in Georgia registered in Gilauri’s name. However, court rulings have also ordered the seizure of other assets and his shares in companies.

Gilauri himself has not commented on the situation. He only responded to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty in writing:

“The legal proceedings are still ongoing, and on my lawyers’ advice, I will not make any comments or give interviews at this stage.”

Gilauri’s return to politics

Nika Gilauri served as energy minister and finance minister under Mikheil Saakashvili. He then headed the government from 2009 to 2012. After leaving public service, he founded the consulting company Reformatics and stayed out of Georgia’s public political life for about 12 years.

The situation changed ahead of the 2024 parliamentary election. A few days before the vote, Gilauri and the Reformatics team presented a 100-page document outlining their vision for a “Third Republic of Georgia”. It addressed Georgia’s exit from Russia’s sphere of influence, judicial independence and European integration.

Media reports said Gilauri was financing the opposition Coalition for Change. Several coalition leaders later confirmed that they had worked with him and received campaign donations.

After security forces violently dispersed protests in November and December 2024, Gilauri called the Georgian Dream government illegitimate. He demanded new elections and the release of detained protesters.

Gilauri also called on business representatives to create a fund to support protesters. His Prosperity foundation raised 246,000 lari (about $94,450) in three months. The money was intended to support protesters and people who had lost their jobs because of their political views.

In March 2025, the prosecutor’s office froze the assets of the Prosperity foundation and four other foundations. Authorities opened an investigation into allegations of sabotage, assisting the activities of a hostile foreign organisation and actions against the constitutional order. The investigation remains ongoing, and the foundations remain suspended.

Gilauri has not appeared in public since then.

Dispute over the construction of three hydropower plants

The multimillion-lari legal dispute involving Gilauri began several years before he returned to politics.

In 2015, Aquahydro signed memorandums with the Georgian government and state-owned companies to build three small hydropower plants in the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region: Ipari, Khelra and Nakra.

Black Sea Group took responsibility for the construction work. Under the agreement, the contractor would receive payment for the completed work as well as a 20% stake in the company operating the hydropower plants.

Ipari and Khelra were completed and brought into operation. However, Black Sea Group halted construction of Nakra in 2020. A few months later, Aquahydro terminated its contract with the company and hired another contractor to complete the project.

In 2021, Black Sea Group went to court. The company said it had not received full payment for the work it had completed. It sought several million lari in compensation, as well as damages for lost profits.

Gilauri’s side filed a counterclaim seeking 14.5 million lari (about $5.57 million) from Black Sea Group. They argued that the suspension of construction at Nakra deprived the company of expected revenue for 2020-2022. Their expert assessment found that the contractor had received $600,000 more than the actual cost of the work, according to official documentation.

Black Sea Group rejected the assessment, arguing that it had not received full payment for the work it had completed.

Why was Gilauri held personally liable?

On 12 February 2025, Tbilisi City Court judge Liana Kajashvili ruled in favour of Black Sea Group. The court ordered the former prime minister and companies under his control to pay Black Sea Group more than $12 million in damages.

The Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court upheld the ruling. It became final in November 2025. The amount owed continues to increase each day until the court order is enforced.

The direct parties to the dispute were Aquahydro and Black Sea Group. Nika Gilauri had no direct contractual relationship with either company. He owned a stake in a firm whose subsidiary acted as the project’s direct client.

Despite this corporate structure, the court held Gilauri personally liable. It also imposed liability on Reformatics, even though the company had no involvement in the hydropower project.

The court concluded that Gilauri and companies linked to him had acted together against Black Sea Group under what it described as a “joint agreement”.

What do the lawyers say?

German and Georgian lawyers Heinz Böling and Giorgi Jughéli analysed the ruling. Their analysis appeared in a German legal journal in June 2026.

The authors argue that the court conflated the common goal of the economic project with the legal liability of the individual companies involved. They believe the ruling effectively erases the distinction between a company and its partners.

“Neither German nor Georgian law provides for such legal consequences. This is incorrect and, moreover, as already stated, simply fabricated,” the lawyers write.

In their assessment, the court imposed personal liability “through three corporate veils” on a person who was not a party to the disputed contract.

“As far as we know, there is no other court ruling allowing such liability — not only in Georgia, but anywhere in the world,” the authors note.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty also asked two other Georgian lawyers to independently review the ruling. Both said there were insufficient legal grounds for holding Gilauri and Reformatics liable.

One of the lawyers said that common ownership does not automatically make companies liable for each other’s obligations. To impose personal liability, the court would have had to prove that Gilauri used the corporate structure to defraud a creditor or pursue other unlawful purposes. The ruling contains no such evidence or reasoning.

There is no documented evidence of a political link between Gilauri’s public criticism, the acceleration of the court proceedings and the final ruling. However, the chronology raises questions. The trial court concluded a four-year dispute about two months after Gilauri made a series of high-profile political statements. The higher courts then reviewed the extensive case file within eight months.

The state has now sold Gilauri’s house at auction. The former prime minister remains silent, while authorities continue to pursue his assets and business interests to recover the money.

Nika Gilauri case

World.title: Aliyev’s Uzbekistan visit: ‘Eternal friendship’ and family business expansion
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Uzbekistan

The state visit to Tashkent was presented by official media as a “new, symbolic and practical stage” in relations between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev held a one-on-one meeting, chaired the third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council, signed a “Treaty on Eternal Friendship”, awarded each other their countries’ highest state honours, and took part in ceremonies marking the opening and laying of foundations for Azerbaijani investment projects in Uzbekistan.

However, behind the official statements and rhetoric about “brotherhood” lie specific financial and business interests. Against the backdrop of the visit, attention has also focused on the parallel expansion of private companies directly or indirectly linked to Ilham Aliyev’s family, including PASHA Holding and Emin Agalarov’s Sea Breeze project.

What happened?

The main document signed during the visit was the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship”. Under the treaty, the two sides intend to build relations based on the principles of eternal friendship, mutual trust, strategic partnership and alliance, as well as support each other’s national development models. They undertake not to join blocs or alliances that could harm the other side’s sovereignty, security or territorial integrity, and not to allow their territory to be used by third parties for such purposes or for the activities of such groups.

Areas of cooperation outlined in the treaty include strengthening the UN’s central role, developing interparliamentary ties, trade and investment, including in energy, transport and logistics, digital development, agriculture, the green and digital economies, e-commerce, ICT and space technologies. The treaty also provides for the development of interconnected transport systems, the preservation of cultural and humanitarian ties, language learning, scientific and educational exchanges, interregional cooperation and tourism.

The heads of state exchanged their countries’ highest state honours, with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev receiving the Heydar Aliyev Order. Ceremonies were also held to open and lay the foundations for specific Azerbaijani projects in Uzbekistan, including hotel and residential complexes, tourism facilities, a building for the Nizami Ganjavi University, an “Azerbaijan” park and other facilities.

Joint projects have been launched in banking and finance, construction materials production, education, the oil and gas sector, tourism, housing construction, mining and agriculture. A corresponding “road map” was also adopted.

Azerbaijan’s state-owned bank enters Uzbek market

President Ilham Aliyev cited several specific examples of cooperation, including the entry of a leading Azerbaijani bank into the Uzbek market, the expansion of SOCAR’s retail network, oil and gas exploration nearing its final stage, and the prospect of drilling production wells next year.

The bank in question is the International Bank of Azerbaijan (ABB), the country’s largest state-owned bank, with around 88–92% of its shares held by the Finance Ministry and other state bodies. ABB is acquiring a 51% controlling stake in the privately owned Uzbek bank Davr Bank, investing more than $100m in the deal.

Despite its state-owned status, ABB was previously implicated in the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal, involving a $2.9bn money-laundering scheme. The bank is now entering the Uzbek market with the backing of state resources and political will. The deal is being presented as a purely commercial decision, but comes against the backdrop of a strengthening political alliance between the two countries.

Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov announced the deal at an interregional forum a day before the visit, and it was formally concluded on the day of the visit. ABB will operate in Uzbekistan under the Davr Bank brand. The bank has assets of around $1bn, a customer base of 1.4 million and a network of 43 branches. Fitch Ratings expects the deal to be completed by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Expansion of businesses linked to Aliyev family

Alongside the official banking deal, several private projects have also attracted attention during the visit and in the preceding period. Some are linked to companies and structures directly or indirectly associated with the president’s family.

Sea Breeze Uzbekistan: A $5bn resort project being developed by Agalarov Development, owned by Emin Agalarov, the former husband of President Aliyev’s daughter Leyla Aliyeva. The complex is planned for a 577-hectare site on the shores of the Charvak Reservoir. In 2025, the project was presented directly to Mirziyoyev and fast-tracked without a tender, while the environmental assessment had not yet been fully completed. A foundation-laying ceremony took place on the day of the visit. Although Agalarov is no longer related to the presidential family by marriage, he continues to enjoy high-level political support.

PASHA Holding projects: The holding company, which has been linked to the president’s daughters Leyla and Arzu Aliyeva, as well as to Mehriban Aliyeva’s father Arif Pashayev, is building a Ritz-Carlton-branded hotel and residential complex in Tashkent. The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates.

SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: "Sabah" advance to UEFA Champions League league phase
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Azerbaijani side "Sabah" secured a convincing victory over Israel's "Hapoel" (Be'er Sheva) in the second leg of the UEFA Champions League play-off round, advancing to the league phase of the tournament.

The match at the Tofiq Bahramov Republican Stadium ended 5-2 in favor of the Baku-based team.

As a result, "Sabah" won 6-4 on aggregate and reached the league phase of the UEFA Champions League for the first time in the club's history.

The first leg in Bucharest ended in a 2-1 victory for "Hapoel."

World.title: Tajikistan, Belarus discuss new prospects for bilateral cooperation
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tajikistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Tajikistan and Belarus discussed prospects for developing bilateral cooperation.

This was announced in a report published by the press service of the Tajik MFA, following the meeting between Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin and newly appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Belarus to Tajikistan Alexander Khudoleyev.

The meeting between the minister and the newly appointed ambassador was held on the occasion of the formal presentation of copies of the ambassador’s credentials.

"During the meeting, the current state and prospects for bilateral cooperation between Tajikistan and Belarus were discussed," the statement said.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs wished the new Ambassador of Belarus success in his diplomatic activities in Tajikistan.

Meanwhile, Tajikistan and Belarus maintain diplomatic relations and cooperate through bilateral and multilateral frameworks. Their cooperation covers areas including trade and economic relations, agriculture, industry, education, and humanitarian ties, while the two countries also maintain regular political contacts.

World.title: Azerbaijan facilitates transit of new Russian shipment to Armenia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Another shipment from Russia to Armenia has been delivered via Azerbaijan.

On August 25, 14 railcars of wheat weighing 976 metric tons and 1 railcar of lumber weighing 65 metric tons were dispatched from the Bilajari station in Boyuk-Kesik.

To date, more than 50,000 metric tons of grain, about 9,000 metric tons of fertilizer, 1,414 metric tons of propane, 133 metric tons of aluminum, 1,114 metric tons of coal, and 67 metric tons of lumber have been shipped from Russia to Armenia via Azerbaijan.

In addition, approximately 15,000 metric tons of diesel fuel and about 5,000 metric tons of RON-92 and RON-95 gasoline have been exported from Azerbaijan to Armenia to date.

World.title: Regional residents furious deliveries they paid for aren't coming
World.content:
Residents in parts of regional Tasmania are furious with a delivery company, after they paid for a door-to-door delivery service that no longer exists.

Miena resident Michael Walls used to reliably receive deliveries from Team Global Express.

"We had a great service up until they've changed their policy about delivering to the Central Highlands," he said.

In recent months, he has been told by the company his deliveries have been taken to the depot in Cambridge near Hobart — a four-hour round trip from Miena.

Michael Walls is considering legal action, as he paid for the items to be delivered to his home. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

After Mr Walls complained to the company, Team Global Express arranged for its state manager to deliver his package, but two others remain at the depot.

"They're obligated to deliver it because they've been contracted to deliver the items," he said.

"They shouldn't have accepted the items that they weren't interested in delivering.

He is looking at launching legal action, believing the failure to deliver may be a violation of consumer law.

Team Global Express told the ABC the Tasmanian towns it recently stopped delivering to were Miena, Liawenee, Waddamana, Levendale, Tunnack, Bradys Lake, Bronte Park, Derwent Bridge, Lake St Clair, Maydena and Colebrook.

'We pay them to deliver'

Laurie Smythe ordered machinery bases from a Queensland company to his home in Colebrook, north of Hobart.

"I received a message from Team Global Express to say that I needed to pick the freight up from their base area at Cambridge," he said.

" I rang them up and I said, 'What's going on? You've got to deliver that to me', and they said, 'No, we don't deliver in that area anymore'. "

Laurie Smythe contacted the seller, which told him it had paid Team Global Express to deliver the items to his door. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Mr Smythe was told it would be sent back to the sender if he did not pick it up within seven days.

He rang the company he purchased the freight from to explain that Team Global Express would not deliver it.

"'He said, 'Well, we pay them to deliver'," Mr Smythe said.

Laurie Smythe eventually made the two-hour trip from his home in Colebrook to the Team Global Express depot in Hobart. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Eventually, Mr Smythe made the two-hour round trip to collect his freight from the depot.

"They were paid for it; they're supposed to be a national company doing deliveries," he said.

"In my mind, that's not acceptable.

" How many others yet don't know that their freight's on the road and they're not going to get it? "

Donna Barratt organised a petition calling for Team Global Express to continue delivering to Maydena. (Supplied)

Donna Barratt, who runs a cafe and an accommodation service in Maydena, said she did not have time to pick up every delivery.

"There's a lot of people in Maydena who actually don't drive, so they won't be able to go and pick it up either," she said.

She organised a petition, signed by about 70 community members, calling on Team Global Express to continue delivering to the area — which she said had gone unanswered.

In most cases when purchasing items online, customers are not able to view or select the delivery company.

"So you won't actually know until that parcel's been sent that it's coming [via] Team Global Express and then you realise that you're not going to get the door-to-door service that you've paid for," Ms Barratt said.

Laurie Smythe received a text from Team Global Express saying his freight was at the company's depot. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Company cites driver safety as reason for decision

Team Global Express, which is owned by Allegro Funds and operates across Australia and New Zealand, said it continued to deliver to the majority of Tasmania.

"Recently, we needed to address four postcodes in the Lakes District (7027 and partial areas of 7030, 7120, and 7140)," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"These areas present operational challenges, including unsafe road conditions for our drivers, particularly during winter.

"We proactively notify our customers when there are changes to delivery networks and in cases where parcels cannot be delivered to door, we work with the receiver on alternate options."

When asked for further details, the spokesperson said customers were notified by phone when their parcel arrived at the depot, and worked with them to find delivery options.

Team Global Express says the non-delivery areas "present operational challenges, including unsafe road conditions for our drivers". (Team Global Express)

They said Miena residents could choose to have their packages taken to an alternative delivery point at Longford, while Maydena residents could have their packages taken to Westerway. The spokesperson said Colebrook residents would need to pick up their deliveries from the depot near Hobart.

"We will always strive to give customers and shoppers the best service possible, whilst taking into account the safety of our people and the sustainable operation of our business," they said.

Mr Walls urged Team Global Express not to "forget about the small customers in the rural areas".

World.title: Anthropic's 'massive' AI data centre plans revealed in emails
World.content:
Internal NSW government emails reveal AI giant Anthropic was interested in building up to 5 gigawatts of AI data centre capacity in NSW alone, a capacity that would be three times the size of Australia's entire data centre infrastructure.

This grand ambition from the US company behind Claude would require tens of billions of dollars in investment and a significant expansion in the number of data centres across the country, to meet just one company's demand in a single state.

"That is a massive amount," Olivia Shen, director of the Strategic Technologies Program at the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney, said.

It comes as the Albanese government negotiates new rules for large-scale data centres with the states, which are vying with each other to attract investment from Silicon Valley.

Know more about this story? Email Cam Wilson on wilson.cameron@abc.net.au or his secure email cmwlsn@protonmail.com

The speed and scale of the AI data centre boom has prompted a growing backlash from local communities concerned about the impacts of building this physical infrastructure in their local communities.

Training and running generative AI needs an enormous amount of computing capacity, which requires expensive computing hardware and tremendous amounts of power. They can also be hot and noisy.

With Silicon Valley rushing out new AI models at a breakneck pace, there has been a race to build the physical infrastructure required to serve the billions of people using popular AI services launched since late 2022.

Will Australia be taken for a ride in the AI boom? More than $150 billion is lined up for data centre development and investment in Australia, but there are questions as to whether the boom will provide benefits beyond a short-term construction boost.

Emails reveal plans to meet Anthropic CEO

Documents released by NSW parliament earlier this year reveal how a senior public servant shared information about Anthropic's interest in building out its AI computing capacity in NSW.

Dena Jacobs, executive director of independent state government agency Infrastructure NSW, wrote to two senior public servants at the Department of Premier's Investment NSW in March about a conversation with Anthropic adviser John Garnaut.

Ms Jacobs told the staff she wanted to organise a meeting between Investment NSW staff and Mr Garnaut ahead of a "a more senior level meeting".

"The context is that the CEO of Anthropic is visiting Sydney and would like to speak to NSW government about the opportunities to locate up to 5GW of AI training capacity in NSW. i.e. there's an opportunity to locate this outside Sydney," she wrote on March 18.

The speed and scale of the data centre boom has prompted backlash from some communities. (Supplied: Microsoft)

Ms Jacobs's email did not specify Anthropic's intended time frame for this computing goal.

The ABC understands the 5 gigawatt goal only reflected initial interest from Anthropic, which was one of a handful of major tech companies that Infrastructure NSW had spoken with about their future computing demands.

Both Anthropic and NSW Investment declined to comment.

The Albanese government is negotiating new rules for large-scale data centres with states. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Mr Garnaut told the ABC that he "work[s] with AI firms" but said he "did not put in this particular request".

Two weeks later, Anthropic's senior executive, including CEO Dario Amodei, visited Australia.

Mr Amodei met the prime minister and treasurer when they signed a memorandum of understanding between the company and the government, which included, among other things, a promise to "expand [Anthropic]'s presence in Australia".

The AI company has not publicly stated how much computing capacity it would like to obtain in Australia.

The ABC reported in June that Anthropic wanted 5 gigawatts of new Australian computing capacity by 2030, with a longer-term goal of 20 gigawatts.

The Australian Financial Review reported in July about a confidential tender sent by the AI company to Australian data centre builders asking for 1.4 gigawatts of capacity, valued at more than $20 billion.

Australia an attractive destination for centres

Anthropic's interest in up to 5 gigawatts for a single state would dwarf the projections for the total amount of computing capacity expected to be built by the end of the decade.

New data released in a report from lobby group Data Centre Australia today calculated that Australia currently has 1.6 gigawatts of computing capacity in total.

The report projects that Australia's data centre capacity will grow to 3.9 gigawatts by 2030.

These figures are a marked increase from data released by the same group earlier this year.

The global fight against data centres heats up Last year in the US alone, projects collectively worth $200 billion were scuppered or delayed as communities protested the construction of new data centres promised to deliver the AI of the future.

In April, Data Centres Australia said there were 1.5 gigawatts of current capacity and 3.2 gigawatts projected by 2030, suggesting demand for computing capacity, and the ability to satisfy that demand, is growing even faster than anticipated.

Analysts estimate global data centre capacity was somewhere around 55 and 82 gigawatts in 2025.

Ms Shen said Australia had emerged as an attractive destination for US AI companies for several reasons.

"One is just that we have lots of land. Another is that we have huge amounts of renewable capacity, particularly solar energy, and the third is that we are a stable democracy," she said.

The artificial intelligence boom requires power-hungry data centres. (ABC News: Rhiannon Stevens)

While Australians are among the most distrustful populations in the world of AI, they are also some of the fastest adopters of the technology.

Anthropic released data in June claiming that Australia ranks first in the world for use of its Claude project, when adjusted for the working-age population.

Ms Shen said Anthropic, out of all of the global tech companies, was particularly incentivised to move some of its operations abroad.

Anthropic remains locked in a high-stakes legal battle with the US government over export controls placed on its cutting-edge models.

The company is also reportedly looking at going public at a US$2 trillion ($2.8 trillion) valuation as soon as late this year.

"In the face of this uncertainty about the regulatory landscape in the US, including a lot of local opposition to data centres, it makes sense for Anthropic to want to diversify its compute and its business outside of the United States," Ms Shen said.

Governments looking to attract business

Australian governments, too, have indicated their interest in attracting US tech companies to establish themselves here.

Other internal NSW government emails released by parliamentary order show that the office of NSW Innovation, Science and Technology Minister Anoulack Chanthivong set up a meeting with one US Anthropic executive during their trip.

The ABC understands that meeting did not go ahead.

Mr Chanthivong told the ABC his government did not comment on private discussions but would regularly discuss investment opportunities with the companies.

"The Minns Labor government continues to welcome investment from leading technology companies," he said.

Last week, NSW announced a set of new energy, water, environmental and community requirements would receive a commitment to have their development applications assessed within 75 days.

The state said qualifying projects must fund additional water and energy supply and impose no net cost on consumers and communities.

The Albanese government is pursuing new requirements around the use of energy and water. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

These rules come on top of Anthony Albanese's recent announcement that the federal government would create a set of "Australian standards" that he hoped would attract investment from top tech companies while avoiding a US-style community backlash.

This comes as polling from multiple outlets shows that a plurality of Australians would oppose data centres being built in their local community.

The Albanese government is pursuing new requirements around the use of energy and water, copyright protections, workers' rights and computing capacity for Australian businesses and researchers.

Mr Albanese is set for a showdown over these standards at national cabinet later today, as both Queensland and the Northern Territory have signalled that they will not accept a requirement to guarantee that all data centres bring enough new renewable energy to account for their added demand.

The rest of the new data centre rules will be developed as the Albanese government seeks to legislate the standards in early 2027.

World.title: From turning down Elvis to opening her own theme park, Dolly Parton did it all
World.content:
Behind a glass display case at a resort in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, is a locked box.

Inside it sits a recording of an unreleased Dolly Parton song.

The tune has been kept secret since 2015, when Parton opened the resort as part of her eponymous theme park, Dollywood.

The idea was that nobody would hear it until the country music legend's 100th birthday, more than 30 years later.

"I don't know if I want to live to be 100 or not. But you never know. I might," she joked.

"And if I do, I'm going to be at that opening."

It wasn't to be. Parton has died, her family announced today, missing her own grand reveal by some 20 years.

But having bowed out at 80 years old as one of the most decorated performers of all time, Dolly Parton lived a life well lived.

From a one-room shack in Tennessee

Dolly Rebecca Parton took her first breath of fresh Tennessee mountain air on January 16, 1946.

The fourth child of Avie Lee and Robert Lee Parton, Dolly grew up with her 11 siblings in a one-room shack in the Great Smoky Mountains.

The family had no electricity, heating or running water and very little money, but they got by with Robert's wages from labouring and farming and Avie's resourceful skills as a homemaker.

Dolly Parton (centre) was among 12 children born to Robert Lee and Avie Lee Parton, one of whom died at just four days old. (Supplied: DollyParton.com)

The day that Dolly was born, they paid the town doctor with a sack of cornmeal.

Dolly was proud to share her family's humble beginnings — a lesson she learnt from her mother very early on in life.

"Wealth is not measured by a dollar," Avie once told a young Dolly who was distraught over schoolyard taunts about her beloved patchwork coat, stitched together from a box of rags.

A replica of the coat that inspired Dolly Parton's song, Coat of Many Colors, remains on display in the Chasing Rainbows museum at the Dollywood theme park in Pigeon Forge. (Supplied: Facebook/Dollywood)

Before she had learned to read or write, Dolly was singing, performing and begging for audiences wherever she could.

"I'd put a tin can on a stick as my microphone and pretend the front porch was my stage. Then I'd sing to whatever was in the front yard — human, animal or dirt," she recalled in her 2020 lyrical autobiography, Dolly Parton: Songteller.

The first song she wrote, at age six, was called Little Tiny Tasseltop — an ode to her favourite toy, a doll made out of an old corn cob wrapped in cloth.

By the time she was eight, Dolly was carting her guitar into local radio and TV stations in pursuit of her big break.

She became a regular on the Cas Walker Farm and Home Hour, where she met Carl and Pearl Butler — a husband-and-wife country duo from Knoxville who took the plucky 10-year-old under their wing.

Before too long, Dolly had released her first record, Puppy Love. Her Uncle Bill Owens, who'd gifted her that first guitar, took her down to Nashville on the weekends to perform, write, and even record with well-known artists.

Dolly Parton released her first record, Puppy Love, at the age of 13. (Supplied: Goldband Records via Public Domain)

In 1959, they booked a guest spot on the Grand Ole Opry — the world-famous home of country music. A young Johnny Cash welcomed the duo to the stage.

" We've got a little girl here from up in East Tennessee. Her daddy's listening to the radio at home, and she's gonna be in real trouble if she doesn't sing tonight, so let's bring her out here. "

Even three encores weren't enough; Dolly couldn't wait for the real deal to begin.

In 1964, she became the first member of her family to graduate from high school. Students at Sevier County High were asked to stand up and tell the class what they wanted to do with their lives.

When Dolly's turn came, she simply announced: "I'm going to Nashville and I'm going to be a star."

To Nashville and the greatest loves of her life

Dolly Parton had set her sights on landing a record deal in Music City.

Living with her Uncle Bill and saving what she could from waitressing shifts and odd jobs, she spent every spare second writing.

She signed as a songwriter with Combine Publishing, penning hits for country stars including her own idol, Kitty Wells.

But Parton said it wasn't until Skeeter Davis recorded an album of her songs that industry folks began to take her seriously.

"My voice was real different — not that it's good, because a lot of people just cannot stand to hear me sing," she told music journalist Jack Hurst in 1970.

"Anybody with a real different voice, a lot of people don't like to hear sing, but people who do like them usually like them especially well."

Fred Foster saw the potential and signed Parton to his independent label, Monument Records. He asked Curly Putman — the man behind the 1965 hit Green, Green Grass of Home — to write something for her debut album.

Parton in the studio in the 1960s, with her Uncle Bill and Fred Foster. (Suppied: DollyParton.com)

"[Foster] figured it would make people forget about whether my voice was any good or not and just listen to the song," Parton explained in her 2020 memoir.

Track 1, Dumb Blonde, would become Parton's first major hit as a singer, sending an iconic message to those foolish enough to have dismissed her talents:

"Just because I'm blonde don't think I'm dumb, 'cause this dumb blonde ain't nobody's fool."

Music City would also introduce Parton to her lifelong love, Carl Dean.

She was just 18 when they met on her very first day in Nashville, outside the laundromat. Dean would later describe it as the day his life began.

Within two years, they were married — a secret that Parton kept hidden from her manager, who'd warned the young musician against distractions.

Parton met the love of her life, Carl Dean, when she was just 18 years old. (Suppied: DollyParton.com)

"After I started doing well, Fred said: 'Aren't you glad you didn't get married?' I said: 'I've been married two years — I got married the same weekend you told me not to,'" she recalled years later.

While he adored her from the moment they met, Dean never shared Parton's love for the spotlight.

In 1966, the newlyweds attended the BMI Country Music Awards, where Parton won Song of the Year for co-writing the Bill Phillips hit, Put It Off Until Tomorrow.

Dean got dressed up in his finest tuxedo and sat through the whole ceremony before telling his wife: "I'm happy for you; I want you to do what you want to do. But don't ever ask me to go to another one of them damn things, because I ain't going."

And he never did. Throughout their 60-year marriage, Parton described Dean as her home and heart.

"He will always be the star of my life story," she wrote after his death in 2025, dedicating a new song to their endless love.

Parton and Dean were married for 60 years. (Supplied: Instagram/Dolly Parton)

The Porter Wagoner years

The chart success of Hello I'm Dolly, her first solo studio album released in 1967, had put Parton on the map — and it wasn't long before a superstar came calling.

Porter Wagoner had released a string of heartbreak and honky-tonk hits throughout the 1950s and was hosting a weekly musical variety show in Nashville.

Wagoner asked Parton to become his duet partner and star performer, replacing Norma Jean, the first woman featured on the show.

It was a match made in country music heaven.

Porter Wagoner invited Parton to become the new star of his weekly variety show. (Supplied: RCA Records/Public Domain)

Parton and Wagoner became one of the decade's most successful duos, releasing 11 studio albums together and earning three Grammy nominations in seven years.

"After four years on that show, Miss Dolly is moving toward a place among the female superstars of the business — women like Loretta Lynn and Tammy Wynette," Jack Hurst wrote after interviewing Dolly in 1970.

"Miss Dolly, meanwhile … she seems to take herself remarkably unseriously, particularly for a country girl who has come so far, so fast.

"She seems to think of her success not so much as something she achieved herself but more as a gift from people … who really believed in her."

But behind closed doors, the relationship between the two stars was tense. Parton felt that Wagoner, 19 years her senior, was becoming jealous and insistent on controlling her career.

While their musical partnership was a huge success, tensions grew between Wagoner and Parton. (Supplied: RCA Records/Public Domain)

And while she was pulling a crowd to the weekly tapings of The Porter Wagoner Show, it wasn't Parton earning the big bucks. She and the rest of the band were paid on union scale, taking home about $200 to $350 a week.

Parton had agreed to stay on the show for five years, but she wanted more.

"I wanted to get on with my life. I didn't want to be known as the 'girl singer' in someone else's band," she reflected years later.

Having tried to convince Wagoner dozens of times that they should part ways, Parton finally wrote it to him in a song.

I Will Always Love You would become arguably Parton's most successful song of all time. What sounded like a romantic break-up anthem really marked the end of a significant chapter in her musical career.

One evening after the show, she sat Wagoner down and asked if she could play him a new song.

"When I started to sing the song, he started to cry," Parton recalled, in one of many retellings of that night.

" He got it. He said, 'That's the best song you ever wrote. And you can go, if I can produce that song.' "

It was a deal. Parton and Wagoner officially parted ways in 1974, paving the way for a new era.

Three of her solo singles hit the top of the chart that same year: I Will Always Love You, Jolene (the iconic track loosely inspired by Dean flirting with a bank teller) and the perhaps lesser-known Love Is Like A Butterfly.

Parton's booking fees soared, and by 1977 she was raking in almost double what she'd earned as a Wagoner employee.

Parton was ready to carve her own path. (Supplied: RCA Records/Public Domain)

As Parton herself observed at the time, it was only through breaking out from the country confines of The Porter Wagoner Show that she was able to reach mainstream audiences.

"I haven't turned my back on Nashville," she told Country Music Magazine in 1977.

"I will be able to do more for the name of country music by going ahead and doing what I feel I should do, by reaching a broader audience and as many people as I can, and by having a universal appeal.

"I'll be able to do more for Nashville than I ever could have done had I stayed there."

Country queen to screen star

Back in control of her own destiny, Parton dropped her Nashville management and hired an LA company working with the likes of Cher and Olivia Newton-John.

She assembled a new band, hired a PR firm and started doing late-night TV shows.

The end of the decade heralded Parton's pop breakthrough with Here You Come Again and her first foray into disco, Baby I'm Burnin'.

Loading Instagram content

Meanwhile, Hollywood was calling. Her new manager, Sandy Gallin, a lifelong friend and collaborator, encouraged Parton to take the plunge.

In her own words, she'd never felt a huge desire to star in movies, but she knew that it could be a lucrative pivot. Box office success would offer her the financial freedom to do whatever she wanted with her music.

Then Jane Fonda pitched Parton her 1980 comedy 9 to 5.

Fonda felt Parton was "perfect" for the role of the plucky secretary Doralee Rhodes, plotting revenge alongside her coworkers (played by Fonda and Lily Tomlin) against their sexist boss.

"I was so picky — I hadn't found a script I had thought was good enough … but 9 to 5 fascinated me, and I knew instantly that I should do it — I knew that it was a career move," Parton told Rolling Stone in 1980.

Parton famously tapped out the film's iconic title track on her acrylic nails, right there on set.

Parton told reporters she learned the entire script, and would help prompt her co-stars Lily Tomlin (left) and Jane Fonda (centre) when they forgot their lines. (AP)

It would be her biggest hit of the decade, hitting number one on the US charts, going three times platinum and earning Parton an Oscar nomination and two Grammys.

The following year, Parton starred alongside Burt Reynolds in The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas — the "complete opposite experience" of the dream run she'd had with Fonda and Tomlin.

But it was another commercial success for Parton, who chalked up her second Golden Globe nomination for best actress and re-recorded I Will Always Love You for the soundtrack, bringing it back to number one on the country charts.

Just as her film career was taking off, Parton's health took a hit.

In the early 1980s, Parton's star was rising. (AP/Humphrey)

After she almost collapsed on stage during a gig in Indiana, doctors urged the star to slow down. She cancelled the rest of the tour and flew to New York for urgent surgery to address debilitating symptoms of endometriosis.

The physical recovery took months, and the emotional toll plunged her into a deep depression.

In an interview years later, Parton summed it up as one of the most difficult periods of her life:

" For about six months there, I woke up every morning feeling dead. "

Through her darkest chapter, Parton turned to faith, friendship and songwriting. And after a brief hiatus, she was ready to re-enter the world.

With a brand new star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, Parton took on her next movie role in 1985, as a country singer trying to turn Sylvester Stallone, a New York City cab driver, into a superstar.

Rhinestone flopped at the box office. Undeterred, Parton set her sights on the next lofty career goal.

She and Gallin started their own production company, Sandollar, pumping out A Smoky Mountain Christmas and the short-lived prime-time variety show, Dolly, within their first couple of years.

Sandollar produced a prime-time variety show, Dolly, but the series was cancelled after a season. (AP: Lennox McLendon)

Sandollar went on to produce Father of the Bride, Kicking and Screaming, Wild Texas Wind and four more Dolly-themed Christmas movies.

But arguably its biggest success was the feature-length 1991 film Buffy the Vampire Slayer, which was later adapted into the hit TV series.

Decades later, Sandollar executive Gail Berman told The New York Times just how integral Parton had been to the show's success.

Upon discovering that the men on staff had allocated Berman a "less than generous share" of the royalties, Parton promptly wrote her a personal check to correct the injustice.

While never officially credited as part of the show, its titular character shares the same birthday as Parton—perhaps a nod to her lasting influence.

Welcome to Dollywood

With Parton busier than ever, releasing album after album and landing one of her biggest roles alongside an A-list cast in Steel Magnolias, her empire was expanding.

In the early '80s, she had announced a wacky dream to open a theme park in her beloved home, the Great Smoky Mountains.

Upon hearing this vision, so the story goes, the owners of an existing theme park in Pigeon Forge decided they'd simply never be able to compete. So Parton bought a stake in Silver Dollar City, and together, they turned it into Dollywood.

Dollywood officially opened in 1986, and remains a major tourist attraction to this day. (Supplied: Facebook/Dollywood)

The star attraction was a little museum dedicated to Parton's life story, built as a replica of the two-room shack where it all began.

Forty years later, the sprawling park nestled in the foothills of the Appalachian Mountains now boasts dozens of rides and attractions, its own coal-fired steam train, a separate water park, and on-site resorts.

"The Great Smoky Mountains were there for a couple million years before I came along … if Dollywood can give some people a little extra incentive to visit there, then I am absolutely tickled," Parton wrote in her 1994 autobiography, Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business.

More than just an ode to her cultural heritage, Dollywood offered Parton a way to give back to her community, through the launch of the Dollywood Foundation in 1988.

Its first project offered every kid who graduated from Parton's old school in Sevier County a modest scholarship to attend the local college.

What became known as the "Buddy Program" decreased the county's dropout rate from more than 30 per cent to less than 10 per cent within a few years.

Access to education had always been an issue close to Parton's heart, having grown up with a beloved father who never learned to read or write.

How Dolly Parton is bringing babies to books Dolly Parton's reading revolution is helping empower children to embrace and conquer literacy in western New South Wales.

"I thought if Daddy had an education, there was no telling what he could have been," she wrote in her 2020 memoir.

"My dad couldn't read and write, and he was always kind of ashamed of that. But it's not a thing to be ashamed of."

An idea to distribute free books to local children eventually became the Imagination Library, which to date has donated more than 260 million books worldwide — one of Parton's proudest achievements.

Cementing her icon status

From the very beginning, Parton was the consummate collaborator, dueting with pop heroes and country legends alike, lending her songwriting skills to countless artists over an illustrious seven-decade career.

From Willie Nelson and Kenny Rogers (pictured), to Sabrina Carpenter and Miley Cyrus, Dolly Parton was the queen of collaborations. (AP: Doug Pizac)

But perhaps the most lucrative deal came in 1992, when Whitney Houston released a cover of I Will Always Love You, for the film The Bodyguard.

Parton had turned down similar requests before — Elvis Presley wanted to cover the song in the 1970s, but had demanded half of the publishing rights, so she reluctantly declined.

"I have often said that my songs are my children and that I expect them to support me when I am old," Parton wrote years later.

"Well, I am old, and they are."

Houston's cover of I Will Always Love You in 1992 took Parton's track to the Grammy Hall of Fame. (Reuters: Rick Musacchio)

Houston's I Will Always Love You did just that, earning Parton millions of dollars in royalties.

When she first heard it on the radio, the songwriter "thought [she] was going to wreck [her] car".

"I have never experienced a greater feeling in my life than hearing Whitney Houston sing that song for the first time," Parton wrote in her 2020 memoir.

" She took that simple heartbroken song of mine and took it worldwide. For what she did with that, I will always love you, Whitney Houston. "

Fuelled by her financial success, Parton released a string of solo and collaborative albums through the 1990s, pivoting from folk, to dance/house, back to country-rock and bluegrass.

By the turn of the millennium, Parton had solidified her status as an American icon.

Inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999 and the National Songwriters' Hall of Fame in 2001, she was described as the most successful female country artist of all time.

Far from slowing down, Parton spent the next two decades at full steam.

Dolly Parton won 13 Country Music Awards over her career, including a Lifetime Achievement Award. (Reuters: Jeff Mitchell)

"I still have dreams of what I want to do next and of course I hope that I will never retire, I will never go to seed," she told graduates of the University of Tennessee in 2009.

"I would certainly rather wear out than rust out."

In 2006, Parton received her second Academy Award nomination for the original song Travellin' Thru, written for Transamerica, a film about a trans woman embarking on a road trip with her estranged son.

While never one to shy away from speaking her mind or calling out intrusive questions about her measurements and marriage, Parton walked a delicate political line.

She celebrated her LGBTQ+ fans (though always careful not to deride the conservative country crowd), openly advocated for same-sex marriage, and offered subtle messages of support for the trans community during inflammatory culture wars.

But for the most part, Parton let her music do the talking.

"I didn't think I had to march in the streets to prove anything," she reflected in her 2020 memoir.

" I would write it in my songs and live it as a woman in business. I never felt like I had to do it any differently than that. Everybody has the right to do things their own way. "

Ever determined to do things "Dolly's way", Parton released the first single from her own record company in 2007, and went on to produce 10 albums under the Dolly Records/Butterfly banner.

The songwriter and screen star made her way to the stage, writing and producing a Broadway musical based on her film debut, 9 to 5.

9 to 5 the Musical debuted on Broadway in 2009 and came to Australia (pictured) in 2022. (Supplied: Crossroads Live/David Hooley)

Her shiny acrylics left virtually no creative endeavour untouched.

By 2014, Parton had sold more than 100 million records and received a dazzling collection of awards recognising her efforts, including the National Medal of Arts, entries in the Library of Congress, a Kennedy Center Honor and a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.

Dolly Parton's legacy

Entering her 70s, Parton embarked on her biggest tour in more than 25 years, selling out back-to-back performances at the Hollywood Bowl in 2016.

Her business ventures spanned everything from cosmetics and clothing (Joleans), to wine, baked goods, homewares and Doggy Parton wigs.

Loading Instagram content

Much of Parton's art became semi-biographical, with children's books, themed memoirs and an eight-part Netflix series showcasing the stories behind her biggest songs.

She also wrote her first fiction novel with best-selling author James Patterson (naturally, accompanied by a studio album and adapted for the screen) and began working on another musical.

The retelling of her life and career, cheekily titled Hello, I'm Dolly, premiered in Nashville in July 2025, and is set to hit Broadway in 2026.
