Almost as quickly as the checks were coming in, Parton was looking for places to spend her money.

After wildfires ravaged her beloved Great Smoky Mountains in 2016, Parton personally established an ongoing fund for local families and helped raise $8.9 million for displaced communities.

The following year, she released her first children's album and made a $1 million donation to a paediatric hospital in her home state, in honour of her niece.

When the global pandemic hit in 2020, Parton donated $1 million for the development of Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine, encouraging her fans to get the jab.

Loading...

When a Tennessee representative proposed a bill to erect a statue in Parton's honour on the grounds of the state capitol in 2021, she politely declined.

"At this point in history, is there a better example, not just in America but in the world, of a leader that is [a] kind, decent, passionate human being?" the politician told reporters at the time.

But Parton felt uncomfortable being "put on a pedestal", suggesting perhaps they could revisit the idea "somewhere down the road several years from now".

It also took some convincing before she agreed to be inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, initially insisting she "hadn't done enough" to deserve it.

In finally accepting legendary status, she promised to earn it, and promptly released her first rock album, collaborating with the likes of Stevie Nicks, Joan Jett and her pop diva goddaughter, Miley Cyrus.

Parton dropped a hint at her next album while performing for her Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

The seemingly inexhaustible star was forced to postpone a six-date Las Vegas residency in 2025 to deal with ongoing health challenges, but in true Dolly Parton style, she promised her fans it wouldn't be long before she was back up and running.

"It must be time for my 100,000-mile check-up, although it's not the usual trip to see my plastic surgeon!" she quipped.

However many hundreds of thousands of miles Parton walked in those six-inch stilettos (she is, after all, a "tiny little person"), there's no doubt she has left an indelible mark behind.

And in her own words, it's this she hoped to be remembered for:

"I think people will remember us for who we were, not how many records we sell, or how much money we make," she told the graduates of the University of Tennessee in 2009.

"I have always counted my blessings far more often than I've counted my money. And my blessings are many."

World.title: Automation and repression — why the two go hand in hand
World.content:
When are the pitchforks coming?

Wealth inequality is becoming extreme. Political corruption is rampant in the United States.

Billionaires are building fortified bunkers to protect themselves from the inevitable social upheaval that lies in our future (they fear).

"What do I see in our future now? I see pitchforks," US tech entrepreneur Nick Hanauer famously warned in 2014.

Democracy cannot survive trillionaires Democracy cannot survive trillionaires. We need to start taxing billionaires properly

"There is no example in human history where wealth accumulated like this and the pitchforks didn't eventually come out.

"You show me a highly unequal society, and I will show you a police state. Or an uprising. There are no counter-examples."

Some tech leaders say it is inevitable that people will revolt against automation.

"This is the real underlying threat posed by automation: tremendous social upheaval, public unrest, and political collapse stemming from widespread unemployment and grotesque inequality," warned Kai-Fu Lee, a former president of Google China, in 2022.

It's why 100 millionaires signed an open letter for the Davos Summit in 2025 with a simple message for their wealthy colleagues: "It's taxes or pitchforks!"

So where is society headed?

Daron Acemoglu, a winner of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences (2024), published a working paper recently, with Mehdi Shadmehr and Arda Gitmez, that grappled with these issues.

It was titled Automation and Repression, and its conclusion was disquieting.

Redistribution or repression?

The economists argued in their paper that, when faced with the threat of a popular revolt against greater automation, political leaders will have two choices, and they'll choose the option most people won't like.

"We show that the capitalist state can use redistribution or repression to reduce the threat of a revolt," they say.

Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James A Robinson awarded the Nobel memorial prize in economics The three laureates were recognised for their work in studying how political institutions are formed, and how they affect prosperity and global inequality.

"[And] greater automation makes repression more attractive to the capitalist state," they argue.

Why is that the result?

Because according to their model, more automation will require more redistribution to cushion the disruptive effects of automation, so as a country automates more, the tax burden will keep increasing on "capitalists".

So, the "capitalist state" will opt for repression, since repression only has a fixed cost (as a proportion of output), whereas the cost of redistribution keeps increasing with the extent of automation.

It's a strange use of language.

They're talking about the "cost" of repression like it's a basic financial cost of running a state, and they write in negative terms about the "cost" of redistribution when that redistribution is being used to keep people alive and democratic society functioning.

But that's the language these economic models use.

A lot of surveillance, forced compliance

And it's the language some wealthy individuals and business leaders employ.

The paper references an interview with Mo Gawdat, former chief business officer at Google X, who has spoken of the attitudes of many tech leaders as rushing toward full-scale automation and then using other tools to control the population who lose their jobs, in these terms:

"And so you're going to see a world where unfortunately there's going to be a lot of control, a lot of surveillance, a lot of forced compliance."

What influence will the new 'tech oligarchy' have on the US? There’s no official ruling on the collective noun for a group of billionaires, but if ever we needed one it was this week, writes Ange Lavoipierre.

According to Acemoglu, Shadmehr and Gitmez, these types of debates have become prominent in popular media and the business world.

So they have tried to incorporate revolts, triggered by inequality between capital and labour, into a task-based model of automation.

In essence, they have modelled how workers would try to coordinate in an uprising, and how a capitalist state would try to prevent an uprising occurring, in an environment in which automation and inequality are increasing.

Their paper contributes to growing literature on the historical evidence on political and social reactions to automation.

They say the novel finding of their paper is that automation and repression complement and reinforce each other.

Its full dynamic model shows that if society develops to the point where there is a credible threat of revolt against automation, "the economy will ultimately converge to repression and the "pitchforks" will be met with "guns" from the capitalist state".

"In a further extension, we show that if society first starts in a democracy, democratic decision-making will become less and less acceptable to capitalists as the level of the capital stock grows, and society will experience an anti-democratic coup, once again transitioning to repression," the paper notes.

Priscilla Chan, Mark Zuckerberg, Lauren Sanchez, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai, and Elon Musk, among other dignitaries, attend Donald Trump's second inauguration on January 20 last year. (AP: Shawn Thew )

Data centre and AI boom at risk from backlash

The three economists acknowledge that their paper is only a "first step" in the investigation of the dynamics between political regimes and technology choices, especially automation.

They say it would be great to incorporate richer political interactions into their model, including the reality of lobbying and political donations and other forms of democratic capture.

Police drones over troubled town Police will control drones from more than 600 kilometres away from a rural town battling high crime rates.

And they say it would be interesting to explore how advances in AI can change politics in other ways that interact with automation and repression.

But their paper comes at an interesting time.

In recent months, The Economist magazine has been warning that the data centre and AI boom is at risk from a growing public backlash in countries like the United States, Britain, and Australia.

In Australia, there has also been public unease about the increasing use of new surveillance tools used by the state.

The NSW Police Force is currently running an Australian-first trial in Moree (an area with a high indigenous population) using rooftop drones to "fight crime" in the area, controlled by people hundreds of kilometres away at Bankstown Airport.

Live facial recognition cameras to be used by WA Police WA Police are set to become the first in the country to trial live facial recognition of crowds, describing the technology as safer than standard CCTV cameras.

The same police force has been using software developed by Israeli digital forensics company Cellebrite to download the contents of a suspected criminal's phone, including deleted messages and images, and new legislation before NSW parliament seeks to extend those powers for police, which is raising concerns that that capability will eventually shift into routine policing.

Back in 2017, the Fairfax Media reported that Centrelink, the Australian Taxation Office, the Australian Securities and Investment Commission, and the Australan Federal Police were already using Cellebrite technology.

In another Australian-first trial, the Western Australian Police have been using live facial recognition software to scan people walking on the streets of Perth and Fremantle, comparing their faces against a police watchlist in real time.

And AFL clubs are now exploring using facial recognition technology instead of digital or paper tickets.

It's clear we're heading in a certain direction with this technology. Is the state already rehearsing for a more repressive role?

World.title: Report fails to set distance between waste-to-energy plants and homes
World.content:
Melbourne's outer suburban residents have called for tougher standards on rubbish burning after the tabling of a waste-to-energy report in parliament.

A parliamentary investigation has made 33 recommendations, including continuous emissions monitoring, a review of the approvals process, and requiring waste-to-energy companies to contribute to the upkeep of local roads.

The state government has 11 waste-to-energy licences making their way to final approval, including at Sunbury in Melbourne's outer north-west, Wollert in the outer north, Laverton in the west and Dandenong in the south-east.

Communities from across outer Melbourne travelled to state parliament to see the report tabled and to voice concerns about the proposed facilities, including community health and safety, proximity to homes and increases in truck traffic on local roads.

Residents worry plants built close to homes will threaten their health and safety and put more trucks on local roads. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A big bin fire to deal with rubbish?

Waste-to-energy (WTE) is designed to divert rubbish from landfill, burning it to produce heat that is used to make power for the grid.

The committee found there is plenty of rubbish to burn.

It found Victoria generated 5.7 million tonnes of residual waste and only about 69 per cent of that was recovered for other uses. By 2053, it is forecast the state will generate 8.9 million tonnes of waste.

"Managing and reducing this waste safely and sustainably is one of Victoria's most significant waste management challenges," the report said.

The proposed waste-to-energy facility in Wollert. (Supplied)

The committee described WTE as a "lower-order waste management option" for waste that cannot be avoided, reused, recycled or composted — "a last resort before landfill", urging the government to do more to prevent waste through education and making businesses take responsibility for their plastics and packaging products.

The peak body for waste managers welcomed the report.

Gayle Sloan, chief executive of the Waste Management and Resource Recovery Association of Australia (WMRR), said the committee recognised Victoria was not on target to divert 80 per cent of waste from landfill by 2030 and more had to be done to reduce waste.

"It must also honestly confront what happens to the millions of tonnes that remain," she said.

"Without energy recovery, genuine residual waste will continue to be buried in increasingly constrained landfills."

She said the association strongly supported moves for mandatory product stewardship schemes, putting more pressure on industries that design products like packaging that become waste.

"The waste and resource recovery sector shares the committee's frustration that governments continue to demand more from the end of the supply chain while doing far too little at the beginning," Ms Sloan said.

Is WTE safe?

One of the main concerns community members raised with the committee was the potential health impacts of emissions, with differing evidence about links to cancer and reproductive dysfunction.

Dr Peter Tait, from the Public Health Association of Australia, told the inquiry waste-to-energy incineration had been linked to a range of health effects, including cancers and reproductive dysfunction.

But the inquiry found there was "disagreement" about whether the available evidence proves emissions are linked to bad health outcomes.

"Some considered that scientific uncertainty warranted a precautionary approach, while others provided reassurance that modern waste to energy facilities are safe," the report found, calling for an independent community health surveillance program.

The planned locations of waste-to-energy plants around Melbourne. (ABC News: Bill Maguire)

The committee found there was community concern about ash from incinerators and it was not clear how fly ash and incinerator ash would be transported and managed.

"Ultimately, determining the level of risk that is acceptable, and whether the potential benefits of waste-to-energy facilities justify that level of risk, is not a matter for the committee, but a matter for the Victorian government," the committee said.

In a series of recommendations, the committee called for clear information about potential health risks to the community, continuous emissions monitoring, and more information about buffers between homes and facilities.

How close to homes?

The report found Victoria's Environment Protection Authority had no minimum buffer between waste-to-energy facilities and homes, instead making assessments on a case-by-case basis.

Distance between the proposed waste‑to‑energy facility and potential housing in Sunbury. (Supplied: Legislative Council Economy and Infrastructure Committee Inquiry)

"Without a clear benchmark, many people are left wondering whether a proposed facility is too close to where they live and what that could mean for their quality of life and enjoyment of their home," it found.

The report didn't recommend a benchmark, instead calling on the government to provide clear information about how buffers are determined.

Sarah Notaro lives in Sunbury, where a proposed waste-to-energy incinerator that will operate 24 hours a day, burning 750,000 tonnes of rubbish a year for 30 years.

"Just having a facility like that on our doorstep, in our backyard, is really concerning," she said.

Sunbury resident Sarah Notaro says she's worried about families who may move into a new residential development near the plant. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The mother-of-four said there was a lot of concern in Sunbury about the planned facility's proximity to homes — just 800m from a proposed housing development.

"Even just the fact there are housing developments directly across the road, so lots of new families moving into the area," she said.

Catherine Rouse, from the Stop Wollert Waste Incinerator Group in Melbourne's outer north, unveiled a banner she said was borrowed from a group opposing a planned waste incinerator in western Sydney.

Wollert's Catherine Rouse wants to replicate Sydney residents' successful campaign against the plants. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"They were successful and then they banned waste incinerators in the whole of Sydney," she said.

"We're going to be successful here and we're going to keep going until they ban waste incinerators in Victoria."

Legalise Cannabis MP David Ettershank said the committee's report doesn't go far enough in requiring the safety of waste-to-energy technology to be established before planning and technology approvals are granted.

He also called for the establishment of minimum buffer distances between facilities and communities, and for all new facilities to undergo an environmental effects statement.

"For residents living near proposed WTE facilities, the fundamental question remains: Why shouldn't the burden be on industry and government to demonstrate these facilities are safe before approval?" he said.

He said community concerns about safety were real.

"The committee found the incinerators produce a witch's brew of toxic chemicals through emissions, and for every four tonnes of waste that are burnt, one tonne of bottom ash is produced that needs to be stored," he said.

Legalise Cannabis MP David Ettershank describes the WTE emissions as "a witch's brew" of toxic chemicals. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The government was contacted for comment.

In a dissenting report, the Liberals and Nationals on the committee said they supported waste-to-energy in principle, but location was "everything".

This month, the Liberals announced they would scrap plans for a waste-to-energy incinerator at Sunbury.

World.title: Domestic violence, guns, bird flu and data centres focus of leaders' talks
World.content:
A stoush over energy rules for data centres will dominate national cabinet as leaders confront a crowded agenda where progress on guns, GST and other contentious issues is unlikely.

Premiers and chief ministers will meet with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Sydney today to discuss AI data centres, bird flu, domestic violence, fuel security and the national gun buyback.

The federal government's plan to impose national standards for data centres, which would require developers to bring their own renewable energy and set other parameters around water usage and community contributions, is expected to be the biggest source of disagreement.

The Queensland and Northern Territory governments are opposed to the renewables-focused standards and have been scathing of threats the Commonwealth would force their will on states if necessary.

Despite a long running public stoush about GST the tax issue is not on the agenda, with multiple state sources telling the ABC their respective views on the current deal were already no secret.

Agreement around progressing the next five-year national plan to end violence against women and children is likely, but Mr Albanese is facing calls from the federal crossbench to use the meeting to progress more reforms to help tackle the scourge.

The leaders are not due to discuss federal Labor's plan to standardise the private health rebate for all ages, effectively reducing the benefit for older Australians, which the South Australian government this week became the latest jurisdiction to oppose.

Premiers and chief ministers will get a briefing from Australia's chief veterinary officer on the outbreak of H5N1 bird flu, which has now been detected in all six states.

Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen will provide an update on the latest moves to ensure Australia's fuel security amid ongoing disruptions caused by the US war with Iran.

Bowen dismisses nuclear reactors powering data centres

The Australian Energy Market Operator has estimated data centres would grow from currently consuming 3 per cent of the nation's electricity supply to 13 per cent in a decade.

Data centre rush doubles in a year The rush of AI data centres is expected to put a larger burden on the electricity grid than previously estimated, with projects in development more than doubling in a year.

Mr Bowen said yesterday if the government got the policy settings "right" he was confident Australia could handle the electricity demands of data centres.

"That's why we're requiring new data centres to bring their own renewable energy, backed by gas firming," he said.

Mr Bowen has maintained the Commonwealth is prepared to legislate over the top of states, if necessary, though he has not outlined specifics.

"The constitution is pretty clear about, if there's a dispute between Commonwealth legislation and state legislation, which legislation prevails," he said.

He also rubbished the suggestion of data centres running on nuclear small modular reactors, which he described as the "most expensive form of energy and the longest to deploy".

Bowen's data centre energy threat dismissed as foolish

Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie told ABC his government would not be "forced" into a particular energy pathway by the Commonwealth.

"We're our own state and we're pushing back," he said.

"We believe that there are potential investment opportunities in Queensland for data centres, but it's going to be all forms of electricity and we're not going to force renewable energy on regional communities."

Mr Bleijie said Mr Bowen was a "fool" for threatening to override states and suggested the federal minister "doesn't understand the constitution".

"Chris Bowen should be trying to work with state and territories government, not be a big brother bully as he's trying to do in this case," he said.

Asked if Queensland would mount a challenge to any Commonwealth attempt to override the state, Mr Bleijie said he did not believe it would be necessary.

"No-one's going to have to challenge anything because the type of investment won't come because businesses will not invest it if there's only one form of electricity on the table," he said.

Crossbench calls for audit of dollars spent tackling DV

Also at national cabinet, Mr Albanese will raise domestic and sexual violence against women, with states and territories expected to agree to accelerate efforts to respond to the epidemic.

They will also discuss priorities areas for the next five-year national action plan to end violence against women and children, which is due to be released early next year.

Yesterday, more than a dozen crossbenchers signed a letter to Mr Albanese asking him to use the national cabinet meeting to prioritise their calls to beef up the powers of the Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commission.

The MPs and senators, including Allegra Spender, Andrew Wilkie, Helen Haines, Dai Le, Lidia Thorpe, Jacqui Lambie and Fatima Payman, have asked that the commission be made a statutory authority and given the ability to compel data, audit spending and track whether measures governments have funded are "actually working".

"A decade of reviews and inquiries into domestic, family and sexual violence has produced more than 1,000 recommendations, yet women and children continue to die, and too many systemic failures remain," the letter said.

"Billions of dollars flow to states and territories every year for these programs, but there is no equivalent oversight of where that money goes or whether it is reducing harm."

Gun buyback far from national

Mr Albanese's attempt to establish a national gun buyback in the wake of the Bondi terror attack will be discussed at the meeting though developments are unlikely.

Only NSW and the ACT have signed up to the proposal so far, while Western Australia recently completed its own voluntary program.

Anthony Albanese is yet convince remaining states to adopt the gun buyback scheme. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

But no further jurisdictions are likely to join the scheme.

Cooperation is far more likely in the ongoing response to the deadly outbreak of H5N1 bird flu, which has reached all the major states and recently been detected in a mammal.

World.title: 'Innocent parcels' caught up illicit tobacco bust
World.content:
Amy Zhang spent 300,000 yuan ($62,000) on a custom-made set of kitchen cabinets from China for her new home in Melbourne.

The cabinets were shipped on July 7 and were expected to arrive in a month's time.

While they did arrive in Australia a few weeks later, they have been held in quarantine in Sydney since.

Ms Zhang believes the logistics company handling her parcel has been affected by a recent crackdown on alleged importations of illicit tobacco and vapes into Australia.

The Multi Agency Strike Team (MAST) says it has dismantled two criminal networks. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

Earlier this month, a multi-agency strike team including detectives from NSW and federal law enforcement agencies dismantled two alleged multimillion-dollar criminal networks and charged seven people.

The ABC has confirmed one of the seven people was 53-year-old Peter Ping Xie, who is also the director of Top Logistics Australia (TLA), the company supposed to be delivering Ms Zhang's kitchen cabinets.

Mr Xie has been accused of multiple offences, including obtaining financial advantages by deception, knowingly dealing with proceeds of crime and possessing an unauthorised pistol.

Ms Zhang tried to look up her cabinets' tracking number on TLA's website, but the latest status said "shipment info received" on July 16.

She also contacted the shipping company, which told her the parcel arrived in Sydney on July 22 and was with the Australian government's quarantine and inspection service.

Ms Zhang said the builders had been waiting for the cabinets to arrive to complete the kitchen and it was costing her hundreds of dollars to rent portable toilets for the workers, fencing and cameras every week the delivery was delayed.

"My construction site has basically stopped, and everyone is waiting for the cabinets to arrive," she said, adding that there was no indication when the furniture would be delivered.

Police seized more than $2.5 million worth of illicit tobacco products during multiple searches. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

An Australian Border Force (ABF) spokesperson told the ABC: "As a result of Strikeforce Borderdale, the ABF issued the immediate suspension of depot licences in Sydney and Brisbane, with a notice of intent to cancel in Melbourne for a national freight forwarding company."

The ABF did not name the company in its response to the ABC.

The ABC also asked the ABF how many legitimate parcels were being held at the impacted depots and what would happen to those goods.

The ABF declined to comment, citing the fact the matter was before the courts.

Book Week costumes fail to arrive

ABF suspended the depot licences for a logistics company caught up in the crackdown. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

Many people with similar experiences to Ms Zhang have taken to social media to express concerns about delayed parcels.

Some said their packages of ski clothing and children's costumes for Book Week had not arrived in time.

Sydney mother Mory Zhao is also waiting for a cubby house she bought from China for her four-year-old son.

The item plus shipping cost about 40,000 yuan ($8,300).

Mory Zhao says her four-year-old son had been looking forward to the cubby house. (Supplied: Mory Zhao)

It left China on July 29 and was due to arrive in Sydney on August 9 but its tracking status on the shipping company's portal has not changed since it was sent.

"My child has been looking forward to it every day … and then this happened. It's really frustrating," Ms Zhao said.

Ms Zhao said her items were shipped as part of a consolidated order with other people's goods, so she could not check the status on the TLA's portal.

On Chinese social media platform RedNote, several people posted TLA tracking information showing their shipments had arrived in Australia, but were still awaiting customs clearance.

Other users posted screenshots showing the status as "customs clearance withdrawn".

The ABC's calls to the TLA went unanswered and the company also did not respond to the ABC's email enquiries.

TLA's online customer service is also available.

'One-stop shops' could create risks

Headquartered in Sydney, TLA said on its website the company is a "one-stop logistics solution provider". Its depots in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane have a combined space of more than 15,000 square metres.

Sharon Kwok, a criminology lecturer from Western Sydney University, said "one-stop shop" logistics companies could make supply chains more efficient but could also create opportunities for organised crime if a part of that chain was compromised.

Seven people have been charged as part of the crackdown. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

"If you have a company that can handle everything in one place, there are fewer [third parties] involved compared with a traditional logistics company," Dr Kwok said.

"There is a high risk that it could be exploited."

Dr Kwok believed that logistics companies could be exploited by organised crime syndicates looking to make large profit margins from illicit tobacco and vaping products.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) estimated that illicitly sourced tobacco accounted for 80 per cent of tobacco consumed in Australia in 2025, up from 12 per cent in 2017.

Kevin Liu, a logistics company owner and industry insider, said it was positive to see the dismantling of the alleged criminal network connected to the logistics company.

He said logistics companies involved in illegal activities could also affect legitimate businesses.

Kevin Liu is the managing director of Pinle Logistics and has worked in the China-Australia freight industry for more than a decade. (Supplied: Kevin Liu)

"They can generate substantial profits through illegal activities, so they don't necessarily need to make money from their legitimate operations.

"That gives them the ability to operate on very thin margins, or even at a loss, which can seriously distort competition and disrupt the industry."

Ms Zhang said she supported the crackdown on the criminal syndicate but wanted authorities to distinguish between illicit goods and legitimate shipments.

"We support the police operation, but it shouldn't affect innocent people," she said.

"They should release the innocent parcels first."

World.title: One Nation has again had to clear up its migration target, so exactly what is the NOM?
World.content:
Three letters are defining the latest migration debate in Australia and catching out political parties.

Net overseas migration, or NOM, has become a de facto measure on how tough each party is on migration but the term is widely misunderstood.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson this week was again forced to clear up the party's NOM target, after their newest MP David Farley suggested the party's figures were "not too different" to Labor's.

Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are all saying they will cut back on net overseas migration, although how exactly each party plans to achieve this remains scant on detail and policy.

So what exactly is the NOM, what kind of factors cause it to fluctuate, and where do the political parties stand?

What is Net Overseas Migration (NOM)?

The NOM figure is the number of people who have arrived in Australia and stayed for a year or more, minus the number of people who have left to live overseas.

But that year doesn't have to be continuous — the NOM is calculated using a "12/16-month rule", meaning it counts people who have stayed in Australia for 12 months out of a 16-month period.

Everybody wants to cut migration The causes of migration are murky and it is harder for politicians to control than they would like to admit.

For example, someone could come to Australia and stay for nine months, go overseas for a month, and then return to Australia for another three months. They would then be counted in the NOM figure and added to our estimated resident population.

Foreign diplomats and their families are not included in the NOM.

It's important to note that the NOM number doesn't just include foreigners coming to Australia on visas — it also includes Australian citizens and permanent residents returning home after a long stint overseas, or New Zealand citizens moving here.

And there are other complexities.

Take, for example, the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme, which aims to fill agricultural gaps in regional and rural Australia by recruiting workers from Pacific islands for short-term jobs of up to nine months, or longer-term jobs of up to four years.

Such workers would not be counted in the NOM if they're recruited for a nine-month role, but they would be if they were employed for a longer-term job.

What's our NOM right now?

The latest data, released in June, puts the NOM at 300,960. That figure represents the year to December 2025.

It's a sharp drop from a post-pandemic peak of 556,000 in 2023.

The budget has forecasted the NOM to decline to 225,000 from 2027-28.

However, the NOM has repeatedly exceeded Treasury forecasts.

What visas contribute to the NOM?

Some visa classes that have been floated for cuts are skilled visas, working holidays visas, family reunion visas, international student visas and graduate visas.

Employer wait for overseas nurses, teachers blows out Business leaders hope the current visa settings will be in place for 'a very short time'.

In 2024-25, the biggest cohort of visas contributing to NOM were international students (156,700), with the vast majority of those being in the higher education sector.

Permanent and temporary skilled visas combined brought in around 86,000 people.

Working holiday-makers were around 78,000. There were 24,000 family visas and just under 15,000 humanitarian visas.

The NOM is a nebulous figure, and because it includes the unpredictable movements of Australians and New Zealanders coming and going, it's not something that can be entirely controlled by limiting visas.

Of overseas migrant arrivals in 2024-25, 64,000 were Australian citizens and 53,000 were New Zealanders.

One Nation confusion

One Nation's Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce have both reiterated they want a NOM figure of 130,000.

The pair were mopping up after One Nation's newest MP, David Farley, suggested his party's figures wouldn't be too far off the number forecast in the budget, during an interview on Insiders.

One Nation say they have a firm NOM target of 130,000. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"Our position's 130,000 net overseas migration," Mr Farley said.

"So when we look at the NOM, we've got to also be cognisant there's about a million Australians living offshore at the moment. Even if half of them decided to return, they'll affect the NOM."

But the numbers became increasingly muddled as he elaborated.

He said "on top of" that "true NOM" of 130,000, there were other programs to account for, such as PALM workers — important in his regional electorate or Farrer — and aged care nurses who would not be included in the NOM.

He agreed this would add up to around 100,000 more places "at a minimum", on top of the 130,000 NOM number.

Treasury's NOM forecast for 2027/28 is 225,000.

"The raw number's not too different," he said.

Loading...

After the interview, Ms Hanson took to X to clarify One Nation's NOM target was 130,000.

She signalled the party wanted a "dramatic" reduction in temporary graduate visas, would reduce the number of international students and their dependents, and wanted "a much more targeted skilled migration program".

"We've reviewed the numbers, we've got far too many, 130,000 Net Overseas Migration is our number and we're sticking to it," Mr Joyce told News24 on Monday.

But Ms Hanson added to the confusion further by recently deleting a social media post from March this year, in which she suggested One Nation wanted to cap arrivals at 130,000 per year and combine that with migrant departures — which she said was 230,000 last year — to reach the NOM. In that example, it would lead to a negative NOM of minus 100,000.

The One Nation website says the party will push for "capping visas at 130,000 per year", which would not influence the number of Australians coming and going visa-free.

Mr Joyce added that people should "ignore" the number of people entering the country under the PALM scheme, because they often stay for under 12 months and would not be counted in the NOM.

What are Labor and the Coalition's targets?

The Coalition has not yet finalised its target, but has repeatedly said it wanted to tie NOM to housing construction rates.

"It'll be set based on the housing supply," Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said on Tuesday.

" It'll be capped based on how many houses we have. Now we expect that'll be well below 200,000. But we'll see what housing looks like over the next little while. "

Earlier this month, Liberal senator Andrew Bragg floated the idea of a NOM of 180,000, saying working holiday-makers, student visas and some skilled visas could be targeted.

"We want fewer pastry chefs and more builders," he said.

Senator Andrew Bragg was counselled for 'freelancing' after suggesting a NOM of 180,000. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

But Nationals leader Matt Canavan said touching working holiday visas, often colloquially described as backpacker visas, was off the cards.

Many in rural and regional areas rely heavily on those workers.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has now labelled the Treasury NOM forecast of 225,000 by 2028 a target.

"We've finalised our numbers. We're headed to 225,000 in two years' time," Mr Albanese told ABC Radio Perth on Tuesday.

But how Labor will get there remains unclear.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke earlier this month postponed a National Press Club address in which he was expected to outline Labor's policies to lower migration numbers.

The focus for the government is ensuring that temporary visa holders stay temporary, cracking down on people who are staying in Australia years longer than expected.

Ahead of a looming migration overhaul, Mr Burke has also moved to stop migrants from coming into Australia by pausing or slowing down processing of working holiday and skilled visas.

Tony Burke delayed a speech in which he was expected to outline Labor's migration policies. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"We have a series of plans in place. There's more work to do, and we'll work on that and make announcements at [the] appropriate time," Mr Albanese said.

He said the Coalition and One Nation were throwing around NOM numbers "like confetti, with no real plan".

He added skilled migration was important for the aged care and agriculture sectors, as well as getting houses built in the construction industry.

"That's the contradiction in the Liberal position as well, which is really just a fudge, because they're frightened of One Nation," Mr Albanese said.

World.title: Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVaccination Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000 Michael Koziol August 26, 2026 — 5:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Two unvaccinated people died from measles in the US state of Pennsylvania, becoming the first deaths there from the disease in 35 years amid a growing national outbreak. Pennsylvania’s Department of Health announced the deaths on Tuesday (US time), and warned that the return of measles after a decades-long absence meant people did not grasp its severity. US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr announced an overhaul of federal guidelines on the childhood vaccine schedule this month. Bloomberg It comes as US President Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr, continue to sow doubts about vaccines, including by pushing an unsubstantiated link with autism. This month, Trump signed an executive order that called for parents to space out their children’s vaccine visits and break up the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) jab - which is not currently possible.



Both deaths were in Lancaster County – an area of southern Pennsylvania with a large Amish population, which has historically had lower rates of vaccination. The department would not release further information about the deceased. So far in 2026, Pennsylvania has detected 393 cases of measles in 28 counties. Across the US, there have been 2777 confirmed cases this year, spanning most states and Washington DC. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is only available as a combined dose at present. AP Photo/Mary Conlon Tuesday’s announcement marked the first time people died from measles in Pennsylvania in 35 years. They are also the first US deaths from the disease this year. Last year, three Americans died, following nearly a decade of zero deaths. Pennsylvania’s health secretary, Debra Bogen, said the virtual elimination of measles in the state for more than three decades meant “people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness”.



The best way to protect against measles was vaccination, she said, with two doses of the MMR vaccine providing 97 per cent lifetime protection. The number of measles cases recorded this year has already eclipsed last year’s total of 2289. Nearly 50 per cent were among young people aged five to 19, and 94 per cent were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, according to the Centres for Disease Control. Trump has issued an executive order to establish a “gold standard” vaccination schedule for children. Bloomberg The 2025 and 2026 figures are the highest measles numbers in decades, with only a 2019 outbreak (1274 cases) coming close. Earlier in August, Trump urged parents to break up the MMR vaccine into three separate shots, even though that is not currently enabled by the medical profession or the pharmaceutical industry.



In a subsequent briefing with reporters, US officials said they would work with the private sector to try to make separate doses available. Related Article Trump's White House Trump’s vaccine order adds more fuel to the anti-vaccine fire At a televised news conference in the Oval Office, Trump said the US was recommending too many vaccines. He claimed without evidence that the MMR vaccine could be “quite lethal”, but when given separately, “it looks like they are not at all lethal but just every effective”. The US president also falsely spoke of an “explosion” in vaccine injury, and claimed that doctors were injecting children with large doses that looked like “a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body”. Trump’s executive order did not mention autism. But in his unscripted remarks, he asserted an unproven link between vaccination and higher rates of autism diagnoses in modern times.



“There’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was,” he said. The president’s order does not change vaccine requirements for schools, or impact the policies of state health departments. Rather, it stands as a recommendation from the US federal government. US Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy J has long been a vaccine sceptic. Bloomberg Following Trump’s announcement, the American Medical Association said that altering the proven childhood vaccination schedule without credible evidence risked weakening public confidence in vaccines, and putting children’s health at risk. “Extensive evidence from decades of scientific studies shows no link between vaccines and autism,” president Willie Underwood said. “Putting our children’s health at risk is not an option.”



The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to questions from this masthead about the measles outbreak and deaths in Pennsylvania. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs Stan Choe August 26, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices are falling again, which is helping to ease worries in the bond market and support stock prices. The S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent and edged a bit closer to its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 107 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.4 per cent higher. UBS’ trading desk said earlier this week that the slide in momentum stocks may be nearing its end, creating an opportunity for investors. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 5.06am AEST pointing to a rise of 29 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.7 per cent on Tuesday. Reporting season continues with Nine Entertainment, WiseTech and Woolworths results due out. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.61¢. Some of the strongest action was in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 3.9 per cent to $US87.05 and was heading for a second decline following 13 gains in 14 days. The drop came even though tensions between the United States and Iran seemed to ratchet higher after the Trump administration announced new sanctions to further hurt Iran’s economy.



Brent’s price zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Related Article Electric vehicles Aussie capitals ‘will be driverless within a decade’, says robotaxi pioneer A delegation from Pakistan left Iran after talks with Iran’s president and other senior officials on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reviving negotiations to end the Iran-US conflict, the Pakistani military said. Pakistan Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had been “very positive and productive.” Tuesday’s drop in oil prices tempered the worries about high inflation that helped drive Treasury yields in the bond market higher through the summer. Yields had gotten so high that the US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase its repurchases of longer-term Treasury notes and bonds. High yields make borrowing more expensive for everyone and can slow the economy’s growth while undercutting prices for stocks, cryptocurrencies and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Monday and from 4.74 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a significant move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains firmly above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher. Canada announced it is targeting more than 700 US-made products as the trade war with America escalates. The list extends well beyond industrial goods, hitting everyday purchases such as seafood, cheese, clothing, cosmetics and toilet paper, with some facing duties as high as 50 per cent. The tariffs on American steel, dairy products, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper and electronics take effect September 8 at rates of 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 50 per cent, with Canada matching the corresponding US tariff rate on each product. Canadian officials said the goal is not to raise revenue but to protect Canadian companies and reduce US imports. On Wall Street, Nvidia and other winners of the boom in artificial-intelligence technology helped lead the way. Nvidia rose 1.8 per cent, a day after its drop of 2.9 per cent was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. AI stocks have veered up and down through the summer on worries that their prices shot too high and that the AI boom may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce enough profits for companies. Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday, which could help steer the next move for AI-related stocks.



The gains for chip stocks helped offset a 30.1 per cent drop for Dick’s Sporting Goods, which reported weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Executive Chairman Ed Stack said the retailer cut prices on some of its footwear and apparel to remain competitive, while launches for some footwear during the quarter ended up being weaker than it expected. Related Article Supermarkets Why Coles won’t copy Woolies’ Ooshies sugar hit The company cut its forecast for an underlying measure of profit in 2026 for both its Dick’s and Foot Locker businesses. The company spent $US2.4 billion last year to acquire the struggling Foot Locker chain as inventory in footwear began to pile up for most retailers. Dick’s stock is potentially heading toward its worst day in history. Worries have been rising about how strong spending can remain generally for U.S. households, which is the main engine of the economy. They’re facing higher prices on everything from food to clothes and a job market that suddenly looks iffier after employers cut more jobs last month than they added. A report from the Conference Board on Tuesday said that confidence among U.S. consumers weakened by more than economists expected.



In stock markets around the world, many indexes drifted modestly higher. South Korea’s Kospi, which is dominated by two AI winners, added 0.7 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. It’s been steadying since plunging 22.2 per cent in July. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaEpstein fallout Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein Michael R. Sisak and Larry Neumeister Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:23am ,first published 11:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Ghislaine Maxwell’s bid to overturn her sex trafficking conviction and be freed from prison was rejected by a US federal judge on Tuesday (US time) who said the claims by Jeffrey Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime associate that new evidence had emerged were “demonstrably meritless”. Maxwell filed a habeas petition – a legal procedure challenging her detention – last December seeking to set aside her conviction and free her from a 20-year prison sentence, claiming exonerating information was withheld and false testimony presented at her trial, resulting in a “complete miscarriage of justice”. Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. Getty Judge Paul A. Engelmayer rejected her arguments, saying in his written ruling they “all or almost all are frivolous” and that she had presented nothing that could upend the outcome of her trial. “Nearly all its claims are procedurally barred; the overwhelming testimonial and documentary evidence adduced at trial conclusively established her guilt; and her petition’s claims are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods,” Engelmayer wrote.





The judge noted that many of Maxwell’s claims of “new evidence” stem from documents released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. As a result of that law, the Justice Department over the last eight months has released 18 categories of investigative materials gathered in the massive sex trafficking probe, including search warrants, financial records, notes from interviews with victims and data from electronic devices. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life Engelmayer said that material is “largely irrelevant to the charges against Maxwell and does not support her claims of error.” “On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges,” he wrote.



The judge also rejected Maxwell’s claim that she was selectively prosecuted and made a “scapegoat” when the Justice Department did not indict four co-conspirators named in a government document or 25 men who settled with victims. Engelmayer said she could have raised that claim on appeal after her trial, but he found it to be frivolous nonetheless. Among the recently released Justice Department documents, “she does not cite any that reveals the existence of an uncharged confederate, let alone one as instrumental as she in facilitating Epstein’s horrific crimes,” the judge said. World.title: Gold has lost its glitter. Does that mean it’s time to buy?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingGold Opinion Gold has lost its glitter. Does that mean it’s time to buy?

Justin Lin August 26, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In February, I walked past a bullion dealer in the Sydney CBD with a queue that wrapped around the corner. Gold had just peaked above $US5600 ($7800) an ounce, capping a 12-month run of more than 80 per cent. Six months later, the queues have gone, gold sits near $US4600, and the question I get from investors has inverted. It used to be: “How high can this go?” Now it’s: “Why did my safe haven fail me during a war?” The positioning that made gold fragile in February has been cleared out and the price has rebased to a level far easier to defend. Trevor Collens It is a fair question. Gold’s first half was a disappointment, but unlike how many investors would paint it, nothing about it was mysterious, nor did it reveal any fundamental flaws in gold. Consider the starting point. At the beginning of this year, gold had been perhaps the best-performing major asset on the planet for three years, at one point rising more than 60 per cent in six months.



When an asset climbs that fast it attracts a particular kind of buyer – the one who arrives because the price is rising, not because of any particular thesis. Those buyers set the price at the top and are the first to leave. Then there is the conflict itself. The Iran war has been the most energy-centric war in modern market history, with more than a fifth of the world’s crude and gas exports at risk. That may instinctively read an oil shock as an inflation shock, and inflation as good news for gold. Central banks have accumulated gold for years as a deliberate act of diversification away from the US dollar. The market did something less intuitive. It priced in a central bank forced to stay tight, or even hike. Yields climbed, and gold, which pays no coupon, always struggles against a rising cost of holding it. Finally, amid the clamouring of gold’s failure as a “haven”, it should be noted that nobody truly wanted insurance. Uncertainty hit decade highs, yes, yet equity markets stayed risk-on, propped up by earnings certainty in semiconductors and AI. Investors do not buy a hedge when the thing they are hedging keeps going up.



Three headwinds, all rational, but none a defect in gold. What has changed, however, is that the froth is gone. The positioning that made gold fragile in February has been cleared out and the price has rebased to a level far easier to defend. Anyone buying today is buying an asset that has had its reckoning. Meanwhile, the core investment case remains rock steady, and the accumulators that drove gold’s rally before are making their return. Central banks have accumulated gold for years as a deliberate act of diversification away from the US dollar. That buying slowed in the first half – exactly what you would expect when a war forces policymakers to prioritise liquidity over strategy. But as of August, despite tensions still simmering in the Middle East, central bank buying may have already resumed. The People’s Bank of China recently extended its streak to 21 straight months in July, adding 20 tonnes, its largest monthly purchase by volume since October 2023. And in the World Gold Council’s annual survey of reserve managers, 89 per cent expected global official gold holdings to keep rising over the next 12 months, while 74 per cent expected the US dollar’s share of global reserves to be lower in five years.



Asian investors, a new force in the market, have proven similarly committed. Regional gold ETFs took in a record $US12 billion in the first half, the largest contribution to global flows, and that held through a brutal June of profit taking. A physical gold fund was, for a while, the largest ETF of any kind in mainland China, bigger than the local equivalent of an S&P 500 tracker. Editor's pick Investing ‘They want a piece of that pie’: Gold FOMO untarnished by price meltdown Which brings us to now. Consolidation is miserable to sit through and obvious only in hindsight, but the conditions that made gold vulnerable have been quietly unwinding. The labour market that spent the first half looking indestructible shed 23,000 US jobs in July. Markets that had priced a September rate rise as a near-certainty, now put the odds closer to one in three. Gold has climbed about 8 per cent in a month to a 10-week high, and its correlation with oil and equities has drifted back towards zero as key accumulators return. Six months ago, gold was a crowded trade at a record high. Today, it is an uncrowded one at a discount, with a structural case that has strengthened rather than weakened. The queues outside the bullion dealers may be shorter, but, ironically, now may be the right time to enter the store.



Justin Lin is an Investment Strategist at Global X ETFs Australia. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Should I sell my $1m investment property and put it into my super?
World.content:
August 26, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m a young retiree at 61 years. I have a $500,000 share portfolio and a 20-year-held investment property worth $1 million. I’m of a mind to sell the property and realise the share portfolio over the next four years, and slowly use concessional contributions to the maximum to get the money into a good super fund. I wonder if I’m putting all my eggs into one basket, so to speak. However, I feel simplicity moving forward in retirement is good. The amount in super should provide a perpetual retirement income, as we intend to take the minimum government limits, i.e. 4 per cent, 5 per cent, etc. What are your thoughts on such a simplification? Topping up your super can be a great way to bolster your retirement savings. Simon Letch Finally, you mentioned the downsizer contribution of $300,000 into super. If you’re already at your cap, i.e. $1.9 million for myself, I take it the $300,000 has to sit in the accumulation bucket and thus have gains taxed. Is this correct? You’ve held the investment property for a long time, so the decision about selling it sooner rather than later should be based primarily on its future potential, not on how long you have owned it.



But I do think money invested in a good super fund should outperform a 20-year-old investment property, particularly once you consider the costs and hassles that come with owning property. I also don’t see why you need to leave all the proceeds in accumulation mode. It would seem you have plenty of room to contribute money to super and then transfer it to pension mode, where the earnings will be tax-free. Shares acquired before September 1985 will lose their CGT-free status on June 30, 2027. As for investing part of the portfolio more aggressively in international shares, there is nothing wrong with that in principle. The important point is that super is merely the structure – you can still have a well-diversified portfolio inside it. Moving your investments into super does not mean putting all your eggs into one investment basket. As far as the downsizer contribution is concerned, the limit is $300,000 per person, which means a couple may be able to put $600,000 into super, irrespective of age or the amount already in super.



There is no requirement that a downsizer contribution must stay in accumulation mode. The transfer balance cap is now $2.1 million, so provided you have sufficient personal transfer balance cap available, you may have plenty of space to move more of your super into pension mode. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 64. Should I use my super to pay off the rest of my mortgage? Paul Benson Money contributor You have mentioned several times that the “old” capital gains tax regime of a 50 per cent discount will apply for pensioners and others in receipt of government assistance rather than the new laws. Does this apply only to shares purchased before July 1, 2027 and will new shares or dividend reinvestments purchased after July 1, 2027 be subject to the new capital gains rules? As I understand it, cost base indexation will apply to determine the amount of CGT for gains that accrue from July 1, 2027, however, anyone who receives at least $1 of government income support in the year the asset is sold won’t be subject to a minimum tax rate of 30 per cent. Shares you own now and liquidated before June 30, 2027 will be subject to the existing CGT rules with the 50 per cent discount applying. If sold after that date, the profit will be split between pre-June 30, 2027 and post-June 30, 2027 gains. The value of the shares at June 30, 2027 will be indexed, with a calculation of CGT on the shares after that date.



I have $1.3 million in mainly bank shares returning about $55,000 in reinvested dividends. After June 30, 2027, if I take the dividends as cash payments, am I right in assuming the existing shares will retain the 50 per cent discount until my death? That is not correct. You will need to record the balance of your shares on June 30, 2027. Any shares sold after that date will be given a notional indexed cost base to ensure that any gain from June 30, 2027 to the date of your sale are taxed after adjustment for inflation. All shares sold before June 30, 2027 will get the 50 per cent discount. I bought and have retained shares in two ASX-listed blue-chip companies in the period between 1974 and September 20, 1985, when the CGT was introduced, and more after that latter date. Do the recent changes to the CGT rules apply to all of these shares, or will the shares I acquired before the introduction of the CGT remain exempt from the CGT when I sell them? Shares acquired before September 1985 will lose their CGT-free status on June 30, 2027 – the cost base for CGT purposes going forward will be their market value at that date. When I was 18 – I’m now 59 – I read your book Making Money Made Simple, and I am now wealthy. I have saturated my super and, as I am on the highest marginal tax rate, have been looking at investment bonds. However, I have read that for some people it may be better simply to invest in an exchange-traded fund (ETF) because the costs are lower. I would welcome your comments on this and wonder whether you have done any modelling comparing the two alternatives.



Think of investment bonds as an alternative to super, but with some similar characteristics. They are both tax-paid investments, which means there is nothing to include on your annual tax return until you cash them in. Unlike super, there is no limit on the amount you can invest in investment bonds, and there is no lack of access, as you can cash them in at any time. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start? Noel Whittaker Money columnist The tax in a super fund will be zero or 15 per cent, depending on whether the balance is in pension mode or accumulation mode, whereas investment bonds pay a maximum tax rate of 30 per cent. If you hold the bond for 10 years, the entire proceeds can be redeemed tax-free. A bonus is that you are allowed to contribute up to 125 per cent of the previous year’s investment without restarting the 10-year period. If you redeem the bond before eight years is up, the profit is fully taxable, less a 30 per cent rebate to compensate you for the tax already paid by the bond fund. The management fees may be slightly higher in an investment bond than in a share-based ETF.



But don’t let fees become the tail that wags the dog. You are in the 47 per cent tax bracket, so the real comparison is not simply the fees on an ETF versus the fees on an investment bond. It is the after-tax return from each. The bond keeps the tax rate at a maximum of 30 per cent and, given you have many years ahead of you, you can take a long-term view and redeem the entire proceeds after 10 years tax-free. In your situation, I think that is a major advantage. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: The alarming reason one in three seniors are giving up aged care
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAged care Opinion The alarming reason one in three seniors are giving up aged care Rachel Lane Money contributor August 26, 2026 — 5:01am

August 26, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The most worrying thing about the new aged care system is not that people are paying more for care. It is that some are deciding they can’t afford care at all. A YouGov survey of 1044 senior Australians found that one in three have reduced or stopped home care since November 1 because they can’t afford the new co-contributions. The impact is greatest among those under financial pressure: almost seven in 10 say the new payments have made them more reluctant to seek help, rising to nearly three in four among those experiencing financial hardship. Sadly, for 6 per cent, the cost of care now means choosing between aged care and essentials such as food and electricity. While it may not sound like a care issue, social isolation has serious consequences for your health. iStock The survey found that seven in 10 believe aged care services are too expensive. However, there is an important distinction that appears to be getting lost. The new system doesn’t apply a co-contribution to every service. Think of your Support at Home funding as one bucket of money, divided into three smaller buckets – clinical care, independence and everyday living – with a different co-contribution applying to each.



Clinical care, which includes nursing and allied health, has a zero co-contribution. These services can cost $150 to $200 an hour, and they will certainly use up funding in your Support at Home package, but they won’t cost you anything out of your own pocket. That’s what makes it particularly alarming that up to 13 per cent of survey respondents have reduced or given up clinical services. If people are refusing nursing or allied health because they believe they cannot afford it, we have a communication problem as well as a care problem. Before saying ‘no’ to care because you think you can’t afford it, check what you will actually have to pay. At the other end of the scale are everyday living services such as cleaning, meal preparation, gardening and home maintenance. The survey showed the highest proportion of recipients (20 per cent) had reduced or eliminated domestic help. These services can cost $100 to $150 an hour and attract a co-contribution of between 17.5 per cent and 80 per cent. For a full pensioner, paying 17.5 per cent of a $150 gardening or home maintenance service means a contribution of $26.25 an hour.



If you can afford it, that may seem reasonable. For a self-funded retiree paying 80 per cent, $120 an hour, it’s a different proposition, and they may be better off buying private services. The survey doesn’t make it clear whether some people are opting for private care instead. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care Half-priced aged care at home sounds like a bargain. Here’s why it isn’t Rachel Lane Money contributor Social support sits in between. It is classified as an independence service which attracts a contribution of between 5 per cent and 50 per cent. With prices of $100 to $130 an hour, that could mean paying anywhere from $5 to $65 an hour. Up to 14 per cent of people receiving social support have reduced or declined these services. While it may not sound like a care issue, social isolation has serious consequences for your health. Under the new system more people are paying more towards their home care, but the cost is not across the board. Clinical care remains free, while the biggest increases are concentrated in independence and everyday living services.



Before saying “no” to care because you think you can’t afford it, check what you will actually have to pay. Rachel Lane is the author of Downsizing Made Simple, a book and website aimed at demystifying downsizing.
