World.title: My daughter wanted to be a nepo baby. I didn’t hire her, now she won’t talk to me
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? My daughter wanted to be a nepo baby. I didn’t hire her, now she won’t talk to me Kirstin Ferguson August 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: putting a stop to nepotism, a morning quiz and job-hunting at 62. A company deserves the strongest candidate, not just someone who shares a surname with the boss. Dionne Gain My adult daughter won’t speak to me after I hired someone else to work in the business I run. She assumed she’d automatically get a job with me after university, but I hired a more experienced candidate for the opening that came up. The whole thing has caused a real rift in our relationship. I know I did the right thing as a boss, but as a mother I feel terrible about the impact it has had. How do you balance both? Related Article Got a Minute? Everyone in my office gets free lunch, except me. How is that fair? You definitely made the right decision for your business, which deserves the strongest candidate, and not someone chosen simply because you are related. Favouring family at the expense of fairness rarely ends well for anyone.



You would also know that sometimes being a good parent means disappointing your child. What matters is helping her to understand one missed opportunity doesn’t define either her career or your relationship. In retrospect, it may have been more helpful to establish the expectation very early with your daughter that she would never get a job automatically – with you or any hiring manager. Gaining employment is a privilege she will need to work for like anyone else, and I think you will be able to help her in future by reviewing her resume, suggesting vacancies (in other businesses) as they come up, and being her biggest cheerleader when she scores her dream job. With time and maturity, I am sure your daughter will come to understand you did what you needed to do. Not just as a professional, but also as a mother. We have a new manager who makes a point of going to every person’s desk each morning with a notebook and pen and asks, “What are you working on today, what do you hope to achieve, and what didn’t you finish yesterday?” He makes notes, but does not offer any advice, assistance or comments, then goes to the next person. We have a very open office plan so it puts the team members on the spot with having to come up with answers quickly and the whole team can hear the conversations. We absolutely dread this time of the morning. Staff are starting to get very stressed with not knowing what he does with his notes. It feels as if we have to justify our roles every day, and as if the company is considering redundancies. He is not the most approachable person. We don’t have an HR manager. What should we do? Related Article Got a Minute? I discovered my married boss is cheating with a co-worker. What do I do? Rather than assume the worst, I wonder whether your manager may genuinely be trying to engage with you and understand what everyone is working on, but is doing so in a completely misguided way. I suspect he has no idea of the impact he is having on trust and culture. He doesn’t sound as if he has much emotional intelligence or self-awareness and is completely unaware of the discomfort he causes.



The uncertainty about why the questions are being asked is almost certainly contributing more to the team’s anxiety than the questions themselves. Rather than speculating, someone needs to ask him what the morning routine is all about. If no one feels comfortable doing it alone, consider approaching him as a group. Simply say, “We’re finding the morning check-ins a little unsettling because we’re not sure how the information is being used. Would you mind explaining what this information might be for?” You might discover there’s an innocent explanation, or your feedback may alert him to an unintended consequence. You need to ask, whatever the response, so everyone is clear. I am 62 and had to leave my workplace due to a workcover claim. I have been applying for roles for months with no success. I have applied for junior roles but am told I’m too qualified. I have applied for similar roles in different industries where my skills are transferable, but I’m finding employers won’t take the risk on me. Any ideas on how to move forward and keep positive? It may be time to think laterally and widen your search. Have you considered options such as short-term contracts, consulting, mentoring, project work or even working with not-for-profit organisations? These can all be pathways to be a permanent position. Many employers are looking for the kind of judgment and reliability that comes only with experience. Your job hunt now needs to focus on finding a company wise enough to recognise your age as one of your strengths. Good luck!

World.title: Plane lovers will adore this bargain Japanese airport hotel
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews Plane lovers will adore this bargain Japanese airport hotel Kristie Kellahan August 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel OMO Kansai Airport The hotel is a short walk from Rinku-Town station, near Osaka’s Kansai Airport. Check-in Getting to OMO Kansai Airport hotel, which opened in 2023, is stress-free, even in my tired and jet-lagged state. The first airport-focused hotel in the OMO collection by Japanese hospitality group Hoshino Resorts, the property is located at Rinku-Town station, one stop from Osaka’s Kansai International Airport. I exit the station, follow signs to the hotel entrance and go to the second floor, where I check in. Automated kiosks display prompts to scan my passport and QR booking code to receive my room key but human attendants are also on hand to offer assistance. I’m excited to have access to communal, hot, carbonated baths and saunas on the third floor (free of charge for in-house guests), and within 15 minutes of arriving at the hotel I’m marinating in 40-degree pools.



The look 



Room configurations include single, twin and triple. There are 700 rooms in multiple configurations including queen, twin and triple. I’ve booked a Queen Room for one person at the Solo Special rate of 9000JPY ($81), such a bargain price I assume at first glance it must be a typo. The room is 18 square metres and includes a queen bed, shower stall and toilet. Room amenities include an air purifier, kettle and tea, slippers and toothbrush. There’s a clean and new feel to everything I touch, which makes for a very comfortable, relaxing stay. Food + drink The hotel has a dedicated craft beer bar and outdoor terrace where it serves a range of ales. The substantial breakfast buffet is available from 6am until 10am at OMO Dining on the 21st floor. It includes a pancake station and Japanese comfort foods. At dinner time the kitchen switches to an a-la-carte menu that includes steak, noodles, burgers and lighter bites. If it’s late and you’re not too hungry you might prefer the 22nd-floor rooftop bar, where the emphasis is on craft beer and bar snacks.



Out + about Related Article Foodie travel In one of the world’s best airports for food, this restaurant stands out You’ll likely be staying here for a night before or after a flight, so you might venture only as far as the heated pools on the third floor, or the dining and bar facilities. A Lawson convenience store, located right at the hotel, is open 24 hours. Nearby is Rinku Premium Outlets, a behemoth of a shopping centre with 250 stores and many dining options. Direct trains run from Rinku station to central Osaka, a city often referred to as Japan’s kitchen. The verdict Japan continues to offer bargain surprises for value-minded travellers, even at new hotels with fancy amenities. At OMO Kansai Airport I had a great sleep and a luxurious hot soak, all for under $100. If you find something to complain about with that deal, the problem isn’t the hotel.



Essentials Queen Rooms from 7728JPY ($70) a night. A “Twin Room (Universal Design)” is wheelchair-accessible. OMO Kansai Airport by Hoshino Resorts, 1-833 Rinku Oraikita, Izumisano, Osaka, Japan. Phone +81 50 3134 8095. See hoshinoresorts.com Our score out of five ★★★★ HIGHLIGHT



A long, hot soak and sauna is an ideal, welcome-to-Japan way to refresh and re-energise after a 10-hour flight. LOWLIGHT Airport hotels located inside airports are more convenient, though the one-stop rail transfer to Rinku isn’t taxing. The writer stayed at her own expense.

World.title: Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVaccination Measles kills two unvaccinated people as US outbreak approaches 3000 Michael Koziol August 26, 2026 — 5:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Two unvaccinated people died from measles in the US state of Pennsylvania, becoming the first deaths there from the disease in 35 years amid a growing national outbreak. Pennsylvania’s Department of Health announced the deaths on Tuesday (US time), and warned that the return of measles after a decades-long absence meant people did not grasp its severity. US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr announced an overhaul of federal guidelines on the childhood vaccine schedule this month. Bloomberg It comes as US President Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr, continue to sow doubts about vaccines, including by pushing an unsubstantiated link with autism. This month, Trump signed an executive order that called for parents to space out their children’s vaccine visits and break up the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) jab - which is not currently possible.



Both deaths were in Lancaster County – an area of southern Pennsylvania with a large Amish population, which has historically had lower rates of vaccination. The department would not release further information about the deceased. So far in 2026, Pennsylvania has detected 393 cases of measles in 28 counties. Across the US, there have been 2777 confirmed cases this year, spanning most states and Washington DC. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is only available as a combined dose at present. AP Photo/Mary Conlon Tuesday’s announcement marked the first time people died from measles in Pennsylvania in 35 years. They are also the first US deaths from the disease this year. Last year, three Americans died, following nearly a decade of zero deaths. Pennsylvania’s health secretary, Debra Bogen, said the virtual elimination of measles in the state for more than three decades meant “people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness”.



The best way to protect against measles was vaccination, she said, with two doses of the MMR vaccine providing 97 per cent lifetime protection. The number of measles cases recorded this year has already eclipsed last year’s total of 2289. Nearly 50 per cent were among young people aged five to 19, and 94 per cent were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, according to the Centres for Disease Control. Trump has issued an executive order to establish a “gold standard” vaccination schedule for children. Bloomberg The 2025 and 2026 figures are the highest measles numbers in decades, with only a 2019 outbreak (1274 cases) coming close. Earlier in August, Trump urged parents to break up the MMR vaccine into three separate shots, even though that is not currently enabled by the medical profession or the pharmaceutical industry.



In a subsequent briefing with reporters, US officials said they would work with the private sector to try to make separate doses available. Related Article Trump's White House Trump’s vaccine order adds more fuel to the anti-vaccine fire At a televised news conference in the Oval Office, Trump said the US was recommending too many vaccines. He claimed without evidence that the MMR vaccine could be “quite lethal”, but when given separately, “it looks like they are not at all lethal but just every effective”. The US president also falsely spoke of an “explosion” in vaccine injury, and claimed that doctors were injecting children with large doses that looked like “a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body”. Trump’s executive order did not mention autism. But in his unscripted remarks, he asserted an unproven link between vaccination and higher rates of autism diagnoses in modern times.



“There’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was,” he said. The president’s order does not change vaccine requirements for schools, or impact the policies of state health departments. Rather, it stands as a recommendation from the US federal government. US Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy J has long been a vaccine sceptic. Bloomberg Following Trump’s announcement, the American Medical Association said that altering the proven childhood vaccination schedule without credible evidence risked weakening public confidence in vaccines, and putting children’s health at risk. “Extensive evidence from decades of scientific studies shows no link between vaccines and autism,” president Willie Underwood said. “Putting our children’s health at risk is not an option.”



The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to questions from this masthead about the measles outbreak and deaths in Pennsylvania. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street boosted by falling oil prices; Canada hits back at US with tariffs Stan Choe August 26, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices are falling again, which is helping to ease worries in the bond market and support stock prices. The S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent and edged a bit closer to its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 107 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.4 per cent higher. UBS’ trading desk said earlier this week that the slide in momentum stocks may be nearing its end, creating an opportunity for investors. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 5.06am AEST pointing to a rise of 29 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.7 per cent on Tuesday. Reporting season continues with Nine Entertainment, WiseTech and Woolworths results due out. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.61¢. Some of the strongest action was in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 3.9 per cent to $US87.05 and was heading for a second decline following 13 gains in 14 days. The drop came even though tensions between the United States and Iran seemed to ratchet higher after the Trump administration announced new sanctions to further hurt Iran’s economy.



Brent’s price zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Related Article Electric vehicles Aussie capitals ‘will be driverless within a decade’, says robotaxi pioneer A delegation from Pakistan left Iran after talks with Iran’s president and other senior officials on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reviving negotiations to end the Iran-US conflict, the Pakistani military said. Pakistan Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had been “very positive and productive.” Tuesday’s drop in oil prices tempered the worries about high inflation that helped drive Treasury yields in the bond market higher through the summer. Yields had gotten so high that the US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase its repurchases of longer-term Treasury notes and bonds. High yields make borrowing more expensive for everyone and can slow the economy’s growth while undercutting prices for stocks, cryptocurrencies and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Monday and from 4.74 per cent at the end of last week. That’s a significant move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains firmly above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation much higher. Canada announced it is targeting more than 700 US-made products as the trade war with America escalates. The list extends well beyond industrial goods, hitting everyday purchases such as seafood, cheese, clothing, cosmetics and toilet paper, with some facing duties as high as 50 per cent. The tariffs on American steel, dairy products, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper and electronics take effect September 8 at rates of 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 50 per cent, with Canada matching the corresponding US tariff rate on each product. Canadian officials said the goal is not to raise revenue but to protect Canadian companies and reduce US imports. On Wall Street, Nvidia and other winners of the boom in artificial-intelligence technology helped lead the way. Nvidia rose 1.8 per cent, a day after its drop of 2.9 per cent was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. AI stocks have veered up and down through the summer on worries that their prices shot too high and that the AI boom may not be sustainable if it doesn’t produce enough profits for companies. Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday, which could help steer the next move for AI-related stocks.



The gains for chip stocks helped offset a 30.1 per cent drop for Dick’s Sporting Goods, which reported weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Executive Chairman Ed Stack said the retailer cut prices on some of its footwear and apparel to remain competitive, while launches for some footwear during the quarter ended up being weaker than it expected. Related Article Supermarkets Why Coles won’t copy Woolies’ Ooshies sugar hit The company cut its forecast for an underlying measure of profit in 2026 for both its Dick’s and Foot Locker businesses. The company spent $US2.4 billion last year to acquire the struggling Foot Locker chain as inventory in footwear began to pile up for most retailers. Dick’s stock is potentially heading toward its worst day in history. Worries have been rising about how strong spending can remain generally for U.S. households, which is the main engine of the economy. They’re facing higher prices on everything from food to clothes and a job market that suddenly looks iffier after employers cut more jobs last month than they added. A report from the Conference Board on Tuesday said that confidence among U.S. consumers weakened by more than economists expected.



In stock markets around the world, many indexes drifted modestly higher. South Korea’s Kospi, which is dominated by two AI winners, added 0.7 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. It’s been steadying since plunging 22.2 per cent in July. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaEpstein fallout Ghislaine Maxwell loses bid to overturn conviction for aiding Epstein Michael R. Sisak and Larry Neumeister Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:23am ,first published 11:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Ghislaine Maxwell’s bid to overturn her sex trafficking conviction and be freed from prison was rejected by a US federal judge on Tuesday (US time) who said the claims by Jeffrey Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime associate that new evidence had emerged were “demonstrably meritless”. Maxwell filed a habeas petition – a legal procedure challenging her detention – last December seeking to set aside her conviction and free her from a 20-year prison sentence, claiming exonerating information was withheld and false testimony presented at her trial, resulting in a “complete miscarriage of justice”. Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. Getty Judge Paul A. Engelmayer rejected her arguments, saying in his written ruling they “all or almost all are frivolous” and that she had presented nothing that could upend the outcome of her trial. “Nearly all its claims are procedurally barred; the overwhelming testimonial and documentary evidence adduced at trial conclusively established her guilt; and her petition’s claims are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods,” Engelmayer wrote.





The judge noted that many of Maxwell’s claims of “new evidence” stem from documents released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. As a result of that law, the Justice Department over the last eight months has released 18 categories of investigative materials gathered in the massive sex trafficking probe, including search warrants, financial records, notes from interviews with victims and data from electronic devices. Related Article Investigation

Good Weekend Isolated, scared, forlorn: The heartbreaking final months of Virginia Giuffre’s life Engelmayer said that material is “largely irrelevant to the charges against Maxwell and does not support her claims of error.” “On the contrary, to the extent it is relevant, far from exculpating her, it incriminates her or reinforces the correctness of the legal rulings Maxwell challenges,” he wrote.



The judge also rejected Maxwell’s claim that she was selectively prosecuted and made a “scapegoat” when the Justice Department did not indict four co-conspirators named in a government document or 25 men who settled with victims. Engelmayer said she could have raised that claim on appeal after her trial, but he found it to be frivolous nonetheless. Among the recently released Justice Department documents, “she does not cite any that reveals the existence of an uncharged confederate, let alone one as instrumental as she in facilitating Epstein’s horrific crimes,” the judge said. World.title: Gold has lost its glitter. Does that mean it’s time to buy?
World.content:
MoneyInvestingGold Opinion Gold has lost its glitter. Does that mean it’s time to buy?

Justin Lin August 26, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In February, I walked past a bullion dealer in the Sydney CBD with a queue that wrapped around the corner. Gold had just peaked above $US5600 ($7800) an ounce, capping a 12-month run of more than 80 per cent. Six months later, the queues have gone, gold sits near $US4600, and the question I get from investors has inverted. It used to be: “How high can this go?” Now it’s: “Why did my safe haven fail me during a war?” The positioning that made gold fragile in February has been cleared out and the price has rebased to a level far easier to defend. Trevor Collens It is a fair question. Gold’s first half was a disappointment, but unlike how many investors would paint it, nothing about it was mysterious, nor did it reveal any fundamental flaws in gold. Consider the starting point. At the beginning of this year, gold had been perhaps the best-performing major asset on the planet for three years, at one point rising more than 60 per cent in six months.



When an asset climbs that fast it attracts a particular kind of buyer – the one who arrives because the price is rising, not because of any particular thesis. Those buyers set the price at the top and are the first to leave. Then there is the conflict itself. The Iran war has been the most energy-centric war in modern market history, with more than a fifth of the world’s crude and gas exports at risk. That may instinctively read an oil shock as an inflation shock, and inflation as good news for gold. Central banks have accumulated gold for years as a deliberate act of diversification away from the US dollar. The market did something less intuitive. It priced in a central bank forced to stay tight, or even hike. Yields climbed, and gold, which pays no coupon, always struggles against a rising cost of holding it. Finally, amid the clamouring of gold’s failure as a “haven”, it should be noted that nobody truly wanted insurance. Uncertainty hit decade highs, yes, yet equity markets stayed risk-on, propped up by earnings certainty in semiconductors and AI. Investors do not buy a hedge when the thing they are hedging keeps going up.



Three headwinds, all rational, but none a defect in gold. What has changed, however, is that the froth is gone. The positioning that made gold fragile in February has been cleared out and the price has rebased to a level far easier to defend. Anyone buying today is buying an asset that has had its reckoning. Meanwhile, the core investment case remains rock steady, and the accumulators that drove gold’s rally before are making their return. Central banks have accumulated gold for years as a deliberate act of diversification away from the US dollar. That buying slowed in the first half – exactly what you would expect when a war forces policymakers to prioritise liquidity over strategy. But as of August, despite tensions still simmering in the Middle East, central bank buying may have already resumed. The People’s Bank of China recently extended its streak to 21 straight months in July, adding 20 tonnes, its largest monthly purchase by volume since October 2023. And in the World Gold Council’s annual survey of reserve managers, 89 per cent expected global official gold holdings to keep rising over the next 12 months, while 74 per cent expected the US dollar’s share of global reserves to be lower in five years.



Asian investors, a new force in the market, have proven similarly committed. Regional gold ETFs took in a record $US12 billion in the first half, the largest contribution to global flows, and that held through a brutal June of profit taking. A physical gold fund was, for a while, the largest ETF of any kind in mainland China, bigger than the local equivalent of an S&P 500 tracker. Editor's pick Investing ‘They want a piece of that pie’: Gold FOMO untarnished by price meltdown Which brings us to now. Consolidation is miserable to sit through and obvious only in hindsight, but the conditions that made gold vulnerable have been quietly unwinding. The labour market that spent the first half looking indestructible shed 23,000 US jobs in July. Markets that had priced a September rate rise as a near-certainty, now put the odds closer to one in three. Gold has climbed about 8 per cent in a month to a 10-week high, and its correlation with oil and equities has drifted back towards zero as key accumulators return. Six months ago, gold was a crowded trade at a record high. Today, it is an uncrowded one at a discount, with a structural case that has strengthened rather than weakened. The queues outside the bullion dealers may be shorter, but, ironically, now may be the right time to enter the store.



Justin Lin is an Investment Strategist at Global X ETFs Australia. World.title: Should I sell my $1m investment property and put it into my super?
World.content:
August 26, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m a young retiree at 61 years. I have a $500,000 share portfolio and a 20-year-held investment property worth $1 million. I’m of a mind to sell the property and realise the share portfolio over the next four years, and slowly use concessional contributions to the maximum to get the money into a good super fund. I wonder if I’m putting all my eggs into one basket, so to speak. However, I feel simplicity moving forward in retirement is good. The amount in super should provide a perpetual retirement income, as we intend to take the minimum government limits, i.e. 4 per cent, 5 per cent, etc. What are your thoughts on such a simplification? Topping up your super can be a great way to bolster your retirement savings. Simon Letch Finally, you mentioned the downsizer contribution of $300,000 into super. If you’re already at your cap, i.e. $1.9 million for myself, I take it the $300,000 has to sit in the accumulation bucket and thus have gains taxed. Is this correct? You’ve held the investment property for a long time, so the decision about selling it sooner rather than later should be based primarily on its future potential, not on how long you have owned it.



But I do think money invested in a good super fund should outperform a 20-year-old investment property, particularly once you consider the costs and hassles that come with owning property. I also don’t see why you need to leave all the proceeds in accumulation mode. It would seem you have plenty of room to contribute money to super and then transfer it to pension mode, where the earnings will be tax-free. Shares acquired before September 1985 will lose their CGT-free status on June 30, 2027. As for investing part of the portfolio more aggressively in international shares, there is nothing wrong with that in principle. The important point is that super is merely the structure – you can still have a well-diversified portfolio inside it. Moving your investments into super does not mean putting all your eggs into one investment basket. As far as the downsizer contribution is concerned, the limit is $300,000 per person, which means a couple may be able to put $600,000 into super, irrespective of age or the amount already in super.



There is no requirement that a downsizer contribution must stay in accumulation mode. The transfer balance cap is now $2.1 million, so provided you have sufficient personal transfer balance cap available, you may have plenty of space to move more of your super into pension mode. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m 64. Should I use my super to pay off the rest of my mortgage? Paul Benson Money contributor You have mentioned several times that the “old” capital gains tax regime of a 50 per cent discount will apply for pensioners and others in receipt of government assistance rather than the new laws. Does this apply only to shares purchased before July 1, 2027 and will new shares or dividend reinvestments purchased after July 1, 2027 be subject to the new capital gains rules? As I understand it, cost base indexation will apply to determine the amount of CGT for gains that accrue from July 1, 2027, however, anyone who receives at least $1 of government income support in the year the asset is sold won’t be subject to a minimum tax rate of 30 per cent. Shares you own now and liquidated before June 30, 2027 will be subject to the existing CGT rules with the 50 per cent discount applying. If sold after that date, the profit will be split between pre-June 30, 2027 and post-June 30, 2027 gains. The value of the shares at June 30, 2027 will be indexed, with a calculation of CGT on the shares after that date.



I have $1.3 million in mainly bank shares returning about $55,000 in reinvested dividends. After June 30, 2027, if I take the dividends as cash payments, am I right in assuming the existing shares will retain the 50 per cent discount until my death? That is not correct. You will need to record the balance of your shares on June 30, 2027. Any shares sold after that date will be given a notional indexed cost base to ensure that any gain from June 30, 2027 to the date of your sale are taxed after adjustment for inflation. All shares sold before June 30, 2027 will get the 50 per cent discount. I bought and have retained shares in two ASX-listed blue-chip companies in the period between 1974 and September 20, 1985, when the CGT was introduced, and more after that latter date. Do the recent changes to the CGT rules apply to all of these shares, or will the shares I acquired before the introduction of the CGT remain exempt from the CGT when I sell them? Shares acquired before September 1985 will lose their CGT-free status on June 30, 2027 – the cost base for CGT purposes going forward will be their market value at that date. When I was 18 – I’m now 59 – I read your book Making Money Made Simple, and I am now wealthy. I have saturated my super and, as I am on the highest marginal tax rate, have been looking at investment bonds. However, I have read that for some people it may be better simply to invest in an exchange-traded fund (ETF) because the costs are lower. I would welcome your comments on this and wonder whether you have done any modelling comparing the two alternatives.



Think of investment bonds as an alternative to super, but with some similar characteristics. They are both tax-paid investments, which means there is nothing to include on your annual tax return until you cash them in. Unlike super, there is no limit on the amount you can invest in investment bonds, and there is no lack of access, as you can cash them in at any time. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert My teenage children want to invest $4000. Where should they start? Noel Whittaker Money columnist The tax in a super fund will be zero or 15 per cent, depending on whether the balance is in pension mode or accumulation mode, whereas investment bonds pay a maximum tax rate of 30 per cent. If you hold the bond for 10 years, the entire proceeds can be redeemed tax-free. A bonus is that you are allowed to contribute up to 125 per cent of the previous year’s investment without restarting the 10-year period. If you redeem the bond before eight years is up, the profit is fully taxable, less a 30 per cent rebate to compensate you for the tax already paid by the bond fund. The management fees may be slightly higher in an investment bond than in a share-based ETF.



But don’t let fees become the tail that wags the dog. You are in the 47 per cent tax bracket, so the real comparison is not simply the fees on an ETF versus the fees on an investment bond. It is the after-tax return from each. The bond keeps the tax rate at a maximum of 30 per cent and, given you have many years ahead of you, you can take a long-term view and redeem the entire proceeds after 10 years tax-free. In your situation, I think that is a major advantage. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. World.title: The alarming reason one in three seniors are giving up aged care
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAged care Opinion The alarming reason one in three seniors are giving up aged care Rachel Lane Money contributor August 26, 2026 — 5:01am

August 26, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The most worrying thing about the new aged care system is not that people are paying more for care. It is that some are deciding they can’t afford care at all. A YouGov survey of 1044 senior Australians found that one in three have reduced or stopped home care since November 1 because they can’t afford the new co-contributions. The impact is greatest among those under financial pressure: almost seven in 10 say the new payments have made them more reluctant to seek help, rising to nearly three in four among those experiencing financial hardship. Sadly, for 6 per cent, the cost of care now means choosing between aged care and essentials such as food and electricity. While it may not sound like a care issue, social isolation has serious consequences for your health. iStock The survey found that seven in 10 believe aged care services are too expensive. However, there is an important distinction that appears to be getting lost. The new system doesn’t apply a co-contribution to every service. Think of your Support at Home funding as one bucket of money, divided into three smaller buckets – clinical care, independence and everyday living – with a different co-contribution applying to each.



Clinical care, which includes nursing and allied health, has a zero co-contribution. These services can cost $150 to $200 an hour, and they will certainly use up funding in your Support at Home package, but they won’t cost you anything out of your own pocket. That’s what makes it particularly alarming that up to 13 per cent of survey respondents have reduced or given up clinical services. If people are refusing nursing or allied health because they believe they cannot afford it, we have a communication problem as well as a care problem. Before saying ‘no’ to care because you think you can’t afford it, check what you will actually have to pay. At the other end of the scale are everyday living services such as cleaning, meal preparation, gardening and home maintenance. The survey showed the highest proportion of recipients (20 per cent) had reduced or eliminated domestic help. These services can cost $100 to $150 an hour and attract a co-contribution of between 17.5 per cent and 80 per cent. For a full pensioner, paying 17.5 per cent of a $150 gardening or home maintenance service means a contribution of $26.25 an hour.



If you can afford it, that may seem reasonable. For a self-funded retiree paying 80 per cent, $120 an hour, it’s a different proposition, and they may be better off buying private services. The survey doesn’t make it clear whether some people are opting for private care instead. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care Half-priced aged care at home sounds like a bargain. Here’s why it isn’t Rachel Lane Money contributor Social support sits in between. It is classified as an independence service which attracts a contribution of between 5 per cent and 50 per cent. With prices of $100 to $130 an hour, that could mean paying anywhere from $5 to $65 an hour. Up to 14 per cent of people receiving social support have reduced or declined these services. While it may not sound like a care issue, social isolation has serious consequences for your health. Under the new system more people are paying more towards their home care, but the cost is not across the board. Clinical care remains free, while the biggest increases are concentrated in independence and everyday living services.



Before saying “no” to care because you think you can’t afford it, check what you will actually have to pay. World.title: My daughter wanted to be a nepo baby. I didn’t hire her, now she won’t talk to me
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? My daughter wanted to be a nepo baby. I didn’t hire her, now she won’t talk to me Kirstin Ferguson August 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: putting a stop to nepotism, a morning quiz and job-hunting at 62. A company deserves the strongest candidate, not just someone who shares a surname with the boss. Dionne Gain My adult daughter won’t speak to me after I hired someone else to work in the business I run. She assumed she’d automatically get a job with me after university, but I hired a more experienced candidate for the opening that came up. The whole thing has caused a real rift in our relationship. I know I did the right thing as a boss, but as a mother I feel terrible about the impact it has had. How do you balance both? Related Article Got a Minute? Everyone in my office gets free lunch, except me. How is that fair? You definitely made the right decision for your business, which deserves the strongest candidate, and not someone chosen simply because you are related. Favouring family at the expense of fairness rarely ends well for anyone.



You would also know that sometimes being a good parent means disappointing your child. What matters is helping her to understand one missed opportunity doesn’t define either her career or your relationship. In retrospect, it may have been more helpful to establish the expectation very early with your daughter that she would never get a job automatically – with you or any hiring manager. Gaining employment is a privilege she will need to work for like anyone else, and I think you will be able to help her in future by reviewing her resume, suggesting vacancies (in other businesses) as they come up, and being her biggest cheerleader when she scores her dream job. With time and maturity, I am sure your daughter will come to understand you did what you needed to do. Not just as a professional, but also as a mother. We have a new manager who makes a point of going to every person’s desk each morning with a notebook and pen and asks, “What are you working on today, what do you hope to achieve, and what didn’t you finish yesterday?” He makes notes, but does not offer any advice, assistance or comments, then goes to the next person. We have a very open office plan so it puts the team members on the spot with having to come up with answers quickly and the whole team can hear the conversations. We absolutely dread this time of the morning. Staff are starting to get very stressed with not knowing what he does with his notes. It feels as if we have to justify our roles every day, and as if the company is considering redundancies. He is not the most approachable person. We don’t have an HR manager. What should we do? Related Article Got a Minute? I discovered my married boss is cheating with a co-worker. What do I do? Rather than assume the worst, I wonder whether your manager may genuinely be trying to engage with you and understand what everyone is working on, but is doing so in a completely misguided way. I suspect he has no idea of the impact he is having on trust and culture. He doesn’t sound as if he has much emotional intelligence or self-awareness and is completely unaware of the discomfort he causes.



The uncertainty about why the questions are being asked is almost certainly contributing more to the team’s anxiety than the questions themselves. Rather than speculating, someone needs to ask him what the morning routine is all about. If no one feels comfortable doing it alone, consider approaching him as a group. Simply say, “We’re finding the morning check-ins a little unsettling because we’re not sure how the information is being used. Would you mind explaining what this information might be for?” You might discover there’s an innocent explanation, or your feedback may alert him to an unintended consequence. You need to ask, whatever the response, so everyone is clear. I am 62 and had to leave my workplace due to a workcover claim. I have been applying for roles for months with no success. I have applied for junior roles but am told I’m too qualified. I have applied for similar roles in different industries where my skills are transferable, but I’m finding employers won’t take the risk on me. Any ideas on how to move forward and keep positive? It may be time to think laterally and widen your search. Have you considered options such as short-term contracts, consulting, mentoring, project work or even working with not-for-profit organisations? These can all be pathways to be a permanent position. Many employers are looking for the kind of judgment and reliability that comes only with experience. Your job hunt now needs to focus on finding a company wise enough to recognise your age as one of your strengths. Good luck!

World.title: Plane lovers will adore this bargain Japanese airport hotel
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews Plane lovers will adore this bargain Japanese airport hotel Kristie Kellahan August 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel OMO Kansai Airport The hotel is a short walk from Rinku-Town station, near Osaka’s Kansai Airport. Check-in Getting to OMO Kansai Airport hotel, which opened in 2023, is stress-free, even in my tired and jet-lagged state. The first airport-focused hotel in the OMO collection by Japanese hospitality group Hoshino Resorts, the property is located at Rinku-Town station, one stop from Osaka’s Kansai International Airport. I exit the station, follow signs to the hotel entrance and go to the second floor, where I check in. Automated kiosks display prompts to scan my passport and QR booking code to receive my room key but human attendants are also on hand to offer assistance. I’m excited to have access to communal, hot, carbonated baths and saunas on the third floor (free of charge for in-house guests), and within 15 minutes of arriving at the hotel I’m marinating in 40-degree pools.



The look 



Room configurations include single, twin and triple. There are 700 rooms in multiple configurations including queen, twin and triple. I’ve booked a Queen Room for one person at the Solo Special rate of 9000JPY ($81), such a bargain price I assume at first glance it must be a typo. The room is 18 square metres and includes a queen bed, shower stall and toilet. Room amenities include an air purifier, kettle and tea, slippers and toothbrush. There’s a clean and new feel to everything I touch, which makes for a very comfortable, relaxing stay. Food + drink The hotel has a dedicated craft beer bar and outdoor terrace where it serves a range of ales. The substantial breakfast buffet is available from 6am until 10am at OMO Dining on the 21st floor. It includes a pancake station and Japanese comfort foods. At dinner time the kitchen switches to an a-la-carte menu that includes steak, noodles, burgers and lighter bites. If it’s late and you’re not too hungry you might prefer the 22nd-floor rooftop bar, where the emphasis is on craft beer and bar snacks.



Out + about Related Article Foodie travel In one of the world’s best airports for food, this restaurant stands out You’ll likely be staying here for a night before or after a flight, so you might venture only as far as the heated pools on the third floor, or the dining and bar facilities. A Lawson convenience store, located right at the hotel, is open 24 hours. Nearby is Rinku Premium Outlets, a behemoth of a shopping centre with 250 stores and many dining options. Direct trains run from Rinku station to central Osaka, a city often referred to as Japan’s kitchen. The verdict Japan continues to offer bargain surprises for value-minded travellers, even at new hotels with fancy amenities. At OMO Kansai Airport I had a great sleep and a luxurious hot soak, all for under $100. If you find something to complain about with that deal, the problem isn’t the hotel.



Essentials Queen Rooms from 7728JPY ($70) a night. A “Twin Room (Universal Design)” is wheelchair-accessible. OMO Kansai Airport by Hoshino Resorts, 1-833 Rinku Oraikita, Izumisano, Osaka, Japan. Phone +81 50 3134 8095. See hoshinoresorts.com Our score out of five ★★★★ HIGHLIGHT



A long, hot soak and sauna is an ideal, welcome-to-Japan way to refresh and re-energise after a 10-hour flight. LOWLIGHT Airport hotels located inside airports are more convenient, though the one-stop rail transfer to Rinku isn’t taxing. The writer stayed at her own expense.

World.title: New Zealand's ATM dead zones
World.content:
New Zealand's network of ATMs has shrunk in recent years, and some parts of the country now don't have any cash machines at all.

RNZ research shows there are now just over 1000 access points for cash around the country, at which there may be more than one ATM. About half of the just over 3000 ATMs are owned by non-bank providers.

But there are some places where there is no ATM anywhere near. People living on Great Barrier Island, in Haast, Tuatapere, Omarama and Milford Sound all have to travel a long way to access a cash machine.

From Haast, they might have to drive 144km, from Omarama it is about 30 kilometres to Twizel, and in Tuatapere 48km.

At the Hard Antler Bar and Restaurant in Haast, a staff member said people would get cash out from a local shop or gas station if they needed it. "It would be nice to have one but we manage just fine without. Being so far away from shops we have no need anyway."

In a Haast community group, residents said it was not a huge problem. "If you live off venison, crayfish, veggies from your garden and coffee you don't need any cash," said one.

Others said it was a potential security problem to have an ATM. "ATMs are bad news for small out of the way quiet towns. It puts them in line for serious robbery… plus it requires being topped up a lot which costs a lot which is then passed on to you, the person withdrawing," said another.

Across the country, about 725,000 people live at least 5km from the nearest ATM as the crow flies, 372,162 more than 10km, 200,629 more than 15km and 301 more than 75km.

New Zealand Banking Association chief executive Roger Beaumont said there was a range of factors taken into account when banks were thinking about where to locate ATMs.

"That would probably include things like customer demand for the service, and the practicality of cash in transit services reaching those locations."

The Reserve Bank has been consulting on its plans for cash. It wants 95 percent of people living in urban areas to have walking-distance access to a free cash point.

It has identified 24 rural settlements it says need cash services, including Ngakawau, Ongaonga, Omakau, Owaka, Whangaroa and Taipa, Te Araroa, Cheviot, Rotheram, Waikari, Kimbolton, Kawhia, Balfour, Ohai, Woodlands, St Andrews, Glenavy, Nuhaka, Tuia, Hampton, Kurow, Taharoa, Harihari, Fox Glacier and Ross.

Some of those areas already have limited ATM access.

University of Otago economist Murat Ungor said it was a significant problem that some areas of the country did not have ATMs.

"Research and practical evidence show that people cannot always simply find other solutions, and the burden of doing so falls unevenly on those who are already vulnerable.

"The Reserve Bank has stated that the cash system is not fully meeting the public's needs and that a significant increase in the quantity and quality of cash services is required, especially in rural areas.

"The assumption that people would find other ways is challenged by the realities in these communities. Research shows that 72 percent small businesses would be adversely affected if cash were unavailable. In towns like Palmerston, the only ATM charges a prohibitive $2.80 fee, and businesses have no local way to deposit cash, forcing them to drive long distances, like to Dunedin, just to bank their takings."

He said research focused on rural towns confirmed that declining access was a bigger disadvantage for older people, people who were disabled, on low incomes or with limited transport.

World.title: All Blacks scrape past Lions to retain perfect record in South Africa
World.content:
The All Blacks survived a massive scare from provincial side the Lions before prevailing 41-35 in the match Johannesburg.

The Lions came out firing and were the first to score with halfback Nico Steyn diving over under the posts after a period of sustained attack close to the All Blacks line.

The conversion was good with the hosts ahead 7-0 after about five minutes.

The All Blacks were soon under their posts again after an intercept try to Lions flanker Siba Mahashe not long after the restart. The conversion was successful with the hosts racing out to a 14-0 lead.

The All Blacks didn't go into their shells and were the next to score with halfback Noah Hotham dotting down under the posts after a clean break from wing Emoni Narawa.

Noah Hotham scores a try. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

Fullback Beauden Barrett added the extras to cut the Lions lead to 14-7.

The All Blacks started to make some inroads into the Lions defence and stretched the hosts out wide with wing Narawa scoring untouched in the right-hand corner.

Barrett missed the sideline conversion, leaving the Lions leading 14-12 midway through the first half.

The hosts though wouldn't go away and they were the next to score with wing Kelly Mpeku diving over acrobatically in the corner.

The sideline conversion was good to extend the Lions advantage to 21-12 with less than 10 minutes left in the first half.

The All Blacks struck back soon after with openside Ethan Blackadder scoring down the left edge after a break by wing Fehi Fineanganofo to cut the Lions lead to 21-17.

Fineanganofo was the next to dot down in the left corner, but the try was disallowed due to a forward pass in the lead up, with the Lions taking a four point lead into halftime.

The second half started just like the first with the Lions bursting out of the blocks to score first, with wing Erich Cronje pouncing on a loose ball after a break from the hosts to extend their advantage.

The conversion was successful to put the Lions ahead 28-17.

The crowd was really getting behind the home side throughout the match and the noise was impressive despite the small numbers in the stadium compared to the opening test between the Springboks and All Blacks last weekend.

The Lions, buoyed by their vocal fans, kept the pressure on the All Blacks and scored a scrum pushover try and the sideline conversion again good to push the host's lead out to 35-17.

The All Blacks were being starved of possession but they kept themselves in the game by being the next to score, with midfielder Rieko Ioane making a break at halfway before outsprinting the cover defence to score.

First-five Richie Mo'unga kicked the extras to cut the Lions lead to 35-24 with half an hour remaining in Johannesburg.

Ioane moved out to the wing when Fineanganofo was subbed off for Anton Lienert-Brown and the Blues star nabbed an intercept of his own, scoring next to the posts to bag his second try of the night and bring the All Blacks right back in it.

Mo'unga kicked the conversion to make it a four point game again at 35-31 to the Lions.

The All Blacks were playing far from flawless rugby but they hit the front with about 20 minutes to go with Blackadder grabbing his second try of the game to put the tourists ahead 36-35 with 18 minutes left.

The All Blacks finally put the game beyond doubt in the 80th minute with Narawa scoring his second try of the game after cutting back inside the scrambling Lions defence and powering over the tryline in the tackle.

Mo'unga missed the conversion on the fulltime siren but it didn't matter, with the All Blacks claiming a nervy 41-35 victory to maintain their perfect record on their tour of South Africa.

See how the match unfolded in our live blog below:

All Blacks match-day 23 (Test caps and non-Test games in brackets. * indicates new All Black):

1. Siale Lauaki (0, 2)

2. Samisoni Taukei'aho (44, 2)

3. Pasilio Tosi (17, 2)

4. Sam Darry (10, 2)

5. Patrick Tuipulotu (57, 4) - Captain

6. Wallace Sititi (21, 2)

7. Ethan Blackadder (14, 2)

8. Semisi Ta'eiloa (0, 1)
